abstract: A neural network is applied to the problem of recognizing Kanji characters. Using a b a c k propagation network learning algorithm. a threelayered. feed-forward network is trained to recognize similar handwritten Kanji characters. In addition. two new methods are utilized to make training effective. The recognition accuracy was higher than that of conventional methods. An analysis of connection weights showed that trained networks can discern the hierarchical structure of Kanji characters. This strategy of trained networks makes high recognition accuracy possible. Our results suggest that neural networks are very effective for Kanji character recognition.

paragraphs: This paper applies a neural network to distinguishing similar handwritten Kanji characters. The task centers on characters whose visual resemblance makes classification demanding. The researchers train a three-layer feedforward network with backpropagation and introduce two additional methods intended to make the training process effective.

The trained network achieves higher recognition accuracy than the conventional methods used in the comparison. The authors also analyze its connection weights to investigate how it reaches its decisions. That analysis indicates that the network can distinguish the hierarchical structure of Kanji characters, linking recognition behavior to the organization of the written forms.

The paper attributes the strong recognition results to this learned strategy. Its contribution therefore includes both a character classifier and an interpretation of the representation supporting its performance. Training appears to make structural distinctions useful to the network, helping it separate characters that look similar. The stated findings support neural networks as an effective approach to the Kanji recognition problem examined in the study.
summary.tldr: A backpropagation network distinguishes similar handwritten Kanji with improved accuracy and learns representations reflecting their hierarchical structure.

title: Neural Networks that Learn to Discriminate Similar Kanji Characters

abstract: In [5], a new incremental cascade network architecture has been presented. This paper discusses the properties of such cascade networks and investigates their generalization abilities under the particular constraint of small data sets. The evaluation is done for cascade networks consisting of local linear maps using the Mackey(cid:173) Glass time series prediction task as a benchmark. Our results in(cid:173) dicate that to bring the potential of large networks to bear on the problem of extracting information from small data sets without run(cid:173) ning the risk of overjitting, deeply cascaded network architectures are more favorable than shallow broad architectures that contain the same number of nodes.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how network architecture affects generalization when training data are scarce. It studies an incremental cascade architecture, focusing on networks composed of local linear maps. The central question is how to use a relatively large network to extract information from a small dataset without fitting that dataset too closely.

The evaluation uses the Mackey-Glass time series prediction task. It compares deeply cascaded networks with shallow, broad networks containing the same number of nodes. Holding node count equal makes the arrangement of the network central to the comparison: the question concerns how computational components are organized, rather than simply how many are available.

The results favor deeper cascades for obtaining useful generalization from small datasets while reducing the risk of overfitting. This suggests that network size alone does not determine whether additional capacity is helpful in the studied setting. The architectural organization matters as well. The finding is grounded in cascade networks of local linear maps evaluated on the stated time series prediction benchmark.
summary.tldr: On a small-data time series task, deeper cascade networks generalize more favorably than equally sized shallow, broad networks.

title: Generalization Abilities of Cascade Network Architecture

abstract: We present a Bayesian framework for inferring the parameters of a mixture of experts model based on ensemble learning by varia(cid:173) tional free energy minimisation. The Bayesian approach avoids the over-fitting and noise level under-estimation problems of traditional maximum likelihood inference. We demonstrate these methods on artificial problems and sunspot time series prediction.
originalAbstract: We present a Bayesian framework for inferring the parameters of a mixture of experts model based on ensemble learning by varia(cid:173) tional free energy minimisation. The Bayesian approach avoids the over-fitting and noise level under-estimation problems of traditional maximum likelihood inference. We demonstrate these methods on artificial problems and sunspot time series prediction.

paragraphs: The paper presents a Bayesian way to infer the parameters of a mixture of experts. Such a model combines multiple component predictors, allowing different experts to contribute to its predictions. The learning problem is to determine the model's parameters while accounting for uncertainty in what the available observations support.

The proposed framework uses ensemble learning through variational free energy minimization. This supplies an optimization-based route to Bayesian inference, allowing the method to work with uncertainty over model parameters. Its purpose is to improve on traditional maximum likelihood inference, which the abstract identifies as vulnerable to overfitting and underestimating noise.

These two problems are related in practical interpretation: a model can fit observations too closely while treating their unexplained variation as smaller than it really is. The authors state that their Bayesian approach avoids both problems and demonstrate it on artificial tasks and sunspot time-series prediction. The contribution connects a probabilistic treatment of model uncertainty with more appropriate fitting and noise estimation in mixtures of experts.
summary.tldr: Variational Bayesian learning addresses overfitting and underestimated noise in mixtures of experts.

title: Bayesian Methods for Mixtures of Experts

abstract: A new on-line learning algorithm which minimizes a statistical de(cid:173) pendency among outputs is derived for blind separation of mixed signals. The dependency is measured by the average mutual in(cid:173) formation (MI) of the outputs. The source signals and the mixing matrix are unknown except for the number of the sources. The Gram-Charlier expansion instead of the Edgeworth expansion is used in evaluating the MI. The natural gradient approach is used to minimize the MI. A novel activation function is proposed for the on-line learning algorithm which has an equivariant property and is easily implemented on a neural network like model. The validity of the new learning algorithm are verified by computer simulations.

The dependency is measured by the average mutual in(cid:173) formation (MI) of the outputs. The source signals and the mixing matrix are unknown except for the number of the sources. paragraphs: Blind signal separation asks how to recover individual sources from observations that mix them together. This paper develops an online learning algorithm for that problem when neither the original signals nor the mixing matrix is known. The number of sources is assumed to be available. Its guiding objective is to make the recovered outputs statistically less dependent on one another.

The algorithm measures dependence using average mutual information, which captures how much information outputs share. To evaluate this quantity, the authors use a Gram–Charlier expansion in place of an Edgeworth expansion. They then apply a natural gradient method to reduce it and introduce an activation function for the resulting online update.

The proposed rule has an equivariance property and can be implemented in a neural-network-like model. Computer simulations support its validity. The contribution brings together a statistical separation objective, an approximation for evaluating that objective, and an update suitable for learning as observations arrive.
summary.tldr: An online signal-separation algorithm uses natural gradients to reduce mutual information between outputs when the sources and mixing matrix are unknown.

title: A New Learning Algorithm for Blind Signal Separation

abstract: A c.:omputational model of song learning in the song sparrow (M elospiza melodia) learns to categorize the different syllables of a song sparrow song and uses this categorization to train itself to reproduce song. The model fills a crucial gap in the computational explanation of birdsong learning by exploring the organization of perception in songbirds. It shows how competitive learning may lead to the organization of a specific nucleus in the bird brain, replicates the song production results of a previous model (Doya and Sejnowski, 1995), and demonstrates how perceptual learning can guide production through reinforcement learning.

It shows how competitive learning may lead to the organization of a specific nucleus in the bird brain, replicates the song production results of a previous model (Doya and Sejnowski, 1995), and demonstrates how perceptual learning can guide production through reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Learning to reproduce a song involves both recognizing its sound patterns and learning how to produce them. This paper models that connection in the song sparrow. Its computational system learns to categorize different song syllables and then uses those learned categories to train its own song production.

The perceptual part uses competitive learning to explore how organization might arise in a particular nucleus of the bird brain. This addresses the formation of the categories that guide behavior, supplying a computational account of perception alongside an account of production. The resulting categories become a basis for learning to reproduce the song.

Reinforcement learning links this perceptual organization to production. The model reproduces the song-production results of an earlier model while showing how learned perception can guide that process. Its main contribution is the connection between the two learning problems: organizing heard syllables provides useful structure for acquiring the actions needed to produce them, within a single computational explanation of song learning.
summary.tldr: A song-sparrow model learns syllable categories and uses them to guide song production through reinforcement learning.

title: How Perception Guides Production in Birdsong Learning

abstract: Given a set of objects in the visual field, how does the the visual system learn to attend to a particular object of interest while ignoring the rest? How are occlusions and background clutter so effortlessly discounted for when rec(cid:173) ognizing a familiar object? In this paper, we attempt to answer these ques(cid:173) tions in the context of a Kalman filter-based model of visual recognition that has previously proved useful in explaining certain neurophysiological phe(cid:173) nomena such as endstopping and related extra-classical receptive field ef(cid:173) fects in the visual cortex. By using results from the field of robust statistics, we describe an extension of the Kalman filter model that can handle multiple objects in the visual field. The resulting robust Kalman filter model demon(cid:173) strates how certain forms of attention can be viewed as an emergent prop(cid:173) erty of the interaction between top-down expectations and bottom-up sig(cid:173) nals. The model also suggests functional interpretations of certain attention(cid:173) related effects that have been observed in visual cortical neurons. Exper(cid:173) imental results are provided to help demonstrate the ability of the model to perform robust segmentation and recognition of objects and image se(cid:173) quences in the presence of varying degrees of occlusions and clutter.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how a visual recognition system can focus on an object while coping with other objects, clutter, and partial obstruction. It builds on a Kalman-filter model previously used to explain certain responses in visual cortex. The new contribution extends that model to scenes containing multiple objects through ideas from robust statistics.

The resulting robust Kalman filter combines top-down expectations with bottom-up sensory signals. In the model, some forms of attention emerge from that interaction. Expected object information and incoming visual evidence jointly shape processing, providing a computational account of how relevant information can be emphasized while distracting or obscured information is discounted.

Experiments demonstrate segmentation and recognition of objects and image sequences under varying amounts of occlusion and clutter. The model also offers possible functional interpretations of attention-related effects observed in visual cortical neurons. Its significance is therefore twofold: it demonstrates robust visual processing and connects that behavior to a proposed explanation of certain neural effects associated with attention.
summary.tldr: A robust Kalman-filter recognition model produces attention-like behavior through interactions between visual expectations and sensory evidence.

title: Correlates of Attention in a Model of Dynamic Visual Recognition

abstract: In the developing nervous system, gradients of target-derived dif(cid:173) fusible factors play an important role in guiding axons to appro(cid:173) priate targets. In this paper, the shape that such a gradient might have is calculated as a function of distance from the target and the time since the start of factor production. Using estimates of the relevant parameter values from the experimental literature, the spatiotemporal domain in which a growth cone could detect such a gradient is derived. For large times, a value for the maximum guidance range of about 1 mm is obtained. This value fits well with experimental data. For smaller times, the analysis predicts that guidance over longer ranges may be possible. This prediction remains to be tested.

paragraphs: Developing axons can follow chemical gradients released by their intended targets. This paper asks how far such a signal can guide a growing axon and how that range changes over time. A mathematical model connects the spatial gradient to the duration of chemical production.

The authors calculate gradient shape as a function of target distance and elapsed time, then use experimentally informed parameter estimates to determine where a growth cone could detect it. This converts a qualitative guidance mechanism into a spatiotemporal prediction about when directional information is available.

At long times, the predicted maximum range is approximately one millimeter, consistent with the cited experimental observations. At earlier times, the model predicts that guidance may operate over longer distances. The contribution combines agreement with an established scale and a distinct testable prediction: transient gradients could provide useful information beyond the eventual long-time guidance range.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-based guidance model predicts about a millimeter of long-time axon guidance and potentially longer transient ranges.

title: A Mathematical Model of Axon Guidance by Diffusible Factors

abstract: Despite the fact that mental arithmetic is based on only a few hun(cid:173) dred basic facts and some simple algorithms, humans have a diffi(cid:173) cult time mastering the subject, and even experienced individuals make mistakes. Associative multiplication, the process of doing multiplication by memory without the use of rules or algorithms, is especially problematic. Humans exhibit certain characteristic phenomena in performing associative multiplications, both in the type of error and in the error frequency. We propose a model for the process of associative multiplication, and compare its perfor(cid:173) mance in both these phenomena with data from normal humans and from the model proposed by Anderson et al (1994).
originalAbstract: Despite the fact that mental arithmetic is based on only a few hun(cid:173) dred basic facts and some simple algorithms, humans have a diffi(cid:173) cult time mastering the subject, and even experienced individuals make mistakes. Associative multiplication, the process of doing multiplication by memory without the use of rules or algorithms, is especially problematic. Humans exhibit certain characteristic phenomena in performing associative multiplications, both in the type of error and in the error frequency. We propose a model for the process of associative multiplication, and compare its perfor(cid:173) mance in both these phenomena with data from normal humans and from the model proposed by Anderson et al (1994).

paragraphs: The paper studies multiplication performed by recalling a memorized answer rather than following a calculation procedure. This kind of arithmetic can be difficult even though the underlying collection of basic facts is relatively small. The authors focus on the characteristic mistakes people make when retrieving multiplication facts, including both which wrong answers occur and how frequently errors happen.

They propose a model of this associative multiplication process and compare its behavior with human data. The comparison examines two aspects of performance: the kinds of errors produced and their frequency. The model is also compared with an earlier model by Anderson and colleagues, giving the investigation another computational account against which to assess its behavior.

The central contribution is an attempt to explain the structure of arithmetic errors through a model of memory-based multiplication. Matching correct answers alone would leave those patterns unexplained. The abstract establishes the proposed model and the comparisons undertaken, but does not report which model better matches human performance.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a model of memorized multiplication and compares its error types and frequencies with human behavior and an earlier model.

title: A Model for Associative Multiplication

abstract: Machine learning has reached a point where many probabilistic methods can be understood as variations, extensions and combinations of a much smaller set of abstract themes, e.g., as different instances of the EM algorithm. This enables the systematic derivation of algorithms customized for different models. Here, we describe the AUTO BAYES system which takes a high-level statistical model specification, uses powerful symbolic techniques based on schema-based program synthesis and computer algebra to derive an efficient specialized algorithm for learning that model, and generates executable code implementing that algorithm. This capability is far beyond that of code collections such as Matlab toolboxes or even tools for model-independent optimization such as BUGS for Gibbs sampling: complex new algorithms can be generated without new programming, algorithms can be highly specialized and tightly crafted for the exact structure of the model and data, and efficient and commented code can be generated for different languages or systems. We present automatically-derived algorithms ranging from closed-form solutions of Bayesian textbook problems to recently-proposed EM algorithms for clustering, regression, and a multinomial form of PCA.

This enables the systematic derivation of algorithms customized for different models. This capability is far beyond that of code collections such as Matlab toolboxes or even tools for model-independent optimization such as BUGS for Gibbs sampling: complex new algorithms can be generated without new programming, algorithms can be highly specialized and tightly crafted for the exact structure of the model and data, and efficient and commented code can be generated for different languages or systems. We present automatically-derived algorithms ranging from closed-form solutions of Bayesian textbook problems to recently-proposed EM algorithms for clustering, regression, and a multinomial form of PCA.

paragraphs: Many probabilistic learning methods share a smaller collection of underlying algorithmic ideas. This paper uses that common structure to automate the derivation of learning algorithms. Its AUTO BAYES system starts with a high-level statistical model specification and produces both a specialized algorithm and executable code that implements it.

The system combines reusable algorithmic schemas with symbolic program synthesis and computer algebra. These tools let it work through the mathematical structure of a model and tailor the resulting computation to that structure. The intended benefit is that a new model need not always require someone to manually derive and program a new learning procedure.

The authors present automatically derived solutions ranging from closed-form Bayesian textbook examples to EM algorithms for clustering, regression, and a multinomial version of principal component analysis. These examples illustrate a scope beyond selecting a routine from a fixed library. The contribution is a model-to-code process that can generate specialized, commented implementations for different languages or systems.
summary.tldr: AUTO BAYES turns statistical model specifications into specialized learning algorithms and executable code using symbolic derivation.

title: Automatic Derivation of Statistical Algorithms: The EM Family and Beyond

abstract: According to a widely held view, neurons in lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) operate on visual stimuli in a linear fashion. There is ample evidence, however, that LGN responses are not entirely linear. To account for nonlinearities we propose a model that synthesizes more than 30 years of research in the field. Model neurons have a linear receptive field, and a nonlinear, divisive suppressive field. The suppressive field computes local root-mean- square contrast. To test this model we recorded responses from LGN of anesthetized paralyzed cats. We estimate model parameters from a basic set of measurements and show that the model can accurately predict responses to novel stimuli. The model might serve as the new standard model of LGN responses. It specifies how visual processing in LGN involves both linear filtering and divisive gain control.
originalAbstract: According to a widely held view, neurons in lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) operate on visual stimuli in a linear fashion. There is ample evidence, however, that LGN responses are not entirely linear. To account for nonlinearities we propose a model that synthesizes more than 30 years of research in the field. Model neurons have a linear receptive field, and a nonlinear, divisive suppressive field. The suppressive field computes local root-mean- square contrast. To test this model we recorded responses from LGN of anesthetized paralyzed cats. We estimate model parameters from a basic set of measurements and show that the model can accurately predict responses to novel stimuli. The model might serve as the new standard model of LGN responses. It specifies how visual processing in LGN involves both linear filtering and divisive gain control.

paragraphs: The paper challenges a purely linear account of how neurons in the lateral geniculate nucleus respond to visual input. Motivated by evidence of nonlinear responses, the authors propose a model combining a linear receptive field with a nonlinear suppressive field. The model brings together findings from more than three decades of research.

The suppressive field measures local root-mean-square contrast and acts divisively on the response. In plain language, the model combines filtering of the visual pattern with a contrast-dependent adjustment of response strength. This gives a specific mechanism for nonlinear behavior while retaining a linear component in the description of what stimulates the neuron.

The authors test the model using recordings from the LGN of anesthetized, paralyzed cats. Parameters estimated from a basic measurement set allow accurate predictions for novel stimuli. These results support the joint use of linear filtering and divisive gain control in the studied responses. The authors propose that the model might become a new standard account of LGN processing, presenting that status as a possibility.
summary.tldr: A model combining linear filtering with contrast-dependent divisive suppression accurately predicts novel-stimulus responses in recorded cat LGN neurons.

title: Nonlinear Processing in LGN Neurons

abstract: We present the software architecture of a robotic system for mapping abandoned mines. The software is capable of acquiring consistent 2D maps of large mines with many cycles, represented as Markov random £elds. 3D C-space maps are acquired from local 3D range scans, which are used to identify navigable paths using A* search. Our system has been deployed in three abandoned mines, two of which inaccessible to people, where it has acquired maps of unprecedented detail and accuracy.
originalAbstract: We present the software architecture of a robotic system for mapping abandoned mines. The software is capable of acquiring consistent 2D maps of large mines with many cycles, represented as Markov random £elds. 3D C-space maps are acquired from local 3D range scans, which are used to identify navigable paths using A* search. Our system has been deployed in three abandoned mines, two of which inaccessible to people, where it has acquired maps of unprecedented detail and accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper describes the software architecture of an autonomous robot for mapping abandoned mines. The system must produce a coherent map of a large environment while also finding places the robot can traverse. Its architecture addresses these needs through a combination of two-dimensional mapping and local three-dimensional information.

The software represents its consistent two-dimensional maps as Markov random fields. It can map large mines containing many cycles, meaning that routes through the mine can reconnect. For navigation, local three-dimensional range scans provide configuration-space maps: representations of the space relevant to the robot’s possible movement. The system then uses A* search to identify navigable paths.

The authors report deployments in three abandoned mines, including two that people could not access. They describe the resulting maps as having unprecedented detail and accuracy. These deployments show the architecture being used in actual underground environments, with global mapping and local route finding serving complementary purposes. The contribution is an integrated robotic mapping system supported by field operation.
summary.tldr: A robotic mapping architecture combines consistent 2D maps with 3D navigation and was deployed in three abandoned mines, including two inaccessible to people.

title: An Autonomous Robotic System for Mapping Abandoned Mines

abstract: The NIPS 2003 workshops included a feature selection competition organized by the authors. We provided participants with five datasets from different application domains and called for classification results using a minimal number of features. The competition took place over a period of 13 weeks and attracted 78 research groups. Participants were asked to make on-line submissions on the validation and test sets, with performance on the validation set being presented immediately to the participant and performance on the test set presented to the participants at the workshop. In total 1863 entries were made on the validation sets during the development period and 135 entries on all test sets for the final competition. The winners used a combination of Bayesian neural networks with ARD priors and Dirichlet diffusion trees. Other top entries used a variety of methods for feature selection, which combined filters and/or wrapper or embedded methods using Random Forests, kernel methods, or neural networks as a classification engine. The results of the benchmark (including the predictions made by the participants and the features they selected) and the scoring software are publicly available. The benchmark is available at www.nipsfsc.ecs.soton.ac.uk for post-challenge submissions to stimulate further research.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes a feature-selection competition that asked participants to classify examples using as few features as possible. Five datasets represented different application domains, and 78 research groups participated over 13 weeks. The challenge therefore examined predictive performance together with the selection of compact sets of input features.

Participants received immediate feedback on validation submissions, while test performance was revealed at the workshop. The development period produced 1,863 validation entries, followed by 135 final entries across the test sets. This organization distinguished the feedback used during method development from the results presented for the final competition.

The winners combined Bayesian neural networks using ARD priors with Dirichlet diffusion trees. Other leading entries used varied feature-selection strategies alongside random forests, kernel methods, or neural networks. The paper also describes publicly released predictions, selected features, and scoring software, with the benchmark open to later submissions. These resources make the competition useful as a basis for further research as well as a comparison of submitted methods.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes a five-dataset feature-selection challenge, its leading methods, and the benchmark resources released for further research.

title: Result Analysis of the NIPS 2003 Feature Selection Challenge

abstract: It is known that determinining whether a DEC-POMDP, namely, a cooperative partially observable stochastic game (POSG), has a cooperative strategy with positive expected reward is complete for NEXP. It was not known until now how cooperation affected that complexity. We show that, for competitive POSGs, the complexity of determining whether one team has a positive-expected-reward strategy is complete for the class NEXP with an oracle for NP.
originalAbstract: It is known that determinining whether a DEC-POMDP, namely, a cooperative partially observable stochastic game (POSG), has a cooperative strategy with positive expected reward is complete for NEXP. It was not known until now how cooperation affected that complexity. We show that, for competitive POSGs, the complexity of determining whether one team has a positive-expected-reward strategy is complete for the class NEXP with an oracle for NP.

paragraphs: The paper studies the computational difficulty of deciding whether agents can obtain positive expected reward in a partially observable stochastic game. Partial observability means decisions must be made without complete access to the underlying situation. The question concerns the existence of a suitable strategy, rather than the measured performance of a particular learning algorithm.

For the cooperative version, also called a DEC-POMDP, this decision problem was already known to be complete for NEXP. That classification characterizes its worst-case computational difficulty. The unresolved issue addressed here is how the classification changes when cooperation within a group is accompanied by competition between teams.

The authors show that deciding whether one team has a positive-expected-reward strategy in a competitive POSG is complete for NEXP with an NP oracle. An oracle represents access to answers for another class of computational problems. The result identifies the complexity class for the competitive setting and clarifies the role of competition in this already demanding planning problem. It is a complexity-theoretic finding, not an empirical runtime comparison.
summary.tldr: Positive-reward strategy existence in competitive partially observable stochastic games is complete for NEXP with an NP oracle.

title: Competition Adds Complexity

abstract: We tackle the problem of simultaneously detecting occlusions and estimating optical flow. We show that, under standard assumptions of Lambertian reflection and static illumination, the task can be posed as a convex minimization problem. Therefore, the solution, computed using efficient algorithms, is guaranteed to be globally optimal, for any number of independently moving objects, and any number of occlusion layers. We test the proposed algorithm on benchmark datasets, expanded to enable evaluation of occlusion detection performance.
originalAbstract: We tackle the problem of simultaneously detecting occlusions and estimating optical flow. We show that, under standard assumptions of Lambertian reflection and static illumination, the task can be posed as a convex minimization problem. Therefore, the solution, computed using efficient algorithms, is guaranteed to be globally optimal, for any number of independently moving objects, and any number of occlusion layers. We test the proposed algorithm on benchmark datasets, expanded to enable evaluation of occlusion detection performance.

paragraphs: Estimating optical flow means estimating apparent motion in images, while detecting occlusions means identifying where visibility is blocked. The paper addresses these tasks jointly. This matters because motion estimation and visibility are connected: interpreting image changes requires accounting for both movement and the disappearance of image content behind other objects.

The authors show that the joint task can be formulated as a convex minimization problem under assumptions of Lambertian reflection and unchanging illumination. Convexity permits efficient algorithms to obtain a globally optimal solution to that formulation. The stated result accommodates any number of independently moving objects and any number of occlusion layers.

The guarantee is tied to the model and its assumptions: global optimality concerns the formulated optimization problem under those imaging conditions. The authors test their algorithm on benchmark datasets expanded to support evaluation of occlusion detection. The contribution is thus both a joint mathematical treatment of motion and visibility and an evaluation setup that explicitly assesses the occlusion component.
summary.tldr: Under Lambertian reflection and static illumination, joint optical-flow and occlusion estimation admits a convex formulation with a globally optimal solution.

title: Occlusion Detection and Motion Estimation with Convex Optimization

abstract: Recent work in unsupervised feature learning has focused on the goal of discovering high-level features from unlabeled images. Much progress has been made in this direction, but in most cases it is still standard to use a large amount of labeled data in order to construct detectors sensitive to object classes or other complex patterns in the data. In this paper, we aim to test the hypothesis that unsupervised feature learning methods, provided with only unlabeled data, can learn high-level, invariant features that are sensitive to commonly-occurring objects. Though a handful of prior results suggest that this is possible when each object class accounts for a large fraction of the data (as in many labeled datasets), it is unclear whether something similar can be accomplished when dealing with completely unlabeled data. A major obstacle to this test, however, is scale: we cannot expect to succeed with small datasets or with small numbers of learned features. Here, we propose a large-scale feature learning system that enables us to carry out this experiment, learning 150,000 features from tens of millions of unlabeled images. Based on two scalable clustering algorithms (K-means and agglomerative clustering), we find that our simple system can discover features sensitive to a commonly occurring object class (human faces) and can also combine these into detectors invariant to significant global distortions like large translations and scale.

abstract: We present a Bayesian nonparametric model that discovers implicit social structure from interaction time-series data. Social groups are often formed implicitly, through actions among members of groups. Yet many models of social networks use explicitly declared relationships to infer social structure. We consider a particular class of Hawkes processes, a doubly stochastic point process, that is able to model reciprocity between groups of individuals. We then extend the Infinite Relational Model by using these reciprocating Hawkes processes to parameterise its edges, making events associated with edges co-dependent through time. Our model outperforms general, unstructured Hawkes processes as well as structured Poisson process-based models at predicting verbal and email turn-taking, and military conflicts among nations.

paragraphs: Social structure can emerge through interactions even when people have not explicitly declared their relationships. This paper develops a Bayesian nonparametric model that discovers such implicit structure from the timing of interactions. The focus is on reciprocity: activity involving groups of individuals can be related to subsequent activity in return.

The authors use a class of Hawkes processes suited to representing that reciprocity. They incorporate these processes into the Infinite Relational Model by using them to parameterize its edges. It outperforms both general unstructured Hawkes processes and structured models based on Poisson processes in those evaluations. These comparisons support the combination of relational structure and temporally dependent events: the model represents both who interacts and how interactions are linked over time.
summary.tldr: A relational model with reciprocating Hawkes processes discovers implicit social structure and improves prediction of timed interactions.

title: Modelling Reciprocating Relationships with Hawkes Processes

abstract: We propose a fast algorithm for ridge regression when the number of features is much larger than the number of observations ($p \gg n$). The standard way to solve ridge regression in this setting works in the dual space and gives a running time of $O(n^2p)$. Our algorithm (SRHT-DRR) runs in time $O(np\log(n))$ and works by preconditioning the design matrix by a Randomized Walsh-Hadamard Transform with a subsequent subsampling of features. We provide risk bounds for our SRHT-DRR algorithm in the fixed design setting and show experimental results on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: This paper targets ridge regression when there are far more features than observations. In this regime, the standard dual-space approach has running time O(n²p), where n counts observations and p counts features. The authors develop SRHT-DRR to reduce this computational cost while also analyzing the statistical risk of the resulting procedure.

The algorithm preconditions the design matrix with a randomized Walsh-Hadamard transform and then subsamples features. The transformation and feature reduction together yield a stated running time of O(np log(n)). Relative to the standard expression, the dependence multiplying np changes from n to log(n), which is the central computational improvement claimed for the targeted high-dimensional setting.

The paper provides risk bounds under a fixed-design formulation and presents experiments using synthetic and real datasets. These components address complementary questions: how the method's estimation risk can be controlled and how it behaves on data. The contribution combines a faster computational route with statistical analysis specifically for ridge regression in the many-features, fewer-observations regime.
summary.tldr: SRHT-DRR accelerates ridge regression with many more features than observations using a randomized transform and feature subsampling.

title: Faster Ridge Regression via the Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform

abstract: Numerous datasets ranging from group memberships within social networks to purchase histories on e-commerce sites are represented by binary matrices. While this data is often either proprietary or sensitive, aggregated data, notably row and column marginals, is often viewed as much less sensitive, and may be furnished for analysis. Here, we investigate how these data can be exploited to make inferences about the underlying matrix H. Instead of assuming a generative model for H, we view the input marginals as constraints on the dataspace of possible realizations of H and compute the probability density function of particular entries H(i,j) of interest. We do this, for all the cells of H simultaneously, without generating realizations but rather via implicitly sampling the datasets that satisfy the input marginals. The end result is an efficient algorithm with running time equal to the time required by standard sampling techniques to generate a single dataset from the same dataspace. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates the efficiency and the efficacy of our framework in multiple settings.

paragraphs: Binary matrices can record sensitive facts such as group memberships or purchase histories. Row and column totals are often released because they appear less revealing than individual entries. This paper investigates how those totals can nevertheless support inferences about particular cells of the hidden matrix.

The method treats the supplied totals as constraints defining a space of compatible matrices. It does not assume a generative model for the original matrix. Instead, it computes probability distributions for entries of interest through implicit sampling of the compatible data space. The procedure handles all cells simultaneously without explicitly generating complete matrix realizations.

The resulting algorithm takes as much time as standard sampling methods need to generate just one compatible dataset. Experiments demonstrate its efficiency and effectiveness across multiple settings. The finding gives aggregate information a concrete interpretation: row and column totals restrict possible underlying datasets enough to support cell-level inference. The output is probabilistic information about entries, allowing the framework to characterize what those constraints reveal without claiming exact reconstruction of every hidden value.
summary.tldr: An efficient algorithm uses row and column totals to infer probabilities for hidden binary-matrix entries without generating complete datasets.

title: What do row and column marginals reveal about your dataset?

abstract: Neural responses in visual cortex are influenced by visual stimuli and by ongoing spiking activity in local circuits. An important challenge in computational neuroscience is to develop models that can account for both of these features in large multi-neuron recordings and to reveal how stimulus representations interact with and depend on cortical dynamics. Here we introduce a statistical model of neural population activity that integrates a nonlinear receptive field model with a latent dynamical model of ongoing cortical activity. This model captures the temporal dynamics, effective network connectivity in large population recordings, and correlations due to shared stimulus drive as well as common noise. Moreover, because the nonlinear stimulus inputs are mixed by the ongoing dynamics, the model can account for a relatively large number of idiosyncratic receptive field shapes with a small number of nonlinear inputs to a low-dimensional latent dynamical model. We introduce a fast estimation method using online expectation maximization with Laplace approximations. Inference scales linearly in both population size and recording duration. We apply this model to multi-channel recordings from primary visual cortex and show that it accounts for a large number of individual neural receptive fields using a small number of nonlinear inputs and a low-dimensional dynamical model.

paragraphs: Visual cortical responses reflect both incoming stimuli and ongoing activity within neural circuits. This paper introduces a statistical population model that combines a nonlinear receptive-field model with a latent dynamical model. The aim is to explain how stimulus responses interact with shared internal dynamics across many recorded neurons.

The model captures temporal patterns, effective network connectivity, and correlations arising from shared stimulus input and common noise. Its key representational idea is that ongoing dynamics mix nonlinear stimulus inputs. A relatively small set of inputs can therefore account for many distinct receptive-field shapes through a low-dimensional dynamical system.

The authors develop a fast fitting procedure using online expectation maximization with Laplace approximations. Inference scales linearly with both the number of neurons and recording duration, making the computational claim directly relevant to large recordings. Applied to multichannel primary visual cortex data, the model accounts for many individual receptive fields with few nonlinear inputs and low-dimensional dynamics. This supports a compact joint description of stimulus sensitivity and ongoing population activity.
summary.tldr: A compact dynamical model combines visual inputs and ongoing cortical activity to explain many neurons' receptive fields with scalable inference.

title: Low-dimensional models of neural population activity in sensory cortical circuits

abstract: We present a general framework for graph clustering where a label is observed to each pair of nodes. This allows a very rich encoding of various types of pairwise interactions between nodes. We propose a new tractable approach to this problem based on maximum likelihood estimator and convex optimization. We analyze our algorithm under a general generative model, and provide both necessary and sufficient conditions for successful recovery of the underlying clusters. Our theoretical results cover and subsume a wide range of existing graph clustering results including planted partition, weighted clustering and partially observed graphs. Furthermore, the result is applicable to novel settings including time-varying graphs such that new insights can be gained on solving these problems. Our theoretical findings are further supported by empirical results on both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: This paper studies graph clustering through a general representation in which each pair of nodes has an observed label. Those labels can encode richer relationships than a simple indication that an edge exists. The aim is to recover underlying groups while accommodating different kinds of pairwise information within one framework.

The authors propose a tractable approach based on maximum likelihood estimation and convex optimization. They analyze it under a general generative model and establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for successful cluster recovery. These results address two complementary questions: what successful recovery requires, and what conditions are enough to make it possible.

It also applies to settings such as graphs that change over time, giving the framework a role beyond unifying earlier results. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings. The main significance is a common analytical and computational treatment of several forms of graph clustering.
summary.tldr: A label-based graph clustering framework combines tractable optimization with recovery conditions covering weighted, partially observed, and time-varying graphs.

title: Clustering from Labels and Time-Varying Graphs

abstract: We describe an approach for unsupervised learning of a generic, distributed sentence encoder. Using the continuity of text from books, we train an encoder-decoder model that tries to reconstruct the surrounding sentences of an encoded passage. Sentences that share semantic and syntactic properties are thus mapped to similar vector representations. We next introduce a simple vocabulary expansion method to encode words that were not seen as part of training, allowing us to expand our vocabulary to a million words. After training our model, we extract and evaluate our vectors with linear models on 8 tasks: semantic relatedness, paraphrase detection, image-sentence ranking, question-type classification and 4 benchmark sentiment and subjectivity datasets. The end result is an off-the-shelf encoder that can produce highly generic sentence representations that are robust and perform well in practice. We will make our encoder publicly available.

paragraphs: The paper develops an unsupervised sentence encoder intended to produce useful representations across different tasks. Training uses the continuity of text in books: an encoder represents a passage, and a decoder attempts to reconstruct the surrounding sentences. The surrounding text supplies a learning signal without requiring labels for a particular downstream application.

Through this objective, sentences with shared semantic and syntactic properties map to similar vectors. The authors also introduce a vocabulary expansion method that allows the encoder to handle words absent from its original training vocabulary. This expands the usable vocabulary to a million words, broadening the range of sentences the encoder can represent.

The learned vectors are evaluated with linear models on eight tasks, covering semantic relatedness, paraphrase detection, image-sentence ranking, question classification, and sentiment or subjectivity datasets. These evaluations support the authors' claim that the representations are broadly useful and perform well in practice. The intended outcome is an off-the-shelf sentence encoder whose learned vectors can serve multiple applications.
summary.tldr: Skip-thought learns reusable sentence vectors by reconstructing neighboring sentences and evaluates them across eight tasks.

title: Skip-Thought Vectors

abstract: We consider cooperative multi-agent consensus optimization problems over an undirected network of agents, where only those agents connected by an edge can directly communicate. The objective is to minimize the sum of agent-specific composite convex functions over agent-specific private conic constraint sets; hence, the optimal consensus decision should lie in the intersection of these private sets. We provide convergence rates in sub-optimality, infeasibility and consensus violation; examine the effect of underlying network topology on the convergence rates of the proposed decentralized algorithms; and show how to extend these methods to handle time-varying communication networks.

We provide convergence rates in sub-optimality, infeasibility and consensus violation; examine the effect of underlying network topology on the convergence rates of the proposed decentralized algorithms; and show how to extend these methods to handle time-varying communication networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a network of agents can agree on a decision while each agent has its own objective and constraints. Communication is restricted: two agents can exchange information directly only when an edge connects them. The shared goal is to minimize the sum of their individual convex objectives, while choosing a decision that satisfies every agent’s private conic constraints.

The proposed primal-dual approach addresses optimization and coordination together. A decision can be attractive according to the combined objective yet violate someone’s constraints, and different agents can hold inconsistent decisions. The paper therefore provides convergence rates for three separate quantities: distance from the optimal objective value, constraint infeasibility, and disagreement among agents.

The analysis also examines how the network’s connection pattern affects convergence. This links the mathematical guarantees to the communication structure through which cooperation must occur. Finally, the authors explain how to extend the decentralized methods to networks whose connections change over time, broadening the setting beyond a fixed communication graph.
summary.tldr: A decentralized primal-dual method coordinates convex optimization under private conic constraints, with convergence guarantees covering accuracy, feasibility, and agreement.

title: A primal-dual method for conic constrained distributed optimization problems

abstract: We introduce a collaborative PAC learning model, in which k players attempt to learn the same underlying concept. We ask how much more information is required to learn an accurate classifier for all players simultaneously. We refer to the ratio between the sample complexity of collaborative PAC learning and its non-collaborative (single-player) counterpart as the overhead. We design learning algorithms with O(ln(k)) and O(ln^2(k)) overhead in the personalized and centralized variants our model. This gives an exponential improvement upon the naive algorithm that does not share information among players. We complement our upper bounds with an Omega(ln(k)) overhead lower bound, showing that our results are tight up to a logarithmic factor.

We design learning algorithms with O(ln(k)) and O(ln^2(k)) overhead in the personalized and centralized variants our model. This gives an exponential improvement upon the naive algorithm that does not share information among players. We complement our upper bounds with an Omega(ln(k)) overhead lower bound, showing that our results are tight up to a logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much data is needed when several players want to learn the same underlying concept and every player needs an accurate classifier. Learning separately wastes opportunities to share information. However, a collaborative procedure must satisfy all players simultaneously, so its data requirements need to be compared with those of an ordinary single-player task.

The authors formalize this comparison through overhead: the collaborative sample complexity divided by the single-player sample complexity. They develop algorithms for personalized and centralized versions of the problem. With k players, the respective overhead bounds are O(ln(k)) and O(ln²(k)), making the additional data requirement grow slowly with the number of participants.

These bounds give an exponential improvement over the naive approach without information sharing. The paper also proves an Ω(ln(k)) lower bound, establishing that some increasing cost of collaboration is unavoidable in this model. Together, the bounds identify the achievable overhead up to a logarithmic factor and show how sharing information changes the statistical cost of serving many learners.
summary.tldr: Collaborative learning algorithms achieve logarithmic or squared-logarithmic sample overhead, with a lower bound showing near-tight dependence on the number of players.

title: Collaborative PAC Learning

abstract: Computational models of visual attention are at the crossroad of disciplines like cognitive science, computational neuroscience, and computer vision. This paper proposes a model of attentional scanpath that is based on the principle that there are foundational laws that drive the emergence of visual attention. We devise variational laws of the eye-movement that rely on a generalized view of the Least Action Principle in physics. The potential energy captures details as well as peripheral visual features, while the kinetic energy corresponds with the classic interpretation in analytic mechanics. In addition, the Lagrangian contains a brightness invariance term, which characterizes significantly the scanpath trajectories. We obtain differential equations of visual attention as the stationary point of the generalized action, and we propose an algorithm to estimate the model parameters. Finally, we report experimental results to validate the model in tasks of saliency detection.

paragraphs: This paper models the sequence of eye movements through a dynamic scene using a principle inspired by physical mechanics. It proposes that attentional scanpaths can emerge from foundational laws expressed through a generalized least-action framework. The aim is to derive movement trajectories from a mathematical description of visual attention.

The model’s potential energy represents visual details and peripheral features, while its kinetic energy follows the classical mechanics interpretation. Its Lagrangian also includes a brightness-invariance term that substantially shapes the resulting scanpaths. The authors derive differential equations for attention by finding stationary points of the generalized action, turning the proposed principle into equations governing movement.

They additionally provide an algorithm for estimating the model’s parameters and report experiments validating it on saliency detection tasks. These steps connect the mathematical formulation to an estimable computational model and an empirical evaluation. The findings support the proposed approach in those tasks; the mechanics-inspired construction is a modeling principle, rather than an established universal law of human eye movement.
summary.tldr: A generalized least-action model derives visual-attention trajectories from image features, movement energy, and brightness invariance.

title: Variational Laws of Visual Attention for Dynamic Scenes

abstract: Cortical circuits exhibit intricate recurrent architectures that are remarkably similar across different brain areas. Such stereotyped structure suggests the existence of common computational principles. However, such principles have remained largely elusive. Inspired by gated-memory networks, namely long short-term memory networks (LSTMs), we introduce a recurrent neural network in which information is gated through inhibitory cells that are subtractive (subLSTM). We propose a natural mapping of subLSTMs onto known canonical excitatory-inhibitory cortical microcircuits. Our empirical evaluation across sequential image classification and language modelling tasks shows that subLSTM units can achieve similar performance to LSTM units. These results suggest that cortical circuits can be optimised to solve complex contextual problems and proposes a novel view on their computational function. Overall our work provides a step towards unifying recurrent networks as used in machine learning with their biological counterparts.

paragraphs: Similar recurrent circuit patterns appear across different areas of the cortex, raising the possibility that they implement shared computational principles. This paper explores that possibility through a recurrent neural network inspired by long short-term memory networks. The aim is to connect a useful machine learning computation with the organization of cortical circuits.

The proposed subLSTM gates information using subtractive inhibitory cells. The authors describe a natural mapping between these units and known cortical microcircuits containing excitatory and inhibitory cells. That mapping makes the network a concrete computational proposal for how familiar circuit components could support gated processing of information across a sequence.

In sequential image classification and language modelling experiments, subLSTM units achieve performance similar to LSTM units. This provides evidence that the proposed form of inhibition can support demanding contextual tasks. The findings suggest a possible computational role for cortical circuitry and a connection to trainable recurrent networks; they do not establish that biological circuits use the proposed mechanism exactly.
summary.tldr: SubLSTM connects subtractive inhibitory gating to cortical microcircuits and achieves performance similar to LSTMs on sequential tasks.

title: Cortical microcircuits as gated-recurrent neural networks

abstract: We study stochastic convex optimization subjected to linear equality constraints. Traditional Stochastic Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers and its Nesterov's acceleration scheme can only achieve ergodic O(1/\sqrt{K}) convergence rates, where K is the number of iteration. By introducing Variance Reduction (VR) techniques, the convergence rates improve to ergodic O(1/K). In this paper, we propose a new stochastic ADMM which elaborately integrates Nesterov's extrapolation and VR techniques. With Nesterov’s extrapolation, our algorithm can achieve a non-ergodic O(1/K) convergence rate which is optimal for separable linearly constrained non-smooth convex problems, while the convergence rates of VR based ADMM methods are actually tight O(1/\sqrt{K}) in non-ergodic sense. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that achieves a truly accelerated, stochastic convergence rate for constrained convex problems. The experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm is significantly faster than the existing state-of-the-art stochastic ADMM methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic convex optimization with linear equality constraints. Its central distinction is between convergence guarantees for averaged iterates, called ergodic guarantees, and guarantees without that averaging, called non-ergodic guarantees. An improvement in the former does not necessarily imply an equally strong improvement in the latter.

Traditional stochastic ADMM and its Nesterov-accelerated version have ergodic rates of O(1/√K), where K counts iterations. Variance reduction improves that averaged rate to O(1/K), but the paper shows that existing variance-reduced ADMM methods still have tight non-ergodic rates of O(1/√K). The proposed algorithm carefully combines variance reduction with Nesterov’s extrapolation to overcome this gap.

The resulting non-ergodic rate is O(1/K), which is optimal for the stated class of separable, linearly constrained, nonsmooth convex problems. This makes the acceleration meaningful beyond averaged outputs. Experiments also show substantially faster performance than existing state-of-the-art stochastic ADMM methods, providing practical evidence alongside the stronger guarantee for the constrained problem class under study.
summary.tldr: Combining extrapolation with variance reduction gives stochastic ADMM an optimal O(1/K) non-ergodic rate for the stated constrained convex problem class.

title: Faster and Non-ergodic O(1/K) Stochastic Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers

abstract: Storing data in synthetic DNA offers the possibility of improving information density and durability by several orders of magnitude compared to current storage technologies. However, DNA data storage requires a computationally intensive process to retrieve the data. In particular, a crucial step in the data retrieval pipeline involves clustering billions of strings with respect to edit distance. Datasets in this domain have many notable properties, such as containing a very large number of small clusters that are well-separated in the edit distance metric space. In this regime, existing algorithms are unsuitable because of either their long running time or low accuracy. To address this issue, we present a novel distributed algorithm for approximately computing the underlying clusters. Our algorithm converges efficiently on any dataset that satisfies certain separability properties, such as those coming from DNA data storage systems. We also prove that, under these assumptions, our algorithm is robust to outliers and high levels of noise. We provide empirical justification of the accuracy, scalability, and convergence of our algorithm on real and synthetic data. Compared to the state-of-the-art algorithm for clustering DNA sequences, our algorithm simultaneously achieves higher accuracy and a 1000x speedup on three real datasets.

Datasets in this domain have many notable properties, such as containing a very large number of small clusters that are well-separated in the edit distance metric space. In this regime, existing algorithms are unsuitable because of either their long running time or low accuracy. To address this issue, we present a novel distributed algorithm for approximately computing the underlying clusters. Our algorithm converges efficiently on any dataset that satisfies certain separability properties, such as those coming from DNA data storage systems. We also prove that, under these assumptions, our algorithm is robust to outliers and high levels of noise. We provide empirical justification of the accuracy, scalability, and convergence of our algorithm on real and synthetic data. Compared to the state-of-the-art algorithm for clustering DNA sequences, our algorithm simultaneously achieves higher accuracy and a 1000x speedup on three real datasets.

paragraphs: Retrieving information stored in synthetic DNA requires grouping enormous numbers of sequence strings by similarity. One crucial step clusters billions of strings using edit distance, which measures the changes needed to transform one string into another. DNA storage data often contains many small groups that are well separated, a combination that existing methods handle too slowly or inaccurately.

The paper proposes a distributed algorithm that approximately recovers these groups. Its theoretical guarantees depend on specified separation properties of the dataset, such as those found in DNA storage systems. Under those assumptions, the algorithm converges efficiently and remains robust to outliers and substantial noise. The separation requirement is central to the regime where these guarantees apply.

Experiments with real and synthetic data examine accuracy, scalability, and convergence. On three real datasets, the algorithm achieves higher accuracy and a 1000-fold speedup over the compared state-of-the-art DNA clustering method. This result shows how exploiting the structure of the clustering problem can substantially reduce a computational bottleneck in data retrieval.
summary.tldr: A distributed clustering algorithm exploits separated DNA sequence groups, achieving higher accuracy and a 1000-fold speedup on three real datasets.

title: Clustering Billions of Reads for DNA Data Storage

abstract: Motivated by online advertising, we study a multiple-play multi-armed bandit problem with position bias that involves several slots and the latter slots yield fewer rewards. We characterize the hardness of the problem by deriving an asymptotic regret bound. We propose the Permutation Minimum Empirical Divergence (PMED) algorithm and derive its asymptotically optimal regret bound. Because of the uncertainty of the position bias, the optimal algorithm for such a problem requires non-convex optimizations that are different from usual partial monitoring and semi-bandit problems. We propose a cutting-plane method and related bi-convex relaxation for these optimizations by using auxiliary variables.

paragraphs: Motivated by online advertising, this paper studies sequential choices involving several display slots. Later slots produce fewer rewards, but the extent of this position bias is unknown. Learning must therefore account for both the options being selected and the effects of their positions, rather than attributing observed rewards entirely to the selected options.

The authors characterize the problem's difficulty through an asymptotic regret bound. Regret measures reward lost through learning and imperfect decisions. They propose the Permutation Minimum Empirical Divergence algorithm, or PMED, and derive an asymptotically optimal regret bound for it. This establishes optimality in the long-run sense specified by the analysis.

Unknown position bias creates non-convex optimization problems within the optimal algorithm, differing from those in usual partial-monitoring and semi-bandit settings. To handle these computations, the paper proposes a cutting-plane method and a related bi-convex relaxation using auxiliary variables. Its contributions therefore address both the statistical difficulty of learning with unknown position effects and the optimization work required by the proposed algorithm.
summary.tldr: PMED achieves asymptotically optimal regret for multi-slot bandits with unknown position bias, alongside methods for its non-convex computations.

title: Position-based Multiple-play Bandit Problem with Unknown Position Bias

abstract: We consider an inexact variant of the popular Riemannian trust-region algorithm for structured big-data minimization problems. The proposed algorithm approximates the gradient and the Hessian in addition to the solution of a trust-region sub-problem. Addressing large-scale finite-sum problems, we specifically propose sub-sampled algorithms with a fixed bound on sub-sampled Hessian and gradient sizes, where the gradient and Hessian are computed by a random sampling technique. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed algorithms outperform state-of-the-art Riemannian deterministic and stochastic gradient algorithms across different applications.

Addressing large-scale finite-sum problems, we specifically propose sub-sampled algorithms with a fixed bound on sub-sampled Hessian and gradient sizes, where the gradient and Hessian are computed by a random sampling technique. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed algorithms outperform state-of-the-art Riemannian deterministic and stochastic gradient algorithms across different applications.

paragraphs: Some large optimization problems have structure expressed through a Riemannian manifold, so the optimization algorithm must respect that geometry. Riemannian trust-region methods are a popular approach to such problems. This paper develops an inexact version aimed at structured problems involving large datasets, where computing all the ingredients of an update can be expensive.

The proposed method approximates the gradient, the Hessian, and the solution of the trust-region subproblem. For finite-sum objectives, the authors use random sampling to compute approximate gradients and Hessians. They specifically propose algorithms with fixed bounds on the numbers of samples used for those two computations, limiting how much data those derivative calculations draw on.

The approach makes approximation part of several stages of the optimization procedure, allowing the method to work with reduced computational inputs while retaining the manifold-based formulation. Numerical evaluations across different applications show the proposed algorithms outperforming the state-of-the-art deterministic and stochastic Riemannian gradient methods considered. The stated evidence supports their practical value for the evaluated large-scale optimization problems.
summary.tldr: Inexact Riemannian trust-region algorithms use sampled derivatives and approximate subproblem solutions to improve performance on evaluated large-scale problems.

title: Inexact trust-region algorithms on Riemannian manifolds

abstract: Despite the advances in the representational capacity of approximate distributions for variational inference, the optimization process can still limit the density that is ultimately learned. We demonstrate the drawbacks of biasing the true posterior to be unimodal, and introduce Annealed Variational Objectives (AVO) into the training of hierarchical variational methods. Inspired by Annealed Importance Sampling, the proposed method facilitates learning by incorporating energy tempering into the optimization objective. In our experiments, we demonstrate our method's robustness to deterministic warm up, and the benefits of encouraging exploration in the latent space.
originalAbstract: Despite the advances in the representational capacity of approximate distributions for variational inference, the optimization process can still limit the density that is ultimately learned. We demonstrate the drawbacks of biasing the true posterior to be unimodal, and introduce Annealed Variational Objectives (AVO) into the training of hierarchical variational methods. Inspired by Annealed Importance Sampling, the proposed method facilitates learning by incorporating energy tempering into the optimization objective. In our experiments, we demonstrate our method's robustness to deterministic warm up, and the benefits of encouraging exploration in the latent space.

paragraphs: Variational inference learns an approximate probability distribution, but a flexible representation alone does not ensure that training finds a useful approximation. The optimization process can restrict which density is ultimately learned. This paper focuses on that gap between what an approximate distribution can represent and what its training procedure actually discovers.

The authors demonstrate drawbacks of biasing the true posterior toward a single mode and introduce Annealed Variational Objectives for hierarchical variational methods. Inspired by Annealed Importance Sampling, the method incorporates energy tempering into the training objective. This changes the optimization problem to facilitate exploration of latent space, addressing the learning process alongside the expressive capacity of the approximation.

Experiments show benefits from encouraging latent-space exploration and report robustness to deterministic warm up. These findings support the idea that the objective used during training can matter even when the distribution family is already expressive. The paper's contribution is therefore an annealed training approach for hierarchical inference, with empirical evidence that improved exploration helps the learned approximation.
summary.tldr: Annealed Variational Objectives use energy tempering to encourage latent-space exploration during hierarchical variational inference.

title: Improving Explorability in Variational Inference with Annealed Variational Objectives

abstract: Uncertainty estimation in large deep-learning models is a computationally challenging task, where it is difficult to form even a Gaussian approximation to the posterior distribution. In such situations, existing methods usually resort to a diagonal approximation of the covariance matrix despite the fact that these matrices are known to give poor uncertainty estimates. To address this issue, we propose a new stochastic, low-rank, approximate natural-gradient (SLANG) method for variational inference in large deep models. Our method estimates a “diagonal plus low-rank” structure based solely on back-propagated gradients of the network log-likelihood. This requires strictly less gradient computations than methods that compute the gradient of the whole variational objective. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks confirm that SLANG enables faster and more accurate estimation of uncertainty than mean-field methods, and performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods.
