paragraphs: SLANG addresses the computational difficulty of estimating uncertainty in large neural networks. Even approximating the posterior with a Gaussian can be expensive. Common diagonal covariance approximations simplify that calculation, but the authors identify their poor uncertainty estimates as a reason to retain more structure without paying the cost of a full covariance representation.

The method uses stochastic, low-rank, approximate natural gradients for variational inference. It estimates a diagonal-plus-low-rank structure using only back-propagated gradients of the network log-likelihood. The low-rank component adds structure beyond a diagonal approximation. The procedure requires strictly fewer gradient computations than methods that differentiate the complete variational objective.

Evaluations on standard benchmarks find faster and more accurate uncertainty estimation than mean-field methods, with performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches. These results support the proposed compromise between computational cost and a richer approximation to uncertainty. The contribution is an inference method that obtains its structured approximation from familiar network gradients while improving the reported uncertainty estimates over simpler approximations.
summary.tldr: SLANG uses a diagonal-plus-low-rank approximation to estimate neural-network uncertainty efficiently from likelihood gradients.

title: SLANG: Fast Structured Covariance Approximations for Bayesian Deep Learning with Natural Gradient

abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is widely used as a similarity measure in various domains. Due to its invariance against warping in the time axis, DTW provides more meaningful discrepancy measurements between two signals than other dis- tance measures. In this paper, we propose a novel component in an artificial neural network. In contrast to the previous successful usage of DTW as a loss function, the proposed framework leverages DTW to obtain a better feature extraction. For the first time, the DTW loss is theoretically analyzed, and a stochastic backpropogation scheme is proposed to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the DTW learning. We also demonstrate that the proposed framework can be used as a data analysis tool to perform data decomposition.
originalAbstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is widely used as a similarity measure in various domains. Due to its invariance against warping in the time axis, DTW provides more meaningful discrepancy measurements between two signals than other dis- tance measures. In this paper, we propose a novel component in an artificial neural network. In contrast to the previous successful usage of DTW as a loss function, the proposed framework leverages DTW to obtain a better feature extraction. For the first time, the DTW loss is theoretically analyzed, and a stochastic backpropogation scheme is proposed to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the DTW learning. We also demonstrate that the proposed framework can be used as a data analysis tool to perform data decomposition.

paragraphs: Dynamic Time Warping compares signals while accommodating changes in their timing. This can make its discrepancy measurements more meaningful when corresponding signal patterns are stretched or compressed along the time axis. DTWNet brings that property into a neural-network component intended to improve the features extracted from data.

The paper’s emphasis is on the role DTW plays inside learning. Previous successful uses had treated it as a loss function; here, the framework uses DTW for feature extraction itself. The timing-aware comparison therefore helps shape the representation produced by the network, making alignment part of the process of obtaining useful features.

The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of the DTW loss and propose a stochastic backpropagation scheme intended to improve the accuracy and efficiency of DTW learning. They demonstrate an additional use of the framework as a data-analysis tool for decomposition. Together, these contributions connect a signal-comparison method, a learning procedure, and an analysis application within the same proposed framework.
summary.tldr: DTWNet incorporates Dynamic Time Warping into feature extraction and proposes stochastic backpropagation for learning with that component.

title: DTWNet: a Dynamic Time Warping Network

abstract: Passing gradient is a widely used scheme in modern multi-node learning system (e.g, distributed training, collaborative learning). In a long time, people used to believe that gradients are safe to share: i.e, the training set will not be leaked by gradient sharing. However, in this paper, we show that we can obtain the private training set from the publicly shared gradients. The leaking only takes few gradient steps to process and can obtain the original training set instead of look-alike alternatives. We name this leakage as \textit{deep leakage from gradient} and practically validate the effectiveness of our algorithm on both computer vision and natural language processing tasks. We empirically show that our attack is much stronger than previous approaches and thereby and raise people's awareness to rethink the gradients' safety. We also discuss some possible strategies to defend this deep leakage.

paragraphs: Distributed and collaborative training commonly exchange gradients, the information used to update model parameters. This paper challenges the belief that sharing these updates keeps the underlying training examples private. It shows that publicly shared gradients can contain enough information to recover private training data, making the exchanged updates themselves a potential source of disclosure.

The authors introduce an attack called deep leakage from gradients. In the demonstrated cases, recovery takes only a few gradient steps and can reconstruct original training examples rather than merely produce similar-looking substitutes. That distinction matters because the claimed leakage concerns the actual source data, beyond a general resemblance to the kinds of examples used in training.

The attack is validated on both computer vision and natural language processing tasks. The authors empirically report stronger leakage than previous approaches and discuss possible defensive strategies. These findings establish a concrete reason to reconsider gradient-sharing safety: exchanging updates can expose data even when the training examples themselves are not directly transmitted.
summary.tldr: Shared gradients can reveal original private training examples, as demonstrated by attacks on vision and language tasks.

title: Deep Leakage from Gradients

abstract: Modern approaches for multi-person pose estimation in video require large amounts of dense annotations. However, labeling every frame in a video is costly and labor intensive. To reduce the need for dense annotations, we propose a PoseWarper network that leverages training videos with sparse annotations (every k frames) to learn to perform dense temporal pose propagation and estimation. Given a pair of video frames---a labeled Frame A and an unlabeled Frame B---we train our model to predict human pose in Frame A using the features from Frame B by means of deformable convolutions to implicitly learn the pose warping between A and B. We demonstrate that we can leverage our trained PoseWarper for several applications. First, at inference time we can reverse the application direction of our network in order to propagate pose information from manually annotated frames to unlabeled frames. This makes it possible to generate pose annotations for the entire video given only a few manually-labeled frames. Compared to modern label propagation methods based on optical flow, our warping mechanism is much more compact (6M vs 39M parameters), and also more accurate (88.7% mAP vs 83.8% mAP). We also show that we can improve the accuracy of a pose estimator by training it on an augmented dataset obtained by adding our propagated poses to the original manual labels. Lastly, we can use our PoseWarper to aggregate temporal pose information from neighboring frames during inference. This allows us to obtain state-of-the-art pose detection results on PoseTrack2017 and PoseTrack2018 datasets.

paragraphs: Estimating human poses throughout a video typically demands expensive frame-by-frame annotations. PoseWarper learns from videos labeled only every k frames, using relationships between frames to extend the value of those sparse labels. Its goal is both to propagate pose annotations and to improve pose estimation over time.

During training, the network predicts the pose in a labeled frame using features from an unlabeled frame. Deformable convolutions let it learn the alignment between their poses implicitly. At inference, reversing the application direction transfers information from manually labeled frames to unlabeled ones, making dense annotations possible from a small set of manual labels.

The reported propagation comparison favors PoseWarper over optical-flow methods in both size and accuracy: 6 million versus 39 million parameters, and 88.7% versus 83.8% mAP. Training a pose estimator with the propagated labels further improves accuracy. The network can also aggregate information from neighboring frames at inference, yielding reported state-of-the-art results on PoseTrack2017 and PoseTrack2018.
summary.tldr: PoseWarper learns temporal pose alignment from sparse video labels to propagate annotations and improve pose estimation.

title: Learning Temporal Pose Estimation from Sparsely-Labeled Videos

abstract: Real-world applications often combine learning and optimization problems on graphs. For instance, our objective may be to cluster the graph in order to detect meaningful communities (or solve other common graph optimization problems such as facility location, maxcut, and so on). However, graphs or related attributes are often only partially observed, introducing learning problems such as link prediction which must be solved prior to optimization. Standard approaches treat learning and optimization entirely separately, while recent machine learning work aims to predict the optimal solution directly from the inputs. Here, we propose an alternative decision-focused learning approach that integrates a differentiable proxy for common graph optimization problems as a layer in learned systems. The main idea is to learn a representation that maps the original optimization problem onto a simpler proxy problem that can be efficiently differentiated through. Experimental results show that our ClusterNet system outperforms both pure end-to-end approaches (that directly predict the optimal solution) and standard approaches that entirely separate learning and optimization. Code for our system is available at https://github.com/bwilder0/clusternet.

paragraphs: Graph applications often require both learning missing information and making an optimized decision. Community detection, facility location, and maxcut can all involve graphs that are only partly observed. A conventional pipeline first predicts missing links or attributes and then solves the optimization problem, treating the two stages as separate tasks.

The paper proposes decision-focused learning that connects them through a differentiable optimization proxy. A learned representation maps the original graph problem into a simpler problem through which training can efficiently differentiate. This proxy becomes a layer within the learned system, allowing the optimization task to influence the representation used to support it.

The resulting system, ClusterNet, outperforms both separate learning-and-optimization pipelines and systems that directly predict an optimal solution in the reported experiments. The findings support using an optimization-aware intermediate representation. Its purpose is to make a difficult graph decision accessible to learning through a tractable proxy, while retaining an explicit connection to the downstream optimization problem.
summary.tldr: ClusterNet trains graph representations through a differentiable optimization proxy, improving decisions in the reported experiments.

title: End to end learning and optimization on graphs

abstract: Lossless compression methods shorten the expected representation size of data without loss of information, using a statistical model. Flow-based models are attractive in this setting because they admit exact likelihood optimization, which is equivalent to minimizing the expected number of bits per message. However, conventional flows assume continuous data, which may lead to reconstruction errors when quantized for compression. For that reason, we introduce a flow-based generative model for ordinal discrete data called Integer Discrete Flow (IDF): a bijective integer map that can learn rich transformations on high-dimensional data. As building blocks for IDFs, we introduce a flexible transformation layer called integer discrete coupling. Our experiments show that IDFs are competitive with other flow-based generative models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that IDF based compression achieves state-of-the-art lossless compression rates on CIFAR10, ImageNet32, and ImageNet64. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first lossless compression method that uses invertible neural networks.

paragraphs: Lossless compression uses a statistical model to shorten data representations while preserving every piece of information. Flow-based models are appealing because optimizing their exact likelihood corresponds to minimizing expected message length. Conventional flows, however, operate on continuous data, and quantizing them for compression can introduce reconstruction errors.

Integer Discrete Flow addresses this mismatch with a bijective mapping between integer-valued representations. Because the mapping is invertible within the discrete domain, it fits the requirement of exact recovery. The authors introduce integer discrete coupling layers as flexible building blocks for learning rich transformations of high-dimensional ordinal data.

The experiments find that these models are competitive with other flow-based generative models and achieve state-of-the-art lossless compression rates on CIFAR10, ImageNet32, and ImageNet64. These results connect the discrete modeling choice to an operational compression benefit, rather than evaluating generative modeling alone. The authors also describe the approach as, to their knowledge, the first lossless compression method based on invertible neural networks.
summary.tldr: Integer Discrete Flows learn invertible integer transformations that support exact reconstruction and strong lossless image compression.

title: Integer Discrete Flows and Lossless Compression

abstract: In structured output prediction tasks, labeling ground-truth training output is often expensive. However, for many tasks, even when the true output is unknown, we can evaluate predictions using a scalar reward function, which may be easily assembled from human knowledge or non-differentiable pipelines. But searching through the entire output space to find the best output with respect to this reward function is typically intractable. In this paper, we instead use efficient truncated randomized search in this reward function to train structured prediction energy networks (SPENs), which provide efficient test-time inference using gradient-based search on a smooth, learned representation of the score landscape, and have previously yielded state-of-the-art results in structured prediction. In particular, this truncated randomized search in the reward function yields previously unknown local improvements, providing effective supervision to SPENs, avoiding their traditional need for labeled training data.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can require expensive labels because each output contains multiple related decisions. In some tasks, however, a scalar reward can judge a proposed output even when the correct output is unavailable. Such a reward may come from human knowledge or a pipeline that cannot be differentiated, while searching every possible output remains intractable.

The paper uses short, randomized searches over that reward to discover local improvements. These improved candidates provide supervision for a structured prediction energy network. The search does not need to solve the entire output problem optimally; finding previously unknown improvements is enough to supply the training signal described by the authors.

At test time, the trained network supports gradient-based search over a smooth, learned score landscape. This separates the reward-based search used to obtain supervision from the efficient inference enabled by the learned representation. The stated contribution is a way to train these networks without their traditional labeled-data requirement, using accessible evaluations of candidate outputs to teach a model how to search effectively.
summary.tldr: Short randomized searches for reward improvements provide supervision for structured prediction energy networks without ground-truth output labels.

title: Search-Guided, Lightly-Supervised Training of Structured Prediction Energy Networks

abstract: The signature is an infinite graded sequence of statistics known to characterise a stream of data up to a negligible equivalence class. It is a transform which has previously been treated as a fixed feature transformation, on top of which a model may be built. We propose a novel approach which combines the advantages of the signature transform with modern deep learning frameworks. By learning an augmentation of the stream prior to the signature transform, the terms of the signature may be selected in a data-dependent way. More generally, we describe how the signature transform may be used as a layer anywhere within a neural network. In this context it may be interpreted as a pooling operation. We present the results of empirical experiments to back up the theoretical justification. Code available at \texttt{github.com/patrick-kidger/Deep-Signature-Transforms}.

We propose a novel approach which combines the advantages of the signature transform with modern deep learning frameworks. By learning an augmentation of the stream prior to the signature transform, the terms of the signature may be selected in a data-dependent way. More generally, we describe how the signature transform may be used as a layer anywhere within a neural network. In this context it may be interpreted as a pooling operation. We present the results of empirical experiments to back up the theoretical justification. Code available at \texttt{github.com/patrick-kidger/Deep-Signature-Transforms}.

paragraphs: A signature transform represents a data stream through an infinite, graded collection of statistics. This collection characterizes the stream up to a negligible equivalence class. Earlier uses treated the transform as fixed preprocessing: compute signature features first, then train a separate model to use them.

This paper makes the transformation part of a learned architecture. A network learns an augmentation of the stream before the signature is computed, allowing signature terms to be selected in a way that depends on the data. The feature construction can therefore adapt during learning instead of being completely specified before the model is trained.

The authors also describe how to place a signature transform at other positions within a neural network, where it can be understood as a pooling operation. This broadens its role from an input representation to an internal component of deep models. The paper provides theoretical justification and supporting empirical experiments. Its main contribution is the integration of a mathematically grounded stream representation with learnable neural processing.
summary.tldr: The paper turns signature transforms from fixed stream features into adaptable components that can appear throughout a neural network.

title: Deep Signature Transforms

abstract: Multiplicative stochasticity such as Dropout improves the robustness and gener- alizability deep neural networks. Here, we further demonstrate that always-on multiplicative stochasticity combined with simple threshold neurons provide a suf- ficient substrate for deep learning machines. We call such models Neural Sampling Machines (NSM). We find that the probability of activation of the NSM exhibits a self-normalizing property that mirrors Weight Normalization, a previously studied mechanism that fulfills many of the features of Batch Normalization in an online fashion. The normalization of activities during training speeds up convergence by preventing internal covariate shift caused by changes in the distribution of inputs. The always-on stochasticity of the NSM confers the following advantages: the network is identical in the inference and learning phases, making the NSM a suitable substrate for continual learning, it can exploit stochasticity inherent to a physical substrate such as analog non-volatile memories for in memory computing, and it is suitable for Monte Carlo sampling, while requiring almost exclusively addition and comparison operations. We demonstrate NSMs on standard classification benchmarks (MNIST and CIFAR) and event-based classification benchmarks (N-MNIST and DVS Gestures). Our results show that NSMs perform comparably or better than conventional artificial neural networks with the same architecture.

The paper shows that this combination is sufficient to build deep learning models. Its central observation is that the probability of neuron activation has a self-normalizing property resembling weight normalization.

The authors connect this normalization to faster convergence through stabilizing activities as input distributions change during training. Keeping randomness active also makes the network identical during learning and inference, which they identify as useful for continual learning. The design supports Monte Carlo sampling and requires almost entirely addition and comparison operations.

The paper also identifies a potential hardware benefit: these models can use randomness inherent in physical devices such as analog non-volatile memories. Experiments cover MNIST and CIFAR as well as the event-based N-MNIST and DVS Gestures benchmarks. On these tasks, Neural Sampling Machines perform comparably to or better than conventional artificial neural networks with the same architecture, supporting the practicality of the stochastic design.
summary.tldr: Neural Sampling Machines use always-on randomness and threshold neurons to obtain inherent normalization and competitive classification performance.

title: Inherent Weight Normalization in Stochastic Neural Networks

abstract: In neural network-based models for natural language processing (NLP), the largest part of the parameters often consists of word embeddings. Conventional models prepare a large embedding matrix whose size depends on the vocabulary size. Therefore, storing these models in memory and disk storage is costly. In this study, to reduce the total number of parameters, the embeddings for all words are represented by transforming a shared embedding. The proposed method, ALONE (all word embeddings from one), constructs the embedding of a word by modifying the shared embedding with a filter vector, which is word-specific but non-trainable. Then, we input the constructed embedding into a feed-forward neural network to increase its expressiveness. Naively, the filter vectors occupy the same memory size as the conventional embedding matrix, which depends on the vocabulary size. To solve this issue, we also introduce a memory-efficient filter construction approach. We indicate our ALONE can be used as word representation sufficiently through an experiment on the reconstruction of pre-trained word embeddings. In addition, we also conduct experiments on NLP application tasks: machine translation and summarization. We combined ALONE with the current state-of-the-art encoder-decoder model, the Transformer [36], and achieved comparable scores on WMT 2014 English-to-German translation and DUC 2004 very short summarization with less parameters.

ALONE replaces that large collection of independently learned embeddings with word representations constructed from one shared embedding. The goal is to reduce the storage burden while retaining useful distinctions between words.

For each word, the method modifies the shared embedding using a word-specific filter that is not trained. A feed-forward neural network then increases the expressiveness of the resulting representation. Simply storing a full filter for every word would recreate the original memory problem, so the paper also introduces a memory-efficient way to construct those filters.

The authors test whether ALONE can reconstruct pretrained embeddings and whether it works in translation and summarization. Combined with a Transformer, it achieves comparable scores on the reported English-to-German translation and short-summarization tasks using fewer parameters. These findings support shared construction as a practical alternative to storing a full learned embedding matrix in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ALONE constructs word embeddings from a shared vector and compact filters, achieving comparable task scores with fewer parameters.

title: All Word Embeddings from One Embedding

abstract: As predictive models are increasingly being deployed in high-stakes decision-making, there has been a lot of interest in developing algorithms which can provide recourses to affected individuals. While developing such tools is important, it is even more critical to analyze and interpret a predictive model, and vet it thoroughly to ensure that the recourses it offers are meaningful and non-discriminatory before it is deployed in the real world. To this end, we propose a novel model agnostic framework called Actionable Recourse Summaries (AReS) to construct global counterfactual explanations which provide an interpretable and accurate summary of recourses for the entire population. We formulate a novel objective which simultaneously optimizes for correctness of the recourses and interpretability of the explanations, while minimizing overall recourse costs across the entire population. More specifically, our objective enables us to learn, with optimality guarantees on recourse correctness, a small number of compact rule sets each of which capture recourses for well defined subpopulations within the data. We also demonstrate theoretically that several of the prior approaches proposed to generate recourses for individuals are special cases of our framework. Experimental evaluation with real world datasets and user studies demonstrate that our framework can provide decision makers with a comprehensive overview of recourses corresponding to any black box model, and consequently help detect undesirable model biases and discrimination.

paragraphs: Recourse describes changes an affected person could make to obtain a different model decision. Individual recommendations are useful, but inspecting them separately makes it difficult to judge whether a model offers meaningful and nondiscriminatory options across a population. Actionable Recourse Summaries, or AReS, addresses this broader evaluation problem through global counterfactual explanations.

The framework constructs a small collection of compact rules describing recourse for clearly defined subpopulations. Its objective combines recourse correctness, explanation interpretability, and overall recourse cost across the population. It supplies optimality guarantees concerning correctness, while its model-agnostic design makes it applicable to black box predictors. The authors also establish that several earlier individual recourse approaches are special cases of their framework.

Experiments with real datasets and user studies indicate that these summaries give decision makers a comprehensive overview of a model's recourses. That overview can help expose undesirable biases and discrimination before deployment. The stated contribution is support for inspecting population-wide patterns of recourse, rather than a guarantee that summarization itself removes discrimination.
summary.tldr: AReS summarizes actionable recourse with compact population-level rules that can help decision makers detect model bias.

title: Beyond Individualized Recourse: Interpretable and Interactive Summaries of Actionable Recourses

abstract: Large-scale distributed training of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) on state-of-the-art platforms are expected to be severely communication constrained. To overcome this limitation, numerous gradient compression techniques have been proposed and have demonstrated high compression ratios. However, most existing compression methods do not scale well to large scale distributed systems (due to gradient build-up) and / or lack evaluations in large datasets. To mitigate these issues, we propose a new compression technique, Scalable Sparsified Gradient Compression (ScaleComp), that (i) leverages similarity in the gradient distribution amongst learners to provide a commutative compressor and keep communication cost constant to worker number and (ii) includes low-pass filter in local gradient accumulations to mitigate the impacts of large batch size training and significantly improve scalability. Using theoretical analysis, we show that ScaleComp provides favorable convergence guarantees and is compatible with gradient all-reduce techniques. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate that ScaleComp has small overheads, directly reduces gradient traffic and provides high compression rates (70-150X) and excellent scalability (up to 64-80 learners and 10X larger batch sizes over normal training) across a wide range of applications (image, language, and speech) without significant accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Distributed neural-network training can spend substantial resources communicating gradients between workers. Compression reduces that traffic, but existing methods may scale poorly as gradients build up or as training uses larger batches. This paper proposes ScaleComp, a sparsified gradient-compression technique designed to retain communication savings as the distributed system grows.

The method exploits similarities in gradient distributions across learners to construct a commutative compressor that keeps communication cost constant with respect to worker count. It also applies a low-pass filter to local gradient accumulations to mitigate large-batch effects. Theoretical analysis supplies convergence guarantees and establishes compatibility with gradient all-reduce, connecting the compression scheme to distributed aggregation.

Experiments across image, language, and speech applications report low overhead and direct reductions in gradient traffic. The method achieves compression rates of 70–150 times and scales to 64–80 learners and batches ten times larger than normal training, without significant accuracy loss. These results support its intended role: making gradient compression useful at larger training scales rather than only in smaller configurations.
summary.tldr: ScaleComp combines commutative gradient compression with filtered accumulation to reduce communication while scaling distributed training.

title: ScaleCom: Scalable Sparsified Gradient Compression for Communication-Efficient Distributed Training

abstract: The search for biologically faithful synaptic plasticity rules has resulted in a large body of models. They are usually inspired by -- and fitted to -- experimental data, but they rarely produce neural dynamics that serve complex functions. These failures suggest that current plasticity models are still under-constrained by existing data. Here, we present an alternative approach that uses meta-learning to discover plausible synaptic plasticity rules. Instead of experimental data, the rules are constrained by the functions they implement and the structure they are meant to produce. Briefly, we parameterize synaptic plasticity rules by a Volterra expansion and then use supervised learning methods (gradient descent or evolutionary strategies) to minimize a problem-dependent loss function that quantifies how effectively a candidate plasticity rule transforms an initially random network into one with the desired function. We first validate our approach by re-discovering previously described plasticity rules, starting at the single-neuron level and ``Oja’s rule'', a simple Hebbian plasticity rule that captures the direction of most variability of inputs to a neuron (i.e., the first principal component). We expand the problem to the network level and ask the framework to find Oja’s rule together with an anti-Hebbian rule such that an initially random two-layer firing-rate network will recover several principal components of the input space after learning. Next, we move to networks of integrate-and-fire neurons with plastic inhibitory afferents. We train for rules that achieve a target firing rate by countering tuned excitation. Our algorithm discovers a specific subset of the manifold of rules that can solve this task. Our work is a proof of principle of an automated and unbiased approach to unveil synaptic plasticity rules that obey biological constraints and can solve complex functions.

paragraphs: This paper searches for synaptic learning rules by asking what a network should become after learning. Existing plasticity models often fit biological observations without producing useful network functions. The authors instead constrain candidate rules through the functions and structures they should produce, using meta-learning to search for plausible solutions.

They express plasticity rules through a Volterra expansion and optimize their parameters using gradient descent or evolutionary strategies. A task-specific loss measures how effectively each rule turns an initially random network into one that performs the desired function. The learned object is therefore the rule governing network change.

The framework rediscovers Oja’s rule for extracting the principal direction of input variation, then finds rules that recover several principal components at the network level. In integrate-and-fire networks, it also discovers a subset of inhibitory plasticity rules that achieve a target firing rate against tuned excitation. These results establish a proof of principle for discovering functionally useful rules under biological constraints, rather than identifying a unique biological learning mechanism.
summary.tldr: Meta-learning discovers plausible synaptic plasticity rules by optimizing the network functions those rules produce.

title: A meta-learning approach to (re)discover plasticity rules that carve a desired function into a neural network

abstract: Molecular geometry prediction of flexible molecules, or conformer search, is a long-standing challenge in computational chemistry. This task is of great importance for predicting structure-activity relationships for a wide variety of substances ranging from biomolecules to ubiquitous materials. Substantial computational resources are invested in Monte Carlo and Molecular Dynamics methods to generate diverse and representative conformer sets for medium to large molecules, which are yet intractable to chemoinformatic conformer search methods. We present TorsionNet, an efficient sequential conformer search technique based on reinforcement learning under the rigid rotor approximation. The model is trained via curriculum learning, whose theoretical benefit is explored in detail, to maximize a novel metric grounded in thermodynamics called the Gibbs Score. Our experimental results show that TorsionNet outperforms the highest-scoring chemoinformatics method by 4x on large branched alkanes, and by several orders of magnitude on the previously unexplored biopolymer lignin, with applications in renewable energy. TorsionNet also outperforms the far more exhaustive but computationally intensive Self-Guided Molecular Dynamics sampling method.

paragraphs: Flexible molecules can adopt many geometries, and finding representative collections of these conformations is computationally demanding. The problem matters for understanding relationships between molecular structure and activity. TorsionNet approaches conformer search as a sequence of decisions learned through reinforcement learning, under the rigid rotor approximation.

The model is trained using curriculum learning and aims to maximize the Gibbs Score, a new evaluation quantity grounded in thermodynamics. The paper also investigates the theoretical benefit of the curriculum. This connects the search policy’s learning objective to a thermodynamic measure, giving the sequential procedure a specific target for judging the conformations it discovers.

In the reported experiments, TorsionNet outperforms the highest-scoring chemoinformatics method by a factor of four on large branched alkanes and by several orders of magnitude on lignin. It also surpasses Self-Guided Molecular Dynamics, described as more exhaustive and computationally intensive. These are performance comparisons on the evaluated search tasks, rather than stated runtime speedups. The results support learned sequential search for difficult molecular systems within the method’s approximation.
summary.tldr: TorsionNet uses curriculum-trained reinforcement learning to search molecular conformations and achieves strong reported results under the rigid rotor approximation.

title: TorsionNet: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to Sequential Conformer Search

abstract: The doubly robust (DR) estimator, which consists of two nuisance parameters, the conditional mean outcome and the logging policy (the probability of choosing an action), is crucial in causal inference. This paper proposes a DR estimator for dependent samples obtained from adaptive experiments. To obtain an asymptotically normal semiparametric estimator from dependent samples without non-Donsker nuisance estimators, we propose adaptive-fitting as a variant of sample-splitting. We also report an empirical paradox that our proposed DR estimator tends to show better performances compared to other estimators utilizing the true logging policy. While a similar phenomenon is known for estimators with i.i.d. samples, traditional explanations based on asymptotic efficiency cannot elucidate our case with dependent samples. We confirm this hypothesis through simulation studies.

paragraphs: Doubly robust estimation combines two quantities: a model of the conditional mean outcome and the logging policy, which gives the probability of selecting an action. This paper adapts that approach to experiments where data collection changes over time. Such adaptive experiments produce dependent samples, making their statistical analysis different from the independent-sample setting.

The authors propose adaptive-fitting, a variant of sample splitting, as part of their estimator construction. Its purpose is to obtain an asymptotically normal semiparametric estimator with dependent observations. Asymptotic normality provides a distributional characterization of estimation error as the sample grows, so the fitting procedure supports statistical analysis as well as the construction of an outcome estimate.

Simulations also reveal a surprising empirical pattern: the proposed estimator tends to perform better than other estimators that use the true logging policy. A related phenomenon is known for independent samples, but the authors explain that traditional arguments based on asymptotic efficiency do not account for their dependent-sample case. The reported advantage is an empirical tendency, rather than a universal claim that estimating a known policy always helps.
summary.tldr: Adaptive-fitting supports doubly robust estimation with dependent experimental data and reveals an empirical advantage over some estimators using the true logging policy.

title: The Adaptive Doubly Robust Estimator and a Paradox Concerning Logging Policy

abstract: Representation learning has served as a key tool for meta-learning, enabling rapid learning of new tasks. Recent works like MAML learn task-specific representations by finding an initial representation requiring minimal per-task adaptation (i.e. a fine-tuning-based objective). We present a theoretical framework for analyzing a MAML-like algorithm, assuming all available tasks require approximately the same representation. We then provide risk bounds on predictors found by fine-tuning via gradient descent, demonstrating that the method provably leverages the shared structure. We illustrate these bounds in the logistic regression and neural network settings. In contrast, we establish settings where learning one representation for all tasks (i.e. using a "frozen representation" objective) fails. Notably, any such algorithm cannot outperform directly learning the target task with no other information, in the worst case. This separation underscores the benefit of fine-tuning-based over “frozen representation” objectives in few-shot learning.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to make new tasks easier to learn by drawing on structure shared across previous tasks. One approach learns a representation that remains fixed; another learns an initialization intended for quick adaptation. This paper develops a theoretical account of the second approach through an algorithm resembling MAML.

The analysis assumes that the available tasks need approximately the same representation. Under that shared-structure assumption, the authors derive risk bounds for predictors obtained by fine-tuning with gradient descent. These bounds demonstrate that the method can provably benefit from what the tasks have in common. The framework is illustrated for logistic regression and neural networks.

The authors also establish settings where a frozen-representation objective fails to provide the same benefit. In the worst case, any such algorithm cannot outperform learning the target task directly without information from other tasks. This separation supports fine-tuning-based objectives for few-shot learning in the studied settings; it does not claim that frozen representations are ineffective for every collection of tasks.
summary.tldr: Under an approximately shared-representation assumption, fine-tuning provably exploits task structure in settings where frozen-representation objectives can fail.

title: How Fine-Tuning Allows for Effective Meta-Learning

abstract: As black box explanations are increasingly being employed to establish model credibility in high stakes settings, it is important to ensure that these explanations are accurate and reliable. However, prior work demonstrates that explanations generated by state-of-the-art techniques are inconsistent, unstable, and provide very little insight into their correctness and reliability. In addition, these methods are also computationally inefficient, and require significant hyper-parameter tuning. In this paper, we address the aforementioned challenges by developing a novel Bayesian framework for generating local explanations along with their associated uncertainty. We instantiate this framework to obtain Bayesian versions of LIME and KernelSHAP which output credible intervals for the feature importances, capturing the associated uncertainty. The resulting explanations not only enable us to make concrete inferences about their quality (e.g., there is a 95% chance that the feature importance lies within the given range), but are also highly consistent and stable. We carry out a detailed theoretical analysis that leverages the aforementioned uncertainty to estimate how many perturbations to sample, and how to sample for faster convergence. This work makes the first attempt at addressing several critical issues with popular explanation methods in one shot, thereby generating consistent, stable, and reliable explanations with guarantees in a computationally efficient manner. Experimental evaluation with multiple real world datasets and user studies demonstrate that the efficacy of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the reliability of local explanations for black-box predictions. Existing explanation techniques can produce unstable feature importances while offering little indication of how uncertain those estimates are. The authors develop a Bayesian framework that generates explanations together with uncertainty, giving users more information about the reliability of the reported feature contributions.

They instantiate the framework as Bayesian versions of LIME and KernelSHAP. These methods return credible intervals around feature importances, expressing uncertainty as a range with an associated posterior probability. The authors also report improved consistency and stability, connecting uncertainty modeling to the repeatability of the resulting explanations.

A theoretical analysis uses the uncertainty estimates to determine how many perturbations to sample and how to sample for faster convergence. This makes uncertainty useful both for interpreting an explanation and for controlling its computational cost. Experiments on multiple real datasets and user studies support the framework's effectiveness, alongside the paper's guarantees for efficient, reliable local explanation.
summary.tldr: Bayesian versions of LIME and KernelSHAP quantify feature-importance uncertainty and use it to improve explanation stability and sampling efficiency.

title: Reliable Post hoc Explanations: Modeling Uncertainty in Explainability

abstract: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) usually suffers from sparse reward and inefficient exploration in long-horizon tasks. Planning can find the shortest path to a distant goal that provides dense reward/guidance but is inaccurate without a precise environment model. We show that RL and planning can collaboratively learn from each other to overcome their own drawbacks. In ''CO-PILOT'', a learnable path-planner and an RL agent produce dense feedback to train each other on a curriculum of tree-structured sub-tasks. Firstly, the planner recursively decomposes a long-horizon task to a tree of sub-tasks in a top-down manner, whose layers construct coarse-to-fine sub-task sequences as plans to complete the original task. The planning policy is trained to minimize the RL agent's cost of completing the sequence in each layer from top to bottom layers, which gradually increases the sub-tasks and thus forms an easy-to-hard curriculum for the planner. Next, a bottom-up traversal of the tree trains the RL agent from easier sub-tasks with denser rewards on bottom layers to harder ones on top layers and collects its cost on each sub-task train the planner in the next episode. CO-PILOT repeats this mutual training for multiple episodes before switching to a new task, so the RL agent and planner are fully optimized to facilitate each other's training. We compare CO-PILOT with RL (SAC, HER, PPO), planning (RRT*, NEXT, SGT), and their combination (SoRB) on navigation and continuous control tasks. CO-PILOT significantly improves the success rate and sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Reaching distant goals is difficult for reinforcement learning when useful rewards arrive rarely. Planning can supply intermediate guidance, but its accuracy depends on its environment model. CO-PILOT couples a learnable planner with a reinforcement learning agent so that each supplies training feedback for the other, organized around progressively harder subtasks.

The planner breaks a long task into a tree. Upper layers describe coarse plans, while lower layers provide finer sequences of subtasks. It learns using the agent's cost of completing those sequences, moving from upper to lower layers as the number of subtasks increases. The agent traverses the curriculum in the opposite direction, starting with easier lower-level subtasks that offer denser rewards before attempting harder tasks above them.

The agent's measured costs then inform the planner's next episode, and this mutual training repeats before changing tasks. On the evaluated navigation and continuous-control problems, CO-PILOT significantly improves success rates and sample efficiency against the tested reinforcement learning, planning, and combined approaches. The results support coordinating both components through a shared subtask curriculum.
summary.tldr: CO-PILOT trains a planner and reinforcement learning agent together through a tree of subtasks, improving success and sample efficiency in the evaluated tasks.

title: CO-PILOT: COllaborative Planning and reInforcement Learning On sub-Task curriculum

abstract: We study a real-time iteration (RTI) scheme for solving online optimization problem appeared in nonlinear optimal control. The proposed RTI scheme modifies the existing RTI-based model predictive control (MPC) algorithm, by selecting the stepsize of each Newton step at each sampling time using a differentiable exact augmented Lagrangian. The scheme can adaptively select the penalty parameters of augmented Lagrangian on the fly, which are shown to be stabilized after certain time periods. We prove under generic assumptions that, by involving stepsize selection instead of always using a full Newton step (like what most of the existing RTIs do), the scheme converges globally: for any initial point, the KKT residuals of the subproblems converge to zero. A key step is to show that augmented Lagrangian keeps decreasing as horizon moves forward. We demonstrate the global convergence behavior of the proposed RTI scheme in a numerical experiment.

A key step is to show that augmented Lagrangian keeps decreasing as horizon moves forward. We demonstrate the global convergence behavior of the proposed RTI scheme in a numerical experiment.

paragraphs: Nonlinear model predictive control repeatedly solves optimization problems as new sampling times arrive and the planning horizon advances. This paper studies a real-time iteration scheme for that setting, focusing on how to make the online optimization converge from arbitrary starting points under the stated generic assumptions.

The proposed change selects the step size of each Newton update using a differentiable exact augmented Lagrangian. Many existing real-time iteration schemes instead always take a full Newton step. The method also adapts the augmented Lagrangian's penalty parameters during operation, and the authors show that these parameters stabilize after certain periods.

The convergence result states that the subproblems' KKT residuals approach zero from any initial point, under the assumptions of the analysis. This specifies convergence in terms of optimality conditions rather than guaranteeing a globally optimal solution to every nonlinear problem. A central proof step establishes continued decrease of the augmented Lagrangian as the horizon moves forward. A numerical experiment demonstrates the claimed convergence behavior.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Newton step sizes yield global convergence of online MPC subproblem KKT residuals under the paper's assumptions.

title: Global Convergence of Online Optimization for Nonlinear Model Predictive Control

abstract: Heavy-tailed statistical distributions have long been considered a more realistic statistical model for the data generating process in financial markets in comparison to their Gaussian counterpart. Nonetheless, mathematical nuisances, including nonconvexities, involved in estimating graphs in heavy-tailed settings pose a significant challenge to the practical design of algorithms for graph learning. In this work, we present graph learning estimators based on the Markov random field framework that assume a Student-$t$ data generating process. We design scalable numerical algorithms, via the alternating direction method of multipliers, to learn both connected and $k$-component graphs along with their theoretical convergence guarantees. The proposed methods outperform state-of-the-art benchmarks in an extensive series of practical experiments with publicly available data from the S\&P500 index, foreign exchanges, and cryptocurrencies.

The authors design scalable numerical methods using the alternating direction method of multipliers. Their algorithms can learn a connected graph or a graph with k connected components. They also establish theoretical convergence guarantees for the proposed numerical procedures.

Experiments use publicly available observations from the S&P500, foreign exchange markets, and cryptocurrencies. The methods outperform leading benchmarks in the reported evaluations. The contribution combines an explicit heavy-tailed statistical assumption with algorithms for different graph connectivity requirements, supported by both convergence analysis and practical financial-data experiments.
summary.tldr: Student-t graphical models and scalable optimization algorithms improve graph estimation in the reported heavy-tailed financial-data experiments.

title: Graphical Models in Heavy-Tailed Markets

abstract: Motivated by the consideration of fairly sharing the cost of exploration between multiple groups in learning problems, we develop the Nash bargaining solution in the context of multi-armed bandits. Specifically, the 'grouped' bandit associated with any multi-armed bandit problem associates, with each time step, a single group from some finite set of groups. The utility gained by a given group under some learning policy is naturally viewed as the reduction in that group's regret relative to the regret that group would have incurred 'on its own'. We derive policies that yield the Nash bargaining solution relative to the set of incremental utilities possible under any policy. We show that on the one hand, the 'price of fairness' under such policies is limited, while on the other hand, regret optimal policies are arbitrarily unfair under generic conditions. Our theoretical development is complemented by a case study on contextual bandits for warfarin dosing where we are concerned with the cost of exploration across multiple races and age groups.

paragraphs: Exploration in a learning system can impose costs unevenly across groups. This paper studies how to share those costs in a multi-armed bandit setting where each time step is associated with one group from a finite collection. It evaluates a group’s benefit through the reduction in its regret compared with learning on its own.

The authors use the Nash bargaining solution to choose among the incremental utilities achievable by learning policies. They derive policies that realize this bargaining solution, giving a formal way to balance the benefits of shared learning across groups. This makes the comparison with independent learning central to the fairness objective.

Their analysis shows that the resulting price of fairness is limited, while regret-optimal policies can be arbitrarily unfair under generic conditions. Thus, optimizing aggregate learning performance can leave substantial disparities unresolved. A contextual-bandit case study on warfarin dosing examines exploration costs across racial and age groups. The study complements the theoretical account of how bargaining can shape the distribution of learning benefits.
summary.tldr: Nash bargaining yields bandit policies that distribute exploration benefits fairly with a limited price of fairness.

title: Fair Exploration via Axiomatic Bargaining

abstract: The ensemble method is a promising way to mitigate the overestimation issue in Q-learning, where multiple function approximators are used to estimate the action values. It is known that the estimation bias hinges heavily on the ensemble size (i.e., the number of Q-function approximators used in the target), and that determining the 'right' ensemble size is highly nontrivial, because of the time-varying nature of the function approximation errors during the learning process. To tackle this challenge, we first derive an upper bound and a lower bound on the estimation bias, based on which the ensemble size is adapted to drive the bias to be nearly zero, thereby coping with the impact of the time-varying approximation errors accordingly. Motivated by the theoretic findings, we advocate that the ensemble method can be combined with Model Identification Adaptive Control (MIAC) for effective ensemble size adaptation. Specifically, we devise Adaptive Ensemble Q-learning (AdaEQ), a generalized ensemble method with two key steps: (a) approximation error characterization which serves as the feedback for flexibly controlling the ensemble size, and (b) ensemble size adaptation tailored towards minimizing the estimation bias. Extensive experiments are carried out to show that AdaEQ can improve the learning performance than the existing methods for the MuJoCo benchmark.

paragraphs: Q-learning uses estimated action values to guide decisions, but these estimates can become systematically too optimistic. Combining several value estimators can help, although the resulting bias depends strongly on how many estimators contribute to the learning target. A fixed choice is difficult to get right because approximation errors change as learning progresses.

The paper derives upper and lower bounds on estimation bias and uses them to motivate adjusting the ensemble size during training. AdaEQ first characterizes approximation error and then treats that information as feedback for changing the ensemble. Drawing on Model Identification Adaptive Control, the method aims to keep bias close to zero as the underlying errors evolve.

This makes ensemble size an actively controlled part of learning rather than a single setting chosen in advance. Experiments on the MuJoCo benchmark show that AdaEQ can improve learning performance over existing methods. The contribution connects a theoretical account of bias with a practical feedback mechanism; the stated goal is nearly unbiased estimation, rather than an unconditional claim that all estimation error disappears.
summary.tldr: AdaEQ adjusts the number of value estimators using error feedback to reduce changing estimation bias during Q-learning.

title: Adaptive Ensemble Q-learning: Minimizing Estimation Bias via Error Feedback

abstract: We consider density estimation for Besov spaces when the estimator is restricted to use only a limited number of bits about each sample. We provide a noninteractive adaptive estimator which exploits the sparsity of wavelet bases, along with a simulate-and-infer technique from parametric estimation under communication constraints. We show that our estimator is nearly rate-optimal by deriving minmax lower bounds that hold even when interactive protocols are allowed. Interestingly, while our wavelet-based estimator is almost rate-optimal for Sobolev spaces as well, it is unclear whether the standard Fourier basis, which arise naturally for those spaces, can be used to achieve the same performance.

We show that our estimator is nearly rate-optimal by deriving minmax lower bounds that hold even when interactive protocols are allowed. Interestingly, while our wavelet-based estimator is almost rate-optimal for Sobolev spaces as well, it is unclear whether the standard Fourier basis, which arise naturally for those spaces, can be used to achieve the same performance.

paragraphs: Density estimation aims to recover a probability distribution's shape from samples. This paper considers the problem when the estimator receives only a limited number of bits about each sample. The restriction makes communication part of the statistical problem: useful information must fit into a small message before it can contribute to the final estimate.

For densities in Besov spaces, the authors construct an adaptive, noninteractive estimator using sparse wavelet representations. They combine this with a simulate-and-infer technique drawn from communication-constrained parametric estimation. To assess its performance, they derive minimax lower bounds, which describe unavoidable estimation difficulty. Those bounds apply even to interactive protocols, giving a stronger comparison than restricting every competitor to noninteractive communication.

The resulting estimator is nearly rate-optimal, showing that its accuracy approaches these fundamental limits. It is also almost rate-optimal for Sobolev spaces. The authors leave open whether the Fourier basis, a natural representation for that class, can achieve equivalent performance. This distinction highlights that a representation well suited to an ordinary estimation problem may still require separate analysis under communication limits.
summary.tldr: A noninteractive wavelet estimator approaches optimal density-estimation rates when each sample can communicate only a limited number of bits.

title: Optimal Rates for Nonparametric Density Estimation under Communication Constraints

abstract: Although deep feedforward neural networks share some characteristics with the primate visual system, a key distinction is their dynamics. Deep nets typically operate in serial stages wherein each layer completes its computation before processing begins in subsequent layers. In contrast, biological systems have cascaded dynamics: information propagates from neurons at all layers in parallel but transmission occurs gradually over time, leading to speed-accuracy trade offs even in feedforward architectures. We explore the consequences of biologically inspired parallel hardware by constructing cascaded ResNets in which each residual block has propagation delays but all blocks update in parallel in a stateful manner. Because information transmitted through skip connections avoids delays, the functional depth of the architecture increases over time, yielding anytime predictions that improve with internal-processing time. We introduce a temporal-difference training loss that achieves a strictly superior speed-accuracy profile over standard losses and enables the cascaded architecture to outperform state-of-the-art anytime-prediction methods. The cascaded architecture has intriguing properties, including: it classifies typical instances more rapidly than atypical instances; it is more robust to both persistent and transient noise than is a conventional ResNet; and its time-varying output trace provides a signal that can be exploited to improve information processing and inference.

paragraphs: An anytime predictor can produce an answer quickly and improve it as more processing time becomes available. This paper explores that behavior through a biologically inspired alternative to ordinary serial neural network computation. It constructs cascaded ResNets whose residual blocks maintain state and update in parallel, while information passing through those blocks experiences delays.

Skip connections allow some information to travel without those delays. As time passes, deeper processing contributes to the output, so the network’s effective depth grows and its predictions improve. The authors introduce a temporal-difference training loss that gives this evolving computation a better speed–accuracy profile than the standard losses considered.

The resulting architecture outperforms state-of-the-art anytime prediction methods in the reported work. It also recognizes typical examples sooner than atypical ones and is more robust to persistent and transient noise than a conventional ResNet. Its changing output over time supplies an additional signal that can improve processing and inference, making the temporal evolution useful beyond the final prediction alone.
summary.tldr: Parallel cascaded ResNets trained with a temporal-difference loss improve predictions over time and achieve a stronger reported speed–accuracy profile.

title: Improving Anytime Prediction with Parallel Cascaded Networks and a Temporal-Difference Loss

abstract: Backward propagation of errors (backpropagation) is a method to minimize objective functions (e.g., loss functions) of deep neural networks by identifying optimal sets of weights and biases. Imposing constraints on weight precision is often required to alleviate prohibitive workloads on hardware. Despite the remarkable success of backpropagation, the algorithm itself is not capable of considering such constraints unless additional algorithms are applied simultaneously. To address this issue, we propose the constrained backpropagation (CBP) algorithm based on the pseudo-Lagrange multiplier method to obtain the optimal set of weights that satisfy a given set of constraints. The defining characteristic of the proposed CBP algorithm is the utilization of a Lagrangian function (loss function plus constraint function) as its objective function. We considered various types of constraints — binary, ternary, one-bit shift, and two-bit shift weight constraints. As a post-training method, CBP applied to AlexNet, ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and GoogLeNet on ImageNet, which were pre-trained using the conventional backpropagation. For most cases, the proposed algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on ImageNet, e.g., 66.6\%, 74.4\%, and 64.0\% top-1 accuracy for ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and GoogLeNet with binary weights, respectively. This highlights CBP as a learning algorithm to address diverse constraints with the minimal performance loss by employing appropriate constraint functions. The code for CBP is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/dooseokjeong/CBP}.

Ordinary backpropagation optimizes a loss function but does not itself enforce a specified precision constraint. This paper introduces constrained backpropagation, or CBP, to incorporate such requirements into the optimization objective.

CBP uses a pseudo-Lagrange multiplier method and a Lagrangian objective that combines the prediction loss with a constraint function. Changing that function allows the method to address different permitted weight representations. The authors consider binary, ternary, one-bit shift, and two-bit shift constraints, making weight precision an explicit part of the learning problem.

The experiments apply CBP after conventional training to AlexNet, ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and GoogLeNet on ImageNet. The method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches in most cases. With binary weights, reported top-1 accuracies are 66.6% for ResNet-18, 74.4% for ResNet-50, and 64.0% for GoogLeNet. These results support CBP as a way to accommodate several hardware-oriented weight constraints while limiting the loss of predictive performance.
summary.tldr: CBP combines prediction loss with explicit weight constraints to adapt pretrained networks to low-precision weights with limited performance loss.

title: CBP: backpropagation with constraint on weight precision using a pseudo-Lagrange multiplier method

abstract: Temporal abstractions in the form of options have been shown to help reinforcement learning (RL) agents learn faster. However, despite prior work on this topic, the problem of discovering options through interaction with an environment remains a challenge. In this paper, we introduce a novel meta-gradient approach for discovering useful options in multi-task RL environments. Our approach is based on a manager-worker decomposition of the RL agent, in which a manager maximises rewards from the environment by learning a task-dependent policy over both a set of task-independent discovered-options and primitive actions. The option-reward and termination functions that define a subgoal for each option are parameterised as neural networks and trained via meta-gradients to maximise their usefulness. Empirical analysis on gridworld and DeepMind Lab tasks show that: (1) our approach can discover meaningful and diverse temporally-extended options in multi-task RL domains, (2) the discovered options are frequently used by the agent while learning to solve the training tasks, and (3) that the discovered options help a randomly initialised manager learn faster in completely new tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn faster when they choose extended behaviors, called options, alongside individual actions. Discovering useful options through interaction remains difficult. This paper addresses that problem in environments containing multiple tasks, aiming to learn reusable behaviors whose value extends beyond a single task.

The agent has a manager-worker organization. A task-dependent manager chooses among primitive actions and a shared set of discovered options. Each option's subgoal is specified by a reward function and a termination function, both represented by neural networks. Meta-gradients train these functions to make the resulting options useful for learning, connecting the definition of a subgoal to its downstream benefit.

Experiments in gridworlds and DeepMind Lab show that the method discovers diverse, meaningful behaviors that extend over time. Agents frequently choose these options while learning the training tasks. The options also help a newly initialized manager learn faster on entirely new tasks. This transfer result matters because it shows empirical usefulness beyond the particular manager and tasks involved in discovering the options.
summary.tldr: Meta-learning option rewards and termination rules discovers reusable behaviors that accelerate learning on new tasks in the reported experiments.

title: Discovery of Options via Meta-Learned Subgoals

abstract: Understanding documents with rich layouts plays a vital role in digitization and hyper-automation but remains a challenging topic in the NLP research community. Additionally, the lack of a commonly accepted benchmark made it difficult to quantify progress in the domain. To empower research in this field, we introduce the Document Understanding Evaluation (DUE) benchmark consisting of both available and reformulated datasets to measure the end-to-end capabilities of systems in real-world scenarios.The benchmark includes Visual Question Answering, Key Information Extraction, and Machine Reading Comprehension tasks over various document domains and layouts featuring tables, graphs, lists, and infographics. In addition, the current study reports systematic baselines and analyzes challenges in currently available datasets using recent advances in layout-aware language modeling. We open both the benchmarks and reference implementations and make them available at https://duebenchmark.com and https://github.com/due-benchmark.

paragraphs: Documents communicate through layout as well as words. Tables, graphs, lists, and infographics create varied reading conditions, making document understanding a challenging evaluation problem. This paper introduces Document Understanding Evaluation, or DUE, to provide a shared benchmark for assessing systems across these kinds of documents.

DUE combines existing datasets with reformulated ones and focuses on end-to-end capabilities in realistic scenarios. It includes visual question answering, key information extraction, and machine reading comprehension across different document domains and layouts. Bringing these tasks together gives researchers a common evaluation resource for several distinct demands placed on document-understanding systems.

The authors also establish systematic baselines using recent layout-aware language-modeling methods and analyze challenges in the available datasets. They release both the benchmark and reference implementations. The contribution therefore includes the evaluation tasks and working comparison systems, helping researchers quantify progress in a field where the lack of a commonly accepted benchmark had made comparisons difficult.
summary.tldr: DUE provides shared tasks and reference systems for evaluating end-to-end understanding of documents with rich, varied layouts.

title: DUE: End-to-End Document Understanding Benchmark

abstract: The lack of accessibility to data on policing has severely limited researchers’ ability to conduct thorough quantitative analyses on police activity and behavior, particularly with regard to predicting and explaining police violence. In the present work, we provide a new dataset that contains information on the personnel, activities, use of force, and complaints in the Chicago Police Department (CPD). The raw data, obtained from the CPD via a series of requests under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), consists of 35 unlinked, inconsistent, and undocumented spreadsheets. Our paper provides a cleaned, linked, and documented version of this data that can be reproducibly generated via open source code. We provide a detailed description of the dataset contents, the procedures for cleaning the data, and summary statistics. The data have a rich variety of uses, such as prediction (e.g., predicting misconduct from officer traits, experience, and assigned units), network analysis (e.g., detecting communities within the social network of officers co-listed on complaints), spatiotemporal data analysis (e.g., investigating patterns of officer shooting events), causal inference (e.g., tracking the effects of new disciplinary practices, new training techniques, and new oversight on complaints and use of force), and much more. Access to this dataset will enable the machine learning community to meaningfully engage with the problem of police violence.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a basic obstacle to quantitative research on policing: relevant records can be difficult to access and use together. It introduces a dataset covering Chicago Police Department personnel, activities, force incidents, and complaints. The underlying records were obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests and arrived as 35 inconsistent, undocumented spreadsheets without links between them.

The authors clean, connect, and document these records, and release open-source code that can reproduce the resulting dataset. They also describe its contents, explain the cleaning procedures, and provide summary statistics. This work turns fragmented source material into a more usable research resource while making the preparation process inspectable and repeatable.

These are proposed uses of the resource. The central contribution is making data available in a form that enables more substantial research engagement with police activity and violence.
summary.tldr: The CPD dataset turns 35 fragmented police-record spreadsheets into a linked, documented resource with reproducible preparation code.

title: The CPD Data Set: Personnel, Use of Force, and Complaints in the Chicago Police Department

abstract: Complex time-varying systems are often studied by abstracting away from the dynamics of individual components to build a model of the population-level dynamics from the start. However, when building a population-level description, it can be easy to lose sight of each individual and how they contribute to the larger picture. In this paper, we present a novel transformer architecture for learning from time-varying data that builds descriptions of both the individual as well as the collective population dynamics. Rather than combining all of our data into our model at the onset, we develop a separable architecture that operates on individual time-series first before passing them forward; this induces a permutation-invariance property and can be used to transfer across systems of different size and order. After demonstrating that our model can be applied to successfully recover complex interactions and dynamics in many-body systems, we apply our approach to populations of neurons in the nervous system. On neural activity datasets, we show that our model not only yields robust decoding performance, but also provides impressive performance in transfer across recordings of different animals without any neuron-level correspondence. By enabling flexible pre-training that can be transferred to neural recordings of different size and order, our work provides a first step towards creating a foundation model for neural decoding.

paragraphs: A model of a changing population can capture collective behavior while obscuring what individual components contribute. This paper develops a transformer architecture that represents both levels. It first processes each component's time series separately, then passes those descriptions onward to build a representation of the population's dynamics.

This separable design gives the model a permutation-invariance property, allowing it to handle changes in the ordering of components. The architecture can also transfer across systems containing different numbers of components. The authors first demonstrate that it recovers complex interactions and dynamics in many-body systems, then apply the approach to populations of neurons.

On neural activity datasets, the model delivers robust decoding and transfers across recordings from different animals without requiring neuron-by-neuron correspondence. That result matters because the architecture can reuse learning when recordings differ in their size and ordering. The authors position flexible pre-training and transfer as a first step toward a foundation model for neural decoding, rather than claiming that such a foundation model is already complete.
summary.tldr: A separable transformer models individual and collective dynamics while supporting transfer across neural recordings with different sizes and neuron orderings.

title: Seeing the forest and the tree: Building representations of both individual and collective dynamics with transformers

abstract: Recent research in the theory of overparametrized learning has sought to establish generalization guarantees in the interpolating regime. Such results have been established for a few common classes of methods, but so far not for ensemble methods. We devise an ensemble classification method that simultaneously interpolates the training data, and is consistent for a broad class of data distributions. To this end, we define the manifold-Hilbert kernel for data distributed on a Riemannian manifold. We prove that kernel smoothing regression using the manifold-Hilbert kernel is weakly consistent in the setting of Devroye et al. 1998. For the sphere, we show that the manifold-Hilbert kernel can be realized as a weighted random partition kernel, which arises as an infinite ensemble of partition-based classifiers.
