We devise an ensemble classification method that simultaneously interpolates the training data, and is consistent for a broad class of data distributions. To this end, we define the manifold-Hilbert kernel for data distributed on a Riemannian manifold. We prove that kernel smoothing regression using the manifold-Hilbert kernel is weakly consistent in the setting of Devroye et al. 1998. For the sphere, we show that the manifold-Hilbert kernel can be realized as a weighted random partition kernel, which arises as an infinite ensemble of partition-based classifiers.

paragraphs: A model can fit every training example exactly and still need a separate explanation for why it generalizes. This paper investigates that question for ensembles, where corresponding guarantees had remained absent despite results for several other method classes. It constructs an ensemble classifier that both interpolates its training data and is statistically consistent for a broad class of distributions.

The construction begins with the manifold-Hilbert kernel, designed for data lying on a Riemannian manifold. The authors prove weak consistency for kernel smoothing regression using this kernel in the specified theoretical setting. This establishes a statistical foundation for combining exact training fit with reliable behavior as the amount of data grows.

For data on a sphere, the paper further shows that the kernel has a representation as a weighted random partition kernel. That representation arises from an infinite ensemble of partition-based classifiers, connecting the kernel analysis to an ensemble construction. The sphere-specific result is the bridge between the two perspectives: a geometrically defined smoothing method and an ensemble with both interpolation and consistency guarantees.
summary.tldr: A manifold-based kernel yields an ensemble construction that exactly fits training data while retaining consistency guarantees.

title: Consistent Interpolating Ensembles via the Manifold-Hilbert Kernel

abstract: Inverse problems are paramount in Science and Engineering. In this paper, we consider the setup of Statistical Inverse Problem (SIP) and demonstrate how Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithms can be used to solve linear SIP. We provide consistency and finite sample bounds for the excess risk. We also propose a modification for the SGD algorithm where we leverage machine learning methods to smooth the stochastic gradients and improve empirical performance. We exemplify the algorithm in a setting of great interest nowadays: the Functional Linear Regression model. In this case we consider a synthetic data example and a classification problem for predicting the main activity of bitcoin addresses based on their balances.

The paper studies linear statistical inverse problems, where this recovery must account for the statistical nature of the data. It shows how stochastic gradient descent can be used as a solution method, linking inverse-problem estimation with a familiar learning algorithm.

The theoretical contribution includes consistency results and finite-sample bounds on excess risk. Consistency addresses the behavior of the estimator as data accumulate, while finite-sample bounds describe its error with a limited amount of data. The authors also modify stochastic gradient descent by using machine-learning methods to smooth its stochastic gradients, improving empirical performance.

The method is illustrated through functional linear regression, where the regression setup involves functional data. The examples include synthetic data and a classification task that predicts the main activity of bitcoin addresses from their balances. Together, the theory and examples connect a statistical guarantee for the basic approach with a practical gradient-smoothing modification and concrete applications.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes statistical guarantees for stochastic-gradient solutions to linear inverse problems and improves empirical performance through gradient smoothing.

title: Statistical Learning and Inverse Problems: A Stochastic Gradient Approach

abstract: The \FedProx~algorithm is a simple yet powerful distributed proximal point optimization method widely used for federated learning (FL) over heterogeneous data. Despite its popularity and remarkable success witnessed in practice, the theoretical understanding of FedProx is largely underinvestigated: the appealing convergence behavior of \FedProx~is so far characterized under certain non-standard and unrealistic dissimilarity assumptions of local functions, and the results are limited to smooth optimization problems. In order to remedy these deficiencies, we develop a novel local dissimilarity invariant convergence theory for \FedProx~and its minibatch stochastic extension through the lens of algorithmic stability. As a result, we contribute to derive several new and deeper insights into \FedProx~for non-convex federated optimization including: 1) convergence guarantees invariant to certain stringent local dissimilarity conditions; 2) convergence guarantees for non-smooth FL problems; and 3) linear speedup with respect to size of minibatch and number of sampled devices. Our theory for the first time reveals that local dissimilarity and smoothness are not must-have for \FedProx~to get favorable complexity bounds.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines optimization across devices whose datasets can differ substantially. FedProx is a distributed proximal optimization method used in this setting, but its theoretical explanation has relied on restrictive assumptions about how local objectives differ. Existing results also focused on smooth objectives, leaving a gap between the method's practical use and the situations covered by theory.

This paper develops a convergence analysis for FedProx and a minibatch stochastic extension through algorithmic stability. The resulting guarantees do not depend on certain stringent local dissimilarity conditions. They also cover non-smooth federated optimization problems, expanding the kinds of objectives for which favorable complexity results can be established.

For the analyzed non-convex problems, the theory additionally gives linear speedups with minibatch size and the number of sampled devices. This connects greater participation and larger batches to improved theoretical efficiency. The result is not that heterogeneity or smoothness never matters; it is that the particular dissimilarity restrictions and smoothness assumptions addressed by the paper are unnecessary for obtaining its favorable FedProx bounds.
summary.tldr: A stability-based analysis gives FedProx convergence guarantees beyond restrictive local-dissimilarity and smoothness assumptions, plus linear minibatch and device speedups.

title: On Convergence of FedProx: Local Dissimilarity Invariant Bounds, Non-smoothness and Beyond

abstract: We study the task of robust feature representations, aiming to generalize well on multiple datasets for action recognition. We build our method on Transformers for its efficacy. Although we have witnessed great progress for video action recognition in the past decade, it remains challenging yet valuable how to train a single model that can perform well across multiple datasets. Here, we propose a novel multi-dataset training paradigm, MultiTrain, with the design of two new loss terms, namely informative loss and projection loss, aiming tolearn robust representations for action recognition. In particular, the informative loss maximizes the expressiveness of the feature embedding while the projection loss for each dataset mines the intrinsic relations between classes across datasets. We verify the effectiveness of our method on five challenging datasets, Kinetics-400, Kinetics-700, Moments-in-Time, Activitynet and Something-something-v2 datasets. Extensive experimental results show that our method can consistently improve state-of-the-art performance. Code and models are released.

paragraphs: A strong action-recognition model should learn video features that remain useful across multiple datasets. Training one model to achieve this is challenging because the learning problem spans multiple collections of examples and action classes. The paper introduces MultiTrain, a Transformer-based training approach designed around this shared representation goal.

MultiTrain adds two loss terms with distinct roles. The informative loss encourages the feature embedding to be expressive. The projection loss works separately for each dataset while uncovering relationships among classes across datasets. Together, these objectives aim to make the learned features informative and connect the class information supplied by different training sources.

The authors evaluate the approach on Kinetics-400, Kinetics-700, Moments-in-Time, Activitynet, and Something-something-v2. They report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art performance in their experiments. The findings support using explicit representation objectives to make multi-dataset training effective, with the contribution centered on how a single model learns across datasets rather than merely adopting a Transformer architecture.
summary.tldr: MultiTrain combines informative and cross-dataset projection losses to improve a single Transformer’s action-recognition representations.

title: Multi-dataset Training of Transformers for Robust Action Recognition

abstract: We present a general vision transformer backbone, called as Orthogonal Transformer, in pursuit of both efficiency and effectiveness. A major challenge for vision transformer is that self-attention, as the key element in capturing long-range dependency, is very computationally expensive for dense prediction tasks (e.g., object detection). Coarse global self-attention and local self-attention are then designed to reduce the cost, but they suffer from either neglecting local correlations or hurting global modeling. We present an orthogonal self-attention mechanism to alleviate these issues. Specifically, self-attention is computed in the orthogonal space that is reversible to the spatial domain but has much lower resolution. The capabilities of learning global dependency and exploring local correlations are maintained because every orthogonal token in self-attention can attend to the entire visual tokens. Remarkably, orthogonality is realized by constructing an endogenously orthogonal matrix that is friendly to neural networks and can be optimized as arbitrary orthogonal matrices. We also introduce Positional MLP to incorporate position information for arbitrary input resolutions as well as enhance the capacity of MLP. Finally, we develop a hierarchical architecture for Orthogonal Transformer. Extensive experiments demonstrate its strong performance on a broad range of vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, instance segmentation and semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Dense vision tasks make global self-attention expensive because the model must reason over many image locations. Coarsening attention can overlook local relationships, while restricting it to local neighborhoods can weaken global modeling. Orthogonal Transformer introduces another way to reduce this cost while preserving access to both kinds of information.

The model computes attention in an orthogonal representation with much lower resolution that can be mapped back to the spatial domain. Every orthogonal token can attend to the full set of visual tokens, supporting global dependencies and local correlations. The transformation uses a matrix constructed to be orthogonal and suitable for optimization within a neural network.

The architecture also includes a Positional MLP to represent position at arbitrary input resolutions and strengthen the MLP component. These pieces are organized into a hierarchical backbone. Experiments show strong performance in classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation, supporting the usefulness of changing the space where attention operates for a broad set of vision tasks.
summary.tldr: Orthogonal Transformer computes attention in a lower-resolution reversible representation to combine efficient processing with local and global visual modeling.

title: Orthogonal Transformer: An Efficient Vision Transformer Backbone with Token Orthogonalization

abstract: 3D Garment modeling is a critical and challenging topic in the area of computer vision and graphics, with increasing attention focused on garment representation learning, garment reconstruction, and controllable garment manipulation, whereas existing methods were constrained to model garments under specific categories or with relatively simple topologies. In this paper, we propose a novel Neural Sewing Machine (NSM), a learning-based framework for structure-preserving 3D garment modeling, which is capable of learning representations for garments with diverse shapes and topologies and is successfully applied to 3D garment reconstruction and controllable manipulation. To model generic garments, we first obtain sewing pattern embedding via a unified sewing pattern encoding module, as the sewing pattern can accurately describe the intrinsic structure and the topology of the 3D garment. Then we use a 3D garment decoder to decode the sewing pattern embedding into a 3D garment using the UV-position maps with masks. To preserve the intrinsic structure of the predicted 3D garment, we introduce an inner-panel structure-preserving loss, an inter-panel structure-preserving loss, and a surface-normal loss in the learning process of our framework. We evaluate NSM on the public 3D garment dataset with sewing patterns with diverse garment shapes and categories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed NSM is capable of representing 3D garments under diverse garment shapes and topologies, realistically reconstructing 3D garments from 2D images with the preserved structure, and accurately manipulating the 3D garment categories, shapes, and topologies, outperforming the state-of-the-art methods by a clear margin.

paragraphs: Neural Sewing Machine represents 3D garments through their sewing patterns. The motivation is that a pattern describes the garment’s underlying structure and topology, allowing the representation to accommodate diverse garment forms. The framework supports both reconstructing clothing from images and controllably changing its category, shape, or topology.

A unified encoder converts the sewing pattern into an embedding. A garment decoder then turns that embedding into a 3D garment using masked UV-position maps. Training includes separate losses for preserving structure within panels and between panels, together with a surface-normal loss. These objectives explicitly connect the predicted geometry to the garment’s panel structure.

The authors evaluate the framework on a public garment dataset containing sewing patterns and varied garment categories and shapes. They report realistic image-based reconstruction, accurate controlled manipulation, and clear improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The stated results support sewing patterns as a useful representation for combining structural preservation with variation across garment types, rather than limiting modeling to a narrow category or simple topology.
summary.tldr: Neural Sewing Machine encodes sewing patterns to reconstruct and manipulate diverse 3D garments while preserving their panel structure.

title: Structure-Preserving 3D Garment Modeling with Neural Sewing Machines

abstract: Computer-aided pathology diagnosis based on the classification of Whole Slide Image (WSI) plays an important role in clinical practice, and it is often formulated as a weakly-supervised Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem. Existing methods solve this problem from either a bag classification or an instance classification perspective. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end weakly supervised knowledge distillation framework (WENO) for WSI classification, which integrates a bag classifier and an instance classifier in a knowledge distillation framework to mutually improve the performance of both classifiers. Specifically, an attention-based bag classifier is used as the teacher network, which is trained with weak bag labels, and an instance classifier is used as the student network, which is trained using the normalized attention scores obtained from the teacher network as soft pseudo labels for the instances in positive bags. An instance feature extractor is shared between the teacher and the student to further enhance the knowledge exchange between them. In addition, we propose a hard positive instance mining strategy based on the output of the student network to force the teacher network to keep mining hard positive instances. WENO is a plug-and-play framework that can be easily applied to any existing attention-based bag classification methods. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate the efficiency of WENO. Code is available at https://github.com/miccaiif/WENO.

paragraphs: WENO connects two ways of classifying whole slide pathology images: predicting a label for an entire collection of image instances, and predicting labels for individual instances. The setting is weakly supervised, meaning the available labels describe the whole collection rather than each member. The paper uses knowledge distillation to let the two classifiers help one another.

An attention-based collection classifier serves as the teacher. Its normalized attention scores provide soft training targets for instances belonging to positive collections. The instance classifier learns from these targets, and both models share an instance feature extractor. This shared component gives their learning processes another route to exchange information.

The information flow also runs back toward the teacher. Predictions from the instance classifier guide a strategy for finding difficult positive instances, encouraging the teacher to continue identifying them. WENO is designed to attach to existing attention-based collection classifiers. Experiments on five datasets support the framework’s efficiency, with the central contribution being mutual improvement through weak supervision at two levels.
summary.tldr: WENO links slide-level and instance-level classifiers so that each helps train the other using weak labels.

title: Bi-directional Weakly Supervised Knowledge Distillation for Whole Slide Image Classification

abstract: Discrimination in machine learning often arises along multiple dimensions (a.k.a. protected attributes); it is then desirable to ensure \emph{intersectional fairness}---i.e., that no subgroup is discriminated against. It is known that ensuring \emph{marginal fairness} for every dimension independently is not sufficient in general. Due to the exponential number of subgroups, however, directly measuring intersectional fairness from data is impossible. In this paper, our primary goal is to understand in detail the relationship between marginal and intersectional fairness through statistical analysis. We first identify a set of sufficient conditions under which an exact relationship can be obtained. Then, we prove bounds (easily computable through marginal fairness and other meaningful statistical quantities) in high-probability on intersectional fairness in the general case. Beyond their descriptive value, we show that these theoretical bounds can be leveraged to derive a heuristic improving the approximation and bounds of intersectional fairness by choosing, in a relevant manner, protected attributes for which we describe intersectional subgroups. Finally, we test the performance of our approximations and bounds on real and synthetic data-sets.

paragraphs: Checking fairness separately for each protected attribute does not generally establish fairness for groups defined by combinations of attributes. A system can therefore pass marginal checks while discriminating against an intersectional subgroup. Directly assessing every combination becomes difficult because the number of subgroups grows exponentially with the number of protected dimensions.

This paper studies how much intersectional fairness can be inferred from marginal fairness and additional statistical information. It identifies sufficient conditions that yield an exact relationship. For the general case, it derives high-probability bounds using quantities that are comparatively easy to compute. These results offer a way to characterize intersectional fairness without treating separate marginal checks as conclusive.

The authors also turn the bounds into a heuristic for selecting which protected attributes to combine when describing subgroups. That selection aims to improve both approximations and bounds by making the subgroup description more informative. Tests on real and synthetic datasets evaluate the resulting estimates, connecting the statistical analysis to the practical problem of assessing many overlapping groups.
summary.tldr: The paper derives conditional relationships and high-probability bounds that help estimate intersectional fairness from marginal fairness and other statistics.

title: Bounding and Approximating Intersectional Fairness through Marginal Fairness

abstract: Distributional shifts in photometry and texture have been extensively studied for unsupervised domain adaptation, but their counterparts in optical distortion have been largely neglected. In this work, we tackle the task of unsupervised domain adaptation for semantic image segmentation where unknown optical distortion exists between source and target images. To this end, we propose a distortion-aware domain adaptation (DaDA) framework that boosts the unsupervised segmentation performance. We first present a relative distortion learning (RDL) approach that is capable of modeling domain shifts in fine-grained geometric deformation based on diffeomorphic transformation. Then, we demonstrate that applying additional global affine transformations to the diffeomorphically transformed source images can further improve the segmentation adaptation. Besides, we find that our distortion-aware adaptation method helps to enhance self-supervised learning by providing higher-quality initial models and pseudo labels. To evaluate, we propose new distortion adaptation benchmarks, where rectilinear source images and fisheye target images are used for unsupervised domain adaptation. Extensive experimental results highlight the effectiveness of our approach over state-of-the-art methods under unknown relative distortion across domains. Datasets and more information are available at https://sait-fdd.github.io/.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to image regions, but transferring a model between image domains becomes difficult when their geometry differs. This paper addresses unknown optical distortion between source and target images. It highlights a gap in adaptation research: changes in lighting and texture have received much more attention than changes in how a lens bends the scene.

The proposed DaDA framework learns relative distortion through diffeomorphic transformations, allowing it to model detailed geometric deformation between domains. The authors also show that adding global affine transformations to the already deformed source images improves adaptation further. These two components address fine-grained deformation and broader geometric changes within the same framework.

The authors introduce benchmarks transferring from rectilinear source images to fisheye target images without target supervision. Experiments report advantages over leading methods under unknown relative distortion. They additionally find that distortion-aware adaptation improves the initial models and pseudo labels used for self-supervised learning. Thus, the geometric adaptation contributes both directly to segmentation and to the quality of the model-generated supervision used afterward.
summary.tldr: DaDA improves unsupervised segmentation transfer by learning geometric distortions between source and target images.

title: DaDA: Distortion-aware Domain Adaptation for Unsupervised Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Data augmentation plays a key role in modern machine learning pipelines. While numerous augmentation strategies have been studied in the context of computer vision and natural language processing, less is known for other data modalities. Our work extends the success of data augmentation to compositional data, i.e., simplex-valued data, which is of particular interest in microbiology, geochemistry, and other applications. Drawing on key principles from compositional data analysis, such as the \emph{Aitchison geometry of the simplex} and subcompositions, we define novel augmentation strategies for this data modality. Incorporating our data augmentations into standard supervised learning pipelines results in consistent performance gains across a wide range of standard benchmark datasets. In particular, we set a new state-of-the-art for key disease prediction tasks including colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, and Crohn's disease. In addition, our data augmentations enable us to define a novel contrastive learning model, which improves on previous representation learning approaches for microbiome compositional data.

paragraphs: Compositional data describe relative parts of a whole and lie on a simplex, making their structure different from ordinary unconstrained numerical features. Such data arise in microbiome analysis, geochemistry, and other applications. This paper develops augmentation methods for that setting, extending an approach widely used in vision and language to a different kind of input.

The proposed transformations draw on compositional data analysis, particularly Aitchison geometry and subcompositions. These principles guide augmentation around the structure of compositional observations. The authors incorporate the resulting methods into standard supervised learning pipelines, making augmentation the intervention rather than requiring an entirely new predictive pipeline.

Across a broad collection of benchmark datasets, the augmentations produce consistent performance gains. The authors report new state-of-the-art results for disease prediction tasks involving colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, and Crohn's disease. They also use the augmentations to build a contrastive learning model that improves on previous microbiome representation-learning approaches, showing benefits for both supervised prediction and learned representations.
summary.tldr: Augmentations designed for compositional data improve microbiome prediction and support a stronger contrastive representation-learning model.

title: Data Augmentation for Compositional Data: Advancing Predictive Models of the Microbiome

abstract: Recent advances in implicit neural representations have achieved impressive results by sampling and fusing individual points along sampling rays in the sampling space. However, due to the explosively growing sampling space, finely representing and synthesizing detailed textures remains a challenge for unbounded large-scale outdoor scenes. To alleviate the dilemma of using individual points to perceive the entire colossal space, we explore learning the surface distribution of the scene to provide structural priors and reduce the samplable space and propose a Point Diffusion implicit Function, PDF, for large-scale scene neural representation. The core of our method is a large-scale point cloud super-resolution diffusion module that enhances the sparse point cloud reconstructed from several training images into a dense point cloud as an explicit prior. Then in the rendering stage, only sampling points with prior points within the sampling radius are retained. That is, the sampling space is reduced from the unbounded space to the scene surface. Meanwhile, to fill in the background of the scene that cannot be provided by point clouds, the region sampling based on Mip-NeRF 360 is employed to model the background representation. Expensive experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method for large-scale scene novel view synthesis, which outperforms relevant state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Representing large outdoor scenes with implicit neural models requires sampling a vast spatial region. This makes detailed texture synthesis difficult because individual samples must help describe an effectively unbounded environment. PDF addresses the problem by learning where scene surfaces lie and using that structure to restrict the locations considered during rendering.

The method starts with a sparse point cloud reconstructed from several training images. A point-cloud super-resolution diffusion module turns it into a dense cloud that serves as an explicit structural prior. During rendering, a sampling point is retained only when a prior point lies within its sampling radius. This concentrates sampling around the estimated surface instead of throughout unbounded space.

Point clouds do not provide all background content, so PDF also uses region sampling based on Mip-NeRF 360 to model the background. Experiments on large-scale novel-view synthesis show effectiveness and better results than relevant state-of-the-art baselines. The approach matters because it connects an explicit estimate of scene structure with neural rendering, reducing the spatial search while separately accounting for background regions.
summary.tldr: PDF densifies a scene's point cloud with diffusion and uses it to focus neural rendering samples near surfaces.

title: PDF: Point Diffusion Implicit Function for Large-scale Scene Neural Representation

abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of smart home automation, the potential of IoT devices is vast. In this realm, rules are the main tool utilized for this automation, which are predefined conditions or triggers that establish connections between devices, enabling seamless automation of specific processes. However, one significant challenge researchers face is the lack of comprehensive datasets to explore and advance the field of smart home rule recommendations. These datasets are essential for developing and evaluating intelligent algorithms that can effectively recommend rules for automating processes while preserving the privacy of the users, as it involves personal information about users' daily lives. To bridge this gap, we present the Wyze Rule Dataset, a large-scale dataset designed specifically for smart home rule recommendation research. Wyze Rule encompasses over 1 million rules gathered from a diverse user base of 300,000 individuals from Wyze Labs, offering an extensive and varied collection of real-world data. With a focus on federated learning, our dataset is tailored to address the unique challenges of a cross-device federated learning setting in the recommendation domain, featuring a large-scale number of clients with widely heterogeneous data. To establish a benchmark for comparison and evaluation, we have meticulously implemented multiple baselines in both centralized and federated settings. Researchers can leverage these baselines to gauge the performance and effectiveness of their rule recommendation systems, driving advancements in the domain. The Wyze Rule Dataset is publicly accessible through [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/datasets/wyzelabs/RuleRecommendation)'s dataset API.

Recommending useful rules requires data about how people actually automate their homes. Such data also concerns daily routines, making user privacy relevant to the development and evaluation of recommendation systems.

The paper introduces the Wyze Rule Dataset to support this research. It contains more than one million rules from 300,000 Wyze Labs users, providing a large collection of real-world automation choices. The dataset is designed around cross-device federated learning challenges, particularly the combination of many clients and substantial differences in the data associated with different users.

The authors implement multiple centralized and federated baselines to establish shared comparison points for future recommendation methods. These baselines let researchers evaluate approaches within both settings using the same dataset resource. Public availability through the HuggingFace dataset API makes the collection accessible for further work. Its main contribution is a realistic research and benchmarking foundation for studying rule recommendation under large-scale, heterogeneous user participation.
summary.tldr: Wyze Rule provides over one million smart-home rules and centralized and federated baselines for recommendation research.

title: Wyze Rule: Federated Rule Dataset for Rule Recommendation Benchmarking

abstract: Experimental results have shown that curriculum learning, i.e., presenting simpler examples before more complex ones, can improve the efficiency of learning. Some recent theoretical results also showed that changing the sampling distribution can help neural networks learn parities, with formal results only for large learning rates and one-step arguments. Here we show a separation result in the number of training steps with standard (bounded) learning rates on a common sample distribution: if the data distribution is a mixture of sparse and dense inputs, there exists a regime in which a 2-layer ReLU neural network trained by a curriculum noisy-GD (or SGD) algorithm that uses sparse examples first, can learn parities of sufficiently large degree, while any fully connected neural network of possibly larger width or depth trained by noisy-GD on the unordered samples cannot learn without additional steps. We also provide experimental results supporting the qualitative separation beyond the specific regime of the theoretical results.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning presents simpler examples before harder ones. Although experiments have often found benefits, proving an advantage under comparable training conditions is difficult. This paper studies parity learning with data drawn from a mixture of sparse and dense inputs, comparing training schedules on a common underlying sample distribution.

The authors identify a regime in which a two-layer ReLU network can learn sufficiently high-degree parity targets by training on sparse examples first. Their curriculum algorithms use noisy gradient descent or stochastic gradient descent with bounded learning rates. The comparison shows that fully connected networks trained by noisy gradient descent on unordered samples require additional steps, even if they have greater width or depth.

The result establishes a training-step separation within the specified regime, making example order a provable source of advantage under those conditions. It extends beyond earlier one-step arguments involving large learning rates. Experiments also support a similar qualitative separation outside the exact theoretical regime, providing broader empirical evidence without extending the theorem's formal scope to every curriculum or dataset.
summary.tldr: For a specified mixed-input parity-learning regime, sparse-first curriculum training provably needs fewer steps than noisy gradient descent on unordered samples.

title: Provable Advantage of Curriculum Learning on Parity Targets with Mixed Inputs

abstract: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a crucial weakly supervised learning method applied across various domains, e.g., medical diagnosis based on whole slide images (WSIs). Recent advancements in MIL algorithms have yielded exceptional performance when the training and test data originate from the same domain, such as WSIs obtained from the same hospital. However, this paper reveals a performance deterioration of MIL models when tested on an out-of-domain test set, exemplified by WSIs sourced from a novel hospital. To address this challenge, this paper introduces the Retrieval-AugMented MIL (RAM-MIL) framework, which integrates Optimal Transport (OT) as the distance metric for nearest neighbor retrieval. The development of RAM-MIL is driven by two key insights. First, a theoretical discovery indicates that reducing the input's intrinsic dimension can minimize the approximation error in attention-based MIL. Second, previous studies highlight a link between input intrinsic dimension and the feature merging process with the retrieved data. Empirical evaluations conducted on WSI classification demonstrate that the proposed RAM-MIL framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in both in-domain scenarios, where the training and retrieval data are in the same domain, and more crucially, in out-of-domain scenarios, where the (unlabeled) retrieval data originates from a different domain. Furthermore, the use of the transportation matrix derived from OT renders the retrieval results interpretable at the instance level, in contrast to the vanilla $l_2$ distance, and allows for visualization for human experts. *Code can be found at \url{https://github.com/ralphc1212/ram-mil*.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning supports weakly supervised tasks such as classifying whole-slide medical images. This paper shows that models performing well within one domain can deteriorate when tested in another, such as a different hospital. RAM-MIL addresses this problem by adding retrieval of related data to the learning framework.

The approach uses optimal transport as the distance measure for nearest-neighbor retrieval. Its motivation connects two ideas: the authors' theoretical finding that lower intrinsic input dimension can reduce approximation error in attention-based MIL, and earlier findings relating intrinsic dimension to merging input features with retrieved data. These ideas motivate using retrieval to improve the representation supplied to the model.

Whole-slide classification experiments report state-of-the-art performance when training and retrieval data share a domain and when unlabeled retrieval data comes from another domain. Optimal transport also supplies a transportation matrix that makes retrieval correspondences interpretable at the instance level. Those correspondences can be visualized for experts, coupling the reported predictive improvements with a way to inspect the retrieved information.
summary.tldr: RAM-MIL uses optimal-transport retrieval to improve whole-slide classification across domains and expose interpretable instance-level correspondences.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Multiple Instance Learning

abstract: This paper studies the fundamental learning problem of the energy-based model (EBM). Learning the EBM can be achieved using the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), which typically involves the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, such as the Langevin dynamics. However, the noise-initialized Langevin dynamics can be challenging in practice and hard to mix. This motivates the exploration of joint training with the generator model where the generator model serves as a complementary model to bypass MCMC sampling. However, such a method can be less accurate than the MCMC and result in biased EBM learning. While the generator can also serve as an initializer model for better MCMC sampling, its learning can be biased since it only matches the EBM and has no access to empirical training examples. Such biased generator learning may limit the potential of learning the EBM. To address this issue, we present a joint learning framework that interweaves the maximum likelihood learning algorithm for both the EBM and the complementary generator model. In particular, the generator model is learned by MLE to match both the EBM and the empirical data distribution, making it a more informative initializer for MCMC sampling of EBM. Learning generator with observed examples typically requires inference of the generator posterior. To ensure accurate and efficient inference, we adopt the MCMC posterior sampling and introduce a complementary inference model to initialize such latent MCMC sampling. We show that three separate models can be seamlessly integrated into our joint framework through two (dual-) MCMC teaching, enabling effective and efficient EBM learning.

paragraphs: Training an energy-based model by maximum likelihood typically requires sampling, often through Langevin dynamics. Starting that sampling from noise can make it difficult to explore the model effectively. A generator can supply better starting points, but replacing sampling with generation can introduce bias, and a generator trained only to match the energy model misses direct guidance from observed data.

The paper proposes jointly learning the energy-based model and its complementary generator through interwoven maximum-likelihood procedures. The generator learns to match both the energy model and the empirical data distribution. This gives it a richer source of information for producing the initial states used by the energy model's sampling process.

Learning the generator from observations introduces another inference problem: determining its latent variables. The framework handles this with a second MCMC process, initialized by a separate inference model. These three models are connected through two sampling-based teaching processes, giving the method its dual-MCMC name. The authors present this integration as a way to make energy-based learning effective and efficient while addressing the generator bias they identify.
summary.tldr: Dual-MCMC teaching jointly trains an energy model, a generator, and an inference model so observed data can improve the generator used to initialize sampling.

title: Learning Energy-based Model via Dual-MCMC Teaching

abstract: The capacity to reason logically is a hallmark of human cognition. Humans excel at integrating multimodal information for locigal reasoning, as exemplified by the Visual Question Answering (VQA) task, which is a challenging multimodal task. VQA tasks and large vision-and-language models aim to tackle reasoning problems, but the accuracy, consistency and fabrication of the generated answers is hard to evaluate in the absence of a VQA dataset that can offer formal, comprehensive and systematic complex logical reasoning questions. To address this gap, we present LoRA, a novel Logical Reasoning Augmented VQA dataset that requires formal and complex description logic reasoning based on a food-and-kitchen knowledge base. Our main objective in creating LoRA is to enhance the complex and formal logical reasoning capabilities of VQA models, which are not adequately measured by existing VQA datasets. We devise strong and flexible programs to automatically generate 200,000 diverse description logic reasoning questions based on the SROIQ Description Logic, along with realistic kitchen scenes and ground truth answers. We fine-tune the latest transformer VQA models and evaluate the zero-shot performance of the state-of-the-art large vision-and-language models on LoRA. The results reveal that LoRA presents a unique challenge in logical reasoning, setting a systematic and comprehensive evaluation standard.

paragraphs: Visual question answering requires a model to connect an image with a question and produce an answer. Assessing complex logical reasoning within that process is difficult without questions whose requirements and correct answers are formally defined. This paper introduces LoRA, a dataset designed to evaluate such reasoning systematically using a food-and-kitchen knowledge base.

The authors build programs that automatically generate 200,000 diverse reasoning questions, accompanied by realistic kitchen scenes and ground-truth answers. This design ties the evaluation to explicit logical questions instead of relying solely on broadly framed image understanding tasks.

The evaluation includes fine-tuning transformer-based visual-question-answering models and testing leading large vision-and-language models without task-specific examples. The results indicate that LoRA poses a distinctive logical reasoning challenge. Its contribution is an evaluation resource aimed at measuring complex formal reasoning more comprehensively, with the longer-term objective of improving those capabilities in models that combine visual and linguistic information.
summary.tldr: LoRA pairs kitchen scenes with 200,000 formally generated questions to test complex logical reasoning in visual question answering.

title: LoRA: A Logical Reasoning Augmented Dataset for Visual Question Answering

abstract: The past few years have seen impressive progress in the development of deep generative models capable of producing high-dimensional, complex, and photo-realistic data. However, current methods for evaluating such models remain incomplete: standard likelihood-based metrics do not always apply and rarely correlate with perceptual fidelity, while sample-based metrics, such as FID, are insensitive to overfitting, i.e., inability to generalize beyond the training set. To address these limitations, we propose a new metric called the Feature Likelihood Divergence (FLD), a parametric sample-based score that uses density estimation to provide a comprehensive trichotomic evaluation accounting for novelty (i.e., different from the training samples), fidelity, and diversity of generated samples. We empirically demonstrate the ability of FLD to identify specific overfitting problem cases, where previously proposed metrics fail. We also extensively evaluate FLD on various image datasets and model classes, demonstrating its ability to match intuitions of previous metrics like FID while offering a more comprehensive evaluation of generative models.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce convincing images while failing to generalize beyond its training examples. This makes evaluation more demanding than judging appearance alone. The paper identifies complementary weaknesses in existing measures: likelihood scores are not always applicable and rarely track perceptual fidelity, while sample-based scores such as FID can miss overfitting.

Feature Likelihood Divergence, or FLD, is a parametric score computed from samples using density estimation. It evaluates three qualities together: novelty relative to the training samples, fidelity, and diversity. Including novelty makes generalization an explicit part of the assessment. This matters because realistic and varied outputs can still leave unanswered whether a model has learned to produce examples beyond those it encountered during training.

The authors demonstrate empirically that FLD detects particular overfitting cases missed by previously proposed metrics. Evaluations across image datasets and model classes also show that it agrees with intuitions captured by metrics such as FID while providing a broader assessment. The evidence supports FLD as a more comprehensive evaluation tool in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: FLD evaluates generated samples for novelty, fidelity, and diversity, detecting overfitting cases that earlier metrics miss.

title: Feature Likelihood Divergence: Evaluating the Generalization of Generative Models Using Samples

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is a pivotal form in machine learning to extend the in-domain model to the distinctive target domains where the data distributions differ. Most prior works focus on capturing the inter-domain transferability but largely overlook rich intra-domain structures, which empirically results in even worse discriminability. In this work, we introduce a novel graph SPectral Alignment (SPA) framework to tackle the tradeoff. The core of our method is briefly condensed as follows: (i)-by casting the DA problem to graph primitives, SPA composes a coarse graph alignment mechanism with a novel spectral regularizer towards aligning the domain graphs in eigenspaces; (ii)-we further develop a fine-grained message propagation module --- upon a novel neighbor-aware self-training mechanism --- in order for enhanced discriminability in the target domain. On standardized benchmarks, the extensive experiments of SPA demonstrate that its performance has surpassed the existing cutting-edge DA methods. Coupled with dense model analysis, we conclude that our approach indeed possesses superior efficacy, robustness, discriminability, and transferability. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/CrownX/SPA.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers a model to a target domain with a different data distribution. The paper argues that methods emphasizing similarity between domains can overlook relationships within each domain, empirically weakening the ability to distinguish categories. SPA aims to preserve useful internal structure while making transfer possible.

The approach represents the adaptation problem using graphs. A coarse alignment mechanism and a spectral regularizer align domain graphs in their eigenspaces, bringing graph structure into the matching process. A finer message-propagation module then uses neighbor-aware self-training to improve discrimination in the target domain. These components address alignment between domains and relationships among examples together.

Experiments on standardized benchmarks report performance beyond existing leading domain-adaptation methods. Additional model analysis supports the authors' claims of stronger robustness, discrimination, and transferability. The contribution is a graph-based way to address the tension between making domains compatible and keeping their examples distinguishable, with coarse structural alignment complemented by local propagation during target-domain learning.
summary.tldr: SPA combines spectral graph alignment with neighbor-aware self-training to improve transfer while preserving target-domain discrimination.

title: SPA: A Graph Spectral Alignment Perspective for Domain Adaptation

abstract: Automated reasoning with unstructured natural text is a key requirement for many potential applications of NLP and for developing robust AI systems. Recently, Language Models (LMs) have demonstrated complex reasoning capacities even without any finetuning. However, existing evaluation for automated reasoning assumes access to a consistent and coherent set of information over which models reason. When reasoning in the real-world, the available information is frequently inconsistent or contradictory, and therefore models need to be equipped with a strategy to resolve such conflicts when they arise. One widely-applicable way of resolving conflicts is to impose preferences over information sources (e.g., based on source credibility or information recency) and adopt the source with higher preference. In this paper, we formulate the problem of reasoning with contradictory information guided by preferences over sources as the classical problem of defeasible reasoning, and develop a dataset called BoardgameQA for measuring the reasoning capacity of LMs in this setting. BoardgameQA also incorporates reasoning with implicit background knowledge, to better reflect reasoning problems in downstream applications. We benchmark various LMs on BoardgameQA and the results reveal a significant gap in the reasoning capacity of state-of-the-art LMs on this problem, showing that reasoning with conflicting information does not surface out-of-the-box in LMs. While performance can be improved with finetuning, it nevertheless remains poor.

paragraphs: BoardgameQA evaluates reasoning when the available information contradicts itself. Many language-model reasoning tests assume that all supplied statements fit together consistently. This dataset instead asks whether models can resolve conflicts using preferences over information sources. A source might receive priority because it is more credible or more recent, giving the model a rule for deciding which information should prevail.

The authors frame this as defeasible reasoning: conclusions can be displaced by information that takes precedence. The challenge therefore involves more than deriving an answer from individual statements. A model must also handle the relationships between conflicting statements and their sources. BoardgameQA includes implicit background knowledge as well, bringing another aspect of practical reasoning into the evaluation.

Experiments with several language models reveal a substantial shortfall on these tasks. Fine-tuning improves performance, but the reported results remain poor. The findings show that the tested models' broader reasoning abilities do not automatically translate into reliable conflict resolution. The dataset provides a focused way to measure progress on that capability.
summary.tldr: BoardgameQA tests whether language models can reason through contradictions using source priorities, revealing persistent weaknesses even after fine-tuning.

title: BoardgameQA: A Dataset for Natural Language Reasoning with Contradictory Information

abstract: The Collaborative Research Cycle (CRC) is a National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) benchmarking program intended to strengthen understanding of tabular data deidentification technologies. Deidentification algorithms are vulnerable to the same bias and privacy issues that impact other data analytics and machine learning applications, and it can even amplify those issues by contaminating downstream applications. This paper summarizes four CRC contributions: theoretical work on the relationship between diverse populations and challenges for equitable deidentification; public benchmark data focused on diverse populations and challenging features; a comprehensive open source suite of evaluation metrology for deidentified datasets; and an archive of more than 450 deidentified data samples from a broad range of techniques. The initial set of evaluation results demonstrate the value of the CRC tools for investigations in this field.

paragraphs: Deidentification aims to make data less identifying, but the algorithms performing it can themselves exhibit privacy and bias problems. Those problems can also propagate into downstream analyses that use the resulting data. This paper describes a benchmarking effort designed to improve understanding of these technologies, with particular attention to diverse populations.

The Collaborative Research Cycle is a program from the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Its contributions combine theoretical work on equitable deidentification with public benchmark data containing diverse populations and challenging features. It also provides an open-source evaluation suite and an archive of more than 450 deidentified data samples produced by a broad range of techniques.

These resources connect questions about population diversity with concrete datasets, transformed outputs, and tools for evaluating them. Researchers can therefore investigate deidentification through a shared collection of materials instead of relying only on isolated examples. Initial evaluation results demonstrate the tools’ value for this research. The paper’s central contribution is this coordinated benchmarking foundation for studying privacy and equity together.
summary.tldr: The Collaborative Research Cycle supplies diverse data, evaluation tools, and deidentified samples for studying privacy and equity in deidentification.

title: Diverse Community Data for Benchmarking Data Privacy Algorithms

abstract: Turn-level dialogue evaluation models (TDEMs), using self-supervised learning (SSL) framework, have achieved state-of-the-art performance in open-domain dialogue evaluation. However, these models inevitably face two potential problems. First, they have low correlations with humans on medium coherence samples as the SSL framework often brings training data with unbalanced coherence distribution. Second, the SSL framework leads TDEM to nonuniform score distribution. There is a danger that the nonuniform score distribution will weaken the robustness of TDEM through our theoretical analysis. To tackle these problems, we propose Better Correlation and Robustness (BCR), a distribution-balanced self-supervised learning framework for TDEM. Given a dialogue dataset, BCR offers an effective training set reconstructing method to provide coherence-balanced training signals and further facilitate balanced evaluating abilities of TDEM. To get a uniform score distribution, a novel loss function is proposed, which can adjust adaptively according to the uniformity of score distribution estimated by kernel density estimation. Comprehensive experiments on 17 benchmark datasets show that vanilla BERT-base using BCR outperforms SOTA methods significantly by 11.3% on average. BCR also demonstrates strong generalization ability as it can lead multiple SOTA methods to attain better correlation and robustness.

paragraphs: Automatic dialogue evaluators score how coherently a response fits a conversation. Self-supervised training has produced strong evaluators, but the training examples can have an uneven distribution of coherence levels. The paper connects this imbalance to poor agreement with people on moderately coherent responses. Its theoretical analysis also identifies a danger that uneven output score distributions can weaken robustness.

The proposed BCR framework addresses the training examples and the resulting scores together. It reconstructs the training set to provide more balanced signals across coherence levels. It also introduces a loss that adapts to the estimated uniformity of the score distribution, using kernel density estimation to measure that distribution. These components aim to improve evaluation across the coherence range.

Across 17 benchmark datasets, a BERT-base evaluator trained with BCR reportedly exceeds state-of-the-art methods by 11.3% on average. Applying BCR to several existing leading methods also improves correlation and robustness. The findings support balancing the learning signals and output scores as a useful intervention for the evaluated dialogue models.
summary.tldr: BCR balances coherence examples and evaluator scores to improve agreement with human dialogue judgments and robustness.

title: Better Correlation and Robustness: A Distribution-Balanced Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Automatic Dialogue Evaluation

abstract: In the medical multi-modal frameworks, the alignment of cross-modality features presents a significant challenge. However, existing works have learned features that are implicitly aligned from the data, without considering the explicit relationships in the medical context. This data-reliance may lead to low generalization of the learned alignment relationships. In this work, we propose the Eye-gaze Guided Multi-modal Alignment (EGMA) framework to harness eye-gaze data for better alignment of medical visual and textual features. We explore the natural auxiliary role of radiologists' eye-gaze data in aligning medical images and text, and introduce a novel approach by using eye-gaze data, collected synchronously by radiologists during diagnostic evaluations. We conduct downstream tasks of image classification and image-text retrieval on four medical datasets, where EGMA achieved state-of-the-art performance and stronger generalization across different datasets. Additionally, we explore the impact of varying amounts of eye-gaze data on model performance, highlighting the feasibility and utility of integrating this auxiliary data into multi-modal alignment framework.

EGMA introduces radiologists’ eye-gaze recordings as an additional source of guidance for connecting medical visual and textual features.

The gaze data is collected synchronously while radiologists perform diagnostic evaluations. This gives the framework an auxiliary signal tied to the expert’s examination of the image. The approach uses that signal to guide multimodal alignment, bringing an explicit connection to medical reading behavior into the representation-learning process.

They also study how performance changes with different quantities of gaze data. Together, these results support the feasibility and usefulness of adding gaze information to medical multimodal learning. The findings concern representation quality and downstream task performance, showing how expert attention can contribute beyond image–text pairings alone.
summary.tldr: EGMA uses radiologists’ eye-gaze data to improve medical image–text alignment and generalization across datasets.

title: Eye-gaze Guided Multi-modal Alignment for Medical Representation Learning

abstract: Counterfactual reasoning is pivotal in human cognition and especially important for providing explanations and making decisions. While Judea Pearl's influential approach is theoretically elegant, its generation of a counterfactual scenario often requires too much deviation from the observed scenarios to be feasible, as we show using simple examples. To mitigate this difficulty, we propose a framework of natural counterfactuals and a method for generating counterfactuals that are more feasible with respect to the actual data distribution. Our methodology incorporates a certain amount of backtracking when needed, allowing changes in causally preceding variables to minimize deviations from realistic scenarios. Specifically, we introduce a novel optimization framework that permits but also controls the extent of backtracking with a "naturalness'' criterion. Empirical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. The code is available at https://github.com/GuangyuanHao/natural_counterfactuals.

paragraphs: Counterfactual reasoning asks what would happen under a different scenario and can support explanations and decisions. This paper argues that scenarios generated by Pearl's approach can sometimes depart too far from observed data to be feasible. The authors illustrate that concern with simple examples and propose a framework for more natural counterfactuals.

Their method allows limited backtracking: when needed, it can change variables that causally precede the variable of interest. The aim is to keep the resulting scenario closer to realistic combinations of values in the actual data distribution. Backtracking is therefore a controlled part of constructing the alternative scenario, rather than an unrestricted revision of its history.

An optimization framework governs these changes through a naturalness criterion, permitting backtracking while controlling its extent. Empirical experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to connect causal counterfactual construction with distributional feasibility, so that an explanation can account for which preceding changes are needed to make an alternative scenario more realistic.
summary.tldr: A naturalness-guided optimization framework permits controlled causal backtracking to generate more distributionally feasible counterfactuals.

title: Natural Counterfactuals With Necessary Backtracking

abstract: The Sharpe ratio is an important and widely-used risk-adjusted return in financial engineering. In modern portfolio management, one may require an m-sparse (no more than m active assets) portfolio to save managerial and financial costs. However, few existing methods can optimize the Sharpe ratio with the m-sparse constraint, due to the nonconvexity and the complexity of this constraint. We propose to convert the m-sparse fractional optimization problem into an equivalent m-sparse quadratic programming problem. The semi-algebraic property of the resulting objective function allows us to exploit the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property to develop an efficient Proximal Gradient Algorithm (PGA) that leads to a portfolio which achieves the globally optimal m-sparse Sharpe ratio under certain conditions. The convergence rates of PGA are also provided. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first proposal that achieves a globally optimal m-sparse Sharpe ratio with a theoretically-sound guarantee.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose a portfolio with a strong Sharpe ratio while holding no more than m assets. This restriction matters because managing fewer active investments can reduce managerial and financial costs. It also makes optimization difficult: the method must determine which assets to include while optimizing a risk-adjusted return expressed as a ratio.

The authors transform this fractional optimization problem into an equivalent quadratic programming problem that preserves the asset-count constraint. This equivalence provides a different mathematical route to the same objective. They then use structural properties of the transformed objective, including the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, to develop a proximal gradient algorithm and analyze its convergence rates.

Under certain conditions, the resulting portfolio attains the globally optimal Sharpe ratio among portfolios satisfying the sparsity constraint. The conditional nature of this guarantee matters: the abstract does not claim global optimality for every possible instance. The contribution is a theoretically supported route to optimizing both portfolio sparsity and risk-adjusted return together.
summary.tldr: An equivalent quadratic formulation enables a proximal gradient method with conditional global-optimality guarantees for Sharpe-ratio portfolios holding at most m assets.

title: A Globally Optimal Portfolio for m-Sparse Sharpe Ratio Maximization

abstract: Diffusion models have been widely utilized for image restoration. However, previous blind image restoration methods still need to assume the type of degradation model while leaving the parameters to be optimized, limiting their real-world applications. Therefore, we aim to tame generative diffusion prior for universal blind image restoration dubbed BIR-D, which utilizes an optimizable convolutional kernel to simulate the degradation model and dynamically update the parameters of the kernel in the diffusion steps, enabling it to achieve blind image restoration results even in various complex situations. Besides, based on mathematical reasoning, we have provided an empirical formula for the chosen of adaptive guidance scale, eliminating the need for a grid search for the optimal parameter. Experimentally, Our BIR-D has demonstrated superior practicality and versatility than off-the-shelf unsupervised methods across various tasks both on real-world and synthetic datasets, qualitatively and quantitatively. BIR-D is able to fulfill multi-guidance blind image restoration. Moreover, BIR-D can also restore images that undergo multiple and complicated degradations, demonstrating the practical applications. The code is available at https://github.com/Tusiwei/BIR-D.

paragraphs: Blind image restoration attempts to recover an image without fully knowing how it was degraded. The paper argues that earlier diffusion-based methods still assume the degradation type and only estimate its parameters. BIR-D aims to handle more varied situations by fitting a flexible degradation representation during the restoration process.

The method uses an optimizable convolutional kernel to simulate degradation and updates the kernel's parameters throughout the diffusion steps. This couples the evolving restoration with an evolving estimate of the degradation. The authors also derive mathematical reasoning for an empirical formula that selects an adaptive guidance scale, removing the need to choose that parameter through grid search.

Experiments on real and synthetic datasets report better practicality and versatility than existing unsupervised methods, supported by qualitative and quantitative comparisons. The method supports multiple guidance signals and restores images affected by multiple complicated degradations in the reported evaluations. These findings support jointly adapting a degradation kernel and diffusion guidance as a useful approach to more varied blind restoration tasks.
summary.tldr: BIR-D updates a learned degradation kernel during diffusion to restore images across varied and combined degradations.

title: Taming Generative Diffusion Prior for Universal Blind Image Restoration

abstract: Current reinforcement-learning methods are unable to directly learn policies that solve the minimum cost reach-avoid problem to minimize cumulative costs subject to the constraints of reaching the goal and avoiding unsafe states, as the structure of this new optimization problem is incompatible with current methods. Instead, a surrogate problem is solved where all objectives are combined with a weighted sum. However, this surrogate objective results in suboptimal policies that do not directly minimize the cumulative cost. In this work, we propose RC-PPO, a reinforcement-learning-based method for solving the minimum-cost reach-avoid problem by using connections to Hamilton-Jacobi reachability. Empirical results demonstrate that RC-PPO learns policies with comparable goal-reaching rates to while achieving up to 57% lower cumulative costs compared to existing methods on a suite of minimum-cost reach-avoid benchmarks on the Mujoco simulator. The project page can be found at https://oswinso.xyz/rcppo.

paragraphs: The minimum-cost reach-avoid problem asks an agent to reach a goal, avoid unsafe states, and minimize accumulated cost subject to those requirements. The paper explains that the structure of this problem is incompatible with existing reinforcement-learning methods. A common workaround combines the different objectives into a weighted sum, but that surrogate can produce policies that do not directly minimize the intended cumulative cost.

The authors propose RC-PPO to address the original problem using connections to Hamilton-Jacobi reachability. This connection provides the basis for a reinforcement-learning method organized around reaching the goal safely while minimizing cost. The distinction matters because the original formulation treats reaching and avoiding as constraints on the cost-minimization problem.

On a suite of MuJoCo minimum-cost reach-avoid benchmarks, RC-PPO learns policies with goal-reaching rates comparable to existing methods while reducing cumulative costs by up to 57%. These empirical results show an advantage in the measured cost objective without a corresponding loss in reported goal-reaching performance. The stated reduction is the largest observed improvement, rather than a uniform gain across every benchmark.
summary.tldr: RC-PPO targets minimum-cost reach-avoid directly, achieving comparable goal-reaching rates with up to 57% lower costs in MuJoCo benchmarks.

title: Solving Minimum-Cost Reach Avoid using Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Tabular data is widely utilized in a wide range of real-world applications. The challenge of few-shot learning with tabular data stands as a crucial problem in both industry and academia, due to the high cost or even impossibility of annotating additional samples. However, the inherent heterogeneity of tabular features, combined with the scarcity of labeled data, presents a significant challenge in tabular few-shot classification. In this paper, we propose a novel approach named Diffusion-based Representation with Random Distance matching (D2R2) for tabular few-shot learning. D2R2 leverages the powerful expression ability of diffusion models to extract essential semantic knowledge crucial for denoising process. This semantic knowledge proves beneficial in few-shot downstream tasks. During the training process of our designed diffusion model, we introduce a random distance matching to preserve distance information in the embeddings, thereby improving effectiveness for classification. During the classification stage, we introduce an instance-wise iterative prototype scheme to improve performance by accommodating the multimodality of embeddings and increasing clustering robustness. Our experiments reveal the significant efficacy of D2R2 across various tabular few-shot learning benchmarks, demonstrating its state-of-the-art performance in this field.

paragraphs: Classifying tabular data from only a few labeled examples is difficult because the features can describe very different kinds of information. Obtaining more labels may also be expensive or impossible. D2R2 addresses this problem by learning a representation that extracts useful information before applying it to classification with limited labels.

The method uses a diffusion model to learn semantic information needed for denoising. During this training, random distance matching encourages the learned embeddings to retain distance information, making their arrangement more useful for classification. The approach therefore combines knowledge obtained through denoising with an explicit effort to preserve relationships between examples in the representation.

At classification time, an instance-wise iterative prototype procedure accounts for embeddings that may form multiple groups and seeks to make clustering more robust. This addresses a separate challenge from representation learning: how to organize the learned features for prediction. Across the evaluated tabular few-shot benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, supporting the usefulness of combining diffusion representations, distance preservation, and adaptive prototypes.
summary.tldr: D2R2 combines diffusion representations, distance preservation, and iterative prototypes to improve tabular classification with few labeled examples.

title: D2R2: Diffusion-based Representation with Random Distance Matching for Tabular Few-shot Learning

abstract: Self-supervised heterogeneous graph learning (SHGL) has shown promising potential in diverse scenarios. However, while existing SHGL methods share a similar essential with clustering approaches, they encounter two significant limitations: (i) noise in graph structures is often introduced during the message-passing process to weaken node representations, and (ii) cluster-level information may be inadequately captured and leveraged, diminishing the performance in downstream tasks. In this paper, we address these limitations by theoretically revisiting SHGL from the spectral clustering perspective and introducing a novel framework enhanced by rank and dual consistency constraints. Specifically, our framework incorporates a rank-constrained spectral clustering method that refines the affinity matrix to exclude noise effectively. Additionally, we integrate node-level and cluster-level consistency constraints that concurrently capture invariant and clustering information to facilitate learning in downstream tasks. We theoretically demonstrate that the learned representations are divided into distinct partitions based on the number of classes and exhibit enhanced generalization ability across tasks. Experimental results affirm the superiority of our method, showcasing remarkable improvements in several downstream tasks compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Self-supervised heterogeneous graph learning builds representations from graphs without relying on task labels for its learning signal. The paper identifies two weaknesses in existing methods: message passing can introduce structural noise into node representations, and learning can make insufficient use of information about clusters. Both can weaken performance on later tasks.

The authors revisit the problem through spectral clustering and propose a framework with rank constraints and two forms of consistency. A rank-constrained clustering method refines the affinity matrix, which represents relationships between nodes, to remove noise. Node-level and cluster-level consistency constraints then capture both invariant information and the broader grouping structure.

The theoretical analysis shows that the learned representations form distinct partitions according to the number of classes and have improved generalization across tasks. Experiments report substantial gains over existing methods on several downstream tasks. Together, the results support treating noise reduction and cluster structure as connected parts of representation learning, rather than relying only on information propagated between neighboring nodes.
summary.tldr: A spectral-clustering framework improves heterogeneous graph representations through affinity refinement and node- and cluster-level consistency.

title: Revisiting Self-Supervised Heterogeneous Graph Learning from Spectral Clustering Perspective

abstract: The ability of learning useful features is one of the major advantages of neural networks. Although recent works show that neural network can operate in a neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime that does not allow feature learning, many works also demonstrate the potential for neural networks to go beyond NTK regime and perform feature learning. Recently, a line of work highlighted the feature learning capabilities of the early stages of gradient-based training. In this paper we consider another mechanism for feature learning via gradient descent through a local convergence analysis. We show that once the loss is below a certain threshold, gradient descent with a carefully regularized objective will capture ground-truth directions. We further strengthen this local convergence analysis by incorporating early-stage feature learning analysis. Our results demonstrate that feature learning not only happens at the initial gradient steps, but can also occur towards the end of training.
