paragraphs: Strategic classification studies prediction when people can change their input features, at some cost, in response to a classifier. The model therefore influences the data it will later see. Most prior analysis has focused on linear classifiers; this paper examines how nonlinear decision rules alter the interaction between a classifier and strategic users.

The authors build their analysis from decision-boundary behavior to expressive power and model-class complexity. They find that strategic responses can either increase or decrease the effective complexity of a nonlinear classifier class. The decrease can be arbitrarily large. Thus, the flexibility available before users respond does not by itself determine the flexibility of the resulting strategic system.

A further result concerns universal approximators, including neural networks: their usual universality no longer holds once the environment is strategic. Empirical demonstrations show that this can create performance gaps even with an unrestricted model class. The findings identify strategic response as a fundamental part of the learning problem, with consequences that cannot be inferred simply from a model's ordinary approximation capacity.
summary.tldr: Strategic user responses can reshape nonlinear classifier complexity and remove the universality ordinarily associated with neural networks.

title: Strategic Classification with Non-Linear Classifiers

abstract: Strategic classification, where individuals modify their features to influence machine learning (ML) decisions, presents critical fairness challenges. While group fairness in this setting has been widely studied, individual fairness remains underexplored. We analyze threshold-based classifiers and prove that deterministic thresholds violate individual fairness. Then, we investigate the possibility of using a randomized classifier to achieve individual fairness. We introduce conditions under which a randomized classifier ensures individual fairness and leverage these conditions to find an optimal and individually fair randomized classifier through a linear programming problem. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach can be extended to group fairness notions. Experiments on real-world datasets confirm that our method effectively mitigates unfairness and improves the fairness-accuracy trade-off.

While group fairness in this setting has been widely studied, individual fairness remains underexplored. We analyze threshold-based classifiers and prove that deterministic thresholds violate individual fairness. Then, we investigate the possibility of using a randomized classifier to achieve individual fairness. We introduce conditions under which a randomized classifier ensures individual fairness and leverage these conditions to find an optimal and individually fair randomized classifier through a linear programming problem. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach can be extended to group fairness notions. Experiments on real-world datasets confirm that our method effectively mitigates unfairness and improves the fairness-accuracy trade-off.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies decisions made about people who can modify their features to influence an outcome. This makes fairness depend on the interaction between a classifier and people’s responses to it. The paper focuses on individual fairness, an aspect that has received less attention in this setting than fairness between groups.

The authors analyze threshold-based classifiers and prove that deterministic thresholds violate individual fairness in the setting they study. They then investigate randomized classifiers, introducing conditions sufficient to ensure individual fairness. Those conditions become constraints in a linear programming problem, allowing them to find an optimal randomized classifier that also satisfies the fairness requirements. Randomization is thus paired with explicit mathematical conditions rather than treated as automatically fair.

The approach can also be extended to group fairness notions. Experiments on real-world datasets show reduced unfairness and an improved fairness–accuracy trade-off. The contribution connects a theoretical problem with deterministic thresholds to a constructive optimization method, showing how fairness requirements can guide classifier design when people respond strategically.
summary.tldr: The paper derives conditions for individually fair randomized classifiers and uses linear programming to optimize them in strategic classification settings.

title: Individual Fairness In Strategic Classification

abstract: Bayesian networks (BNs), represented by directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), provide a principled framework for modeling complex dependencies among random variables. As data dimensionality increases into the tens of thousands, fitting and marginalizing a full BN becomes computationally prohibitive—particularly when inference is only needed for a small subset of variables. Estimation-collapsibility addresses this challenge by ensuring that directly fitting a submodel, obtained by ignoring non-essential variables, still yields exact inference on target variables. However, current DAG-based criterion for checking estimation-collapsibility is computationally intensive, involving exhaustive vertex searches and iterative removals. Additionally, practical applications typically identify the underlying DAG only up to its Markov equivalence class, represented by a completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG). To bridge this gap, we introduce sequential $c$-simplicial sets—a novel graphical characterization of estimation-collapsibility applicable directly to CPDAGs. We further propose DSCS, a computationally efficient algorithm for verifying estimation-collapsibility within CPDAG framework that scales effectively to high-dimensional BNs. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the practicality, scalability, and efficiency of our proposed approach.

However, current DAG-based criterion for checking estimation-collapsibility is computationally intensive, involving exhaustive vertex searches and iterative removals. Additionally, practical applications typically identify the underlying DAG only up to its Markov equivalence class, represented by a completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG). To bridge this gap, we introduce sequential $c$-simplicial sets—a novel graphical characterization of estimation-collapsibility applicable directly to CPDAGs. We further propose DSCS, a computationally efficient algorithm for verifying estimation-collapsibility within CPDAG framework that scales effectively to high-dimensional BNs. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the practicality, scalability, and efficiency of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: Bayesian networks describe dependencies among variables using directed acyclic graphs. When a network contains tens of thousands of variables, fitting the full model and then removing irrelevant variables can become computationally prohibitive. Estimation-collapsibility identifies cases where fitting a smaller submodel directly still permits exact inference about the target variables.

Checking that property presents two difficulties. Existing criteria require expensive searches and repeated vertex removals. They also assume a fully directed graph, whereas practical learning often identifies only a class of graphs with equivalent dependency information. That class is represented by a completed partially directed acyclic graph, or CPDAG. The paper introduces sequential c-simplicial sets to characterize estimation-collapsibility directly in this representation.

The resulting DSCS algorithm verifies the property without requiring the problem to be expressed solely through a fully specified directed graph. Numerical experiments demonstrate efficiency and scalability in high-dimensional networks. The practical value is identifying when a smaller fitted model can preserve exact target inference, rather than assuming that dropping variables is always harmless.
summary.tldr: DSCS efficiently checks when a smaller Bayesian-network model preserves exact target inference, working directly with partially directed graph representations.

title: DSCS: Fast CPDAG-Based Verification of Collapsible Submodels in High-Dimensional Bayesian Networks

abstract: To enable egocentric contextual AI in always-on smart glasses, it is crucial to be able to keep a record of the user's interactions with the world, including during reading. In this paper, we introduce a new task of reading recognition to determine when the user is reading. We first introduce the first-of-its-kind large-scale multimodal Reading in the Wild dataset, containing 100 hours of reading and non-reading videos in diverse and realistic scenarios. We then identify three modalities (egocentric RGB, eye gaze, head pose) that can be used to solve the task, and present a flexible transformer model that performs the task using these modalities, either individually or combined. We show that these modalities are relevant and complementary to the task, and investigate how to efficiently and effectively encode each modality. Additionally, we show the usefulness of this dataset towards classifying types of reading, extending current reading understanding studies conducted in constrained settings to larger scale, diversity and realism. Code, model, and data will be public.
originalAbstract: To enable egocentric contextual AI in always-on smart glasses, it is crucial to be able to keep a record of the user's interactions with the world, including during reading. In this paper, we introduce a new task of reading recognition to determine when the user is reading. We first introduce the first-of-its-kind large-scale multimodal Reading in the Wild dataset, containing 100 hours of reading and non-reading videos in diverse and realistic scenarios. We then identify three modalities (egocentric RGB, eye gaze, head pose) that can be used to solve the task, and present a flexible transformer model that performs the task using these modalities, either individually or combined. We show that these modalities are relevant and complementary to the task, and investigate how to efficiently and effectively encode each modality. Additionally, we show the usefulness of this dataset towards classifying types of reading, extending current reading understanding studies conducted in constrained settings to larger scale, diversity and realism. Code, model, and data will be public.

The motivation is contextual AI in always-on smart glasses, which would need to recognize reading as part of a user’s interactions with the world. The task focuses on identifying the activity itself.

The authors create Reading in the Wild, a multimodal dataset containing 100 hours of reading and non-reading videos in diverse, realistic situations. They investigate three signals: first-person RGB video, eye gaze, and head pose. A flexible Transformer model can process each signal independently or combine them, allowing the contribution of different information sources to be studied.

The results show that all three modalities are relevant and provide complementary information. The paper also investigates efficient and effective ways of encoding them. Beyond detecting reading, the dataset proves useful for classifying reading types. Together, these contributions extend reading-understanding research beyond constrained settings through a larger and more varied evaluation resource and a model designed to accommodate different sensor combinations.
summary.tldr: A 100-hour dataset and flexible multimodal Transformer advance recognition of when people are reading in realistic settings.

title: Reading Recognition in the Wild

abstract: We introduce AutoPartGen, a model that generates objects composed of 3D parts in an autoregressive manner. This model can take as input an image of an object, 2D masks of the object's parts, or an existing 3D object, and generate a corresponding compositional 3D reconstruction. Our approach builds upon 3DShape2VecSet, a recent latent 3D representation with powerful geometric expressiveness. We observe that this latent space exhibits strong compositional properties, making it particularly well-suited for part-based generation tasks. Specifically, AutoPartGen generates object parts autoregressively, predicting one part at a time while conditioning on previously generated parts and additional inputs, such as 2D images, masks, or 3D objects. This process continues until the model decides that all parts have been generated, thus determining automatically the type and number of parts. The resulting parts can be seamlessly assembled into coherent objects or scenes without requiring additional optimization. We evaluate both the overall 3D generation capabilities and the part-level generation quality of AutoPartGen, demonstrating that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D part generation.

paragraphs: AutoPartGen reconstructs 3D objects as collections of parts, giving the generation process an explicit compositional structure. It can start from an object image, two-dimensional masks identifying parts, or an existing 3D object. Across these input types, the goal is to produce corresponding three-dimensional components that fit together into a coherent whole.

The model builds on 3DShape2VecSet, a learned representation of 3D geometry. The authors observe that this representation supports composition particularly well. AutoPartGen predicts one part at a time, using both the supplied input and the parts it has already generated. It also decides when generation is complete, allowing the type and number of parts to emerge during reconstruction.

The resulting components can be assembled into objects or scenes without an additional optimization stage. This matters because producing plausible individual pieces is only useful if their combined geometry also makes sense. Evaluations examine both complete-object generation and part-level quality, with the authors reporting state-of-the-art performance in 3D part generation.
summary.tldr: AutoPartGen builds coherent 3D objects one part at a time and automatically determines which parts, and how many, to generate.

title: AutoPartGen: Autoregressive 3D Part Generation and Discovery

abstract: Humans can efficiently extract knowledge and learn skills from the videos within only a few trials and errors. However, it poses a big challenge to replicate this learning process for autonomous agents, due to the complexity of visual input, the absence of action or reward signals, and the limitations of interaction steps. In this paper, we propose a novel, unsupervised, and sample-efficient framework to achieve imitation learning from videos (ILV), named Behavior Cloning from Videos via Latent Representations (BCV-LR). BCV-LR extracts action-related latent features from high-dimensional video inputs through self-supervised tasks, and then leverages a dynamics-based unsupervised objective to predict latent actions between consecutive frames. The pre-trained latent actions are fine-tuned and efficiently aligned to the real action space online (with collected interactions) for policy behavior cloning. The cloned policy in turn enriches the agent experience for further latent action finetuning, resulting in an iterative policy improvement that is highly sample-efficient. We conduct extensive experiments on a set of challenging visual tasks, including both discrete control and continuous control. BCV-LR enables effective (even expert-level on some tasks) policy performance with only a few interactions, surpassing state-of-the-art ILV baselines and reinforcement learning methods (provided with environmental rewards) in terms of sample efficiency across 24/28 tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this work for the first time demonstrates that videos can support extremely sample-efficient visual policy learning, without the need to access any other expert supervision.

paragraphs: Learning a skill from video is difficult for an autonomous agent because the footage supplies visual observations without action labels or rewards. BCV-LR addresses this by learning latent representations of actions, then connecting those representations to actions the agent can actually execute. The goal is to learn useful behavior with few environment interactions.

The framework first uses self-supervised tasks to extract action-related features from video. A dynamics-based unsupervised objective then predicts latent actions between consecutive frames. Online interactions align these pretrained latent actions with the real action space, enabling behavior cloning. The cloned policy collects additional experience, which supports further latent-action refinement and another round of policy improvement.

Across challenging discrete- and continuous-control tasks, the method achieves effective policies with few interactions, reaching expert-level performance on some tasks. It surpasses imitation-from-video baselines and reward-equipped reinforcement-learning methods in sample efficiency on 24 of 28 tasks. The result supports videos as a strong source of supervision without other expert annotations, while the learning process still uses online interaction to connect inferred actions to executable behavior.
summary.tldr: BCV-LR learns latent actions from videos and aligns them through limited interaction, improving sample efficiency over comparison methods on 24 of 28 tasks.

title: Videos are Sample-Efficient Supervisions: Behavior Cloning from Videos via Latent Representations

abstract: Liquid cooling is critical for thermal management in high-density data centers with the rising AI workloads. However, machine learning-based controllers are essential to unlock greater energy efficiency and reliability, promoting sustainability. We present LC-Opt, a Sustainable Liquid Cooling (LC) benchmark environment, for reinforcement learning (RL) control strategies in energy-efficient liquid cooling of high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Built on the baseline of a high-fidelity digital twin of Oak Ridge National Lab's Frontier Supercomputer cooling system, LC-Opt provides detailed Modelica-based end-to-end models spanning site-level cooling towers to data center cabinets and server blade groups. RL agents optimize critical thermal controls like liquid supply temperature, flow rate, and granular valve actuation at the IT cabinet level, as well as cooling tower (CT) setpoints through a Gymnasium interface, with dynamic changes in workloads. This environment creates a multi-objective real-time optimization challenge balancing local thermal regulation and global energy efficiency, and also supports additional components like a heat recovery unit (HRU). We benchmark centralized and decentralized multi-agent RL approaches, demonstrate policy distillation into decision and regression trees for interpretable control, and explore LLM-based methods that explain control actions in natural language through an agentic mesh architecture designed to foster user trust and simplify system management. LC-Opt democratizes access to detailed, customizable liquid cooling models, enabling the ML community, operators, and vendors to develop sustainable data center liquid cooling control solutions.

paragraphs: Liquid cooling control must keep computing equipment within suitable thermal conditions while limiting energy use across the wider cooling system. LC-Opt provides a benchmark for studying that coupled problem under changing workloads. It builds on a high-fidelity digital twin of the Frontier supercomputer’s cooling infrastructure, covering equipment from site cooling towers to server blade groups.

The environment uses Modelica models and exposes controls through a Gymnasium interface. Reinforcement-learning agents can adjust supply temperature, liquid flow, cabinet-level valves, and cooling-tower setpoints. Because actions affect both local temperatures and overall energy consumption, the task involves multiple objectives. The environment also supports additional components, including a heat recovery unit.

The paper benchmarks centralized and decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning. It also demonstrates transferring learned policies into decision and regression trees for interpretable control, and explores language-model explanations of control actions through an agentic mesh architecture. Its main contribution is a detailed, customizable evaluation setting that brings thermal control, energy optimization, and operator-facing interpretability into the same research workflow.
summary.tldr: LC-Opt benchmarks liquid-cooling controllers using a detailed digital twin that connects equipment temperatures, system energy use, and interpretable control.

title: LC-Opt: Benchmarking Reinforcement Learning and Agentic AI for End-to-End Liquid Cooling Optimization in Data Centers

abstract: We consider the transfer learning scenario, where the learner does not have access to the source domain directly, but rather operates on the basis of hypotheses induced from it – the Hypothesis Transfer Learning (HTL) problem. Particularly, we conduct a theoretical analysis of HTL by considering the algorithmic stability of a class of HTL algorithms based on Regularized Least Squares with biased regularization. We show that the relatedness of source and target domains accelerates the convergence of the Leave-One-Out error to the generalization error, thus enabling the use of the Leave-One-Out error to find the optimal transfer parameters, even in the presence of a small training set. In case of unrelated domains we also suggest a theoretically principled way to prevent negative transfer, so that in the limit we recover the performance of the algorithm not using any knowledge from the source domain.

paragraphs: Hypothesis transfer learning uses models learned in a source domain when the source data themselves are unavailable. The paper analyzes a class of these methods based on regularized least squares with biased regularization. Its theoretical tool is algorithmic stability, used to understand how transfer affects the relationship between estimated and actual predictive error.

The authors show that related source and target domains accelerate convergence of leave-one-out error to generalization error. This supports using leave-one-out error to select transfer parameters, even when the target training set is small. The benefit is conditional on domain relatedness, linking the usefulness of source knowledge to reliable parameter selection.

The paper also addresses unrelated domains, where transfer can harm performance. It proposes a theoretically principled way to prevent negative transfer such that, in the limit, performance returns to that of the algorithm using no source knowledge. The analysis thus covers both exploiting helpful prior models and limiting the effects of unhelpful ones.
summary.tldr: A stability analysis explains transfer-parameter selection for related domains and gives an asymptotic safeguard against negative transfer from unrelated ones.

title: Stability and Hypothesis Transfer Learning

abstract: This paper introduces the Deep Recurrent Attentive Writer (DRAW) architecture for image generation with neural networks. DRAW networks combine a novel spatial attention mechanism that mimics the foveation of the human eye, with a sequential variational auto-encoding framework that allows for the iterative construction of complex images. The system substantially improves on the state of the art for generative models on MNIST, and, when trained on the Street View House Numbers dataset, it is able to generate images that are indistinguishable from real data with the naked eye.

The system substantially improves on the state of the art for generative models on MNIST, and, when trained on the Street View House Numbers dataset, it is able to generate images that are indistinguishable from real data with the naked eye.

paragraphs: DRAW is a neural-network architecture that generates images through a sequence of construction steps. Its name expands to Deep Recurrent Attentive Writer. The central idea is to combine repeated image construction with spatial attention, allowing the generation process to focus on selected regions as an image develops.

The attention mechanism is inspired by the eye's ability to concentrate visual attention in a localized area. DRAW combines this mechanism with a sequential variational auto-encoding framework. These components give the model a way to construct complex images iteratively, making spatial focus and sequential generation parts of the same architecture.

The paper reports a substantial improvement over previous generative-model results on MNIST. It also reports that, after training on Street View House Numbers, DRAW produces images that look indistinguishable from real examples to the naked eye. The latter is a claim about visual appearance, while the MNIST result concerns comparative generative performance. Together, the findings support the usefulness of combining attention with iterative image generation.
summary.tldr: DRAW combines spatial attention and sequential variational auto-encoding to construct images iteratively, with strong reported results on handwritten and street-view digits.

title: DRAW: A Recurrent Neural Network For Image Generation

abstract: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Descent (DCD) is one of the most efficient ways to solve the family of L2-regularized empirical risk minimization problems, including linear SVM, logistic regression, and many others. The vanilla implementation of DCD is quite slow; however, by maintaining primal variables while updating dual variables, the time complexity of DCD can be significantly reduced. Such a strategy forms the core algorithm in the widely-used LIBLINEAR package. In this paper, we parallelize the DCD algorithms in LIBLINEAR. In recent research, several synchronized parallel DCD algorithms have been proposed, however, they fail to achieve good speedup in the shared memory multi-core setting. In this paper, we propose a family of parallel asynchronous stochastic dual coordinate descent algorithms (PASSCoDe). Each thread repeatedly selects a random dual variable and conducts coordinate updates using the primal variables that are stored in the shared memory. We analyze the convergence properties of DCD when different locking/atomic mechanisms are applied. For implementation with atomic operations, we show linear convergence under mild conditions. For implementation without any atomic operations or locking, we present a novel error analysis for PASSCoDe under the multi-core environment, showing that the converged solution is the exact solution for a primal problem with a perturbed regularizer. Experimental results show that our methods are much faster than previous parallel coordinate descent solvers.

paragraphs: Dual coordinate descent efficiently solves L2-regularized learning problems such as linear SVMs and logistic regression. Its practical implementation becomes faster by maintaining primal variables while updating dual variables, a strategy used in LIBLINEAR. This paper parallelizes that approach for shared-memory multicore machines, where synchronized alternatives have struggled to obtain good speedups.

PASSCoDe lets each thread repeatedly select a random dual coordinate and update it using shared primal variables. The authors analyze how different locking and atomic-operation choices affect convergence. With atomic operations, they establish linear convergence under mild conditions, providing a theoretical guarantee for a particular way of coordinating shared updates.

For an implementation with neither locking nor atomic operations, the analysis characterizes the converged answer as the exact solution of a primal problem with a perturbed regularizer. This specifies how the result relates to the original optimization objective. Experiments show substantially faster performance than previous parallel coordinate-descent solvers, connecting the reduced coordination requirements to practical speed while distinguishing the guarantees of the different implementations.
summary.tldr: PASSCoDe accelerates dual coordinate descent through asynchronous shared-memory updates with guarantees that depend on synchronization choices.

title: PASSCoDe: Parallel ASynchronous Stochastic dual Co-ordinate Descent

abstract: While the authors of Batch Normalization (BN) identify and address an important problem involved in training deep networks– \textitInternal Covariate Shift– the current solution has certain drawbacks. For instance, BN depends on batch statistics for layerwise input normalization during training which makes the estimates of mean and standard deviation of input (distribution) to hidden layers inaccurate due to shifting parameter values (especially during initial training epochs). Another fundamental problem with BN is that it cannot be used with batch-size 1 during training. We address these drawbacks of BN by proposing a non-adaptive normalization technique for removing covariate shift, that we call \textitNormalization Propagation. Our approach does not depend on batch statistics, but rather uses a data-independent parametric estimate of mean and standard-deviation in every layer thus being computationally faster compared with BN. We exploit the observation that the pre-activation before Rectified Linear Units follow Gaussian distribution in deep networks, and that once the first and second order statistics of any given dataset are normalized, we can forward propagate this normalization without the need for recalculating the approximate statistics for hidden layers.

paragraphs: This paper proposes Normalization Propagation as a way to normalize hidden-layer inputs without relying on batch statistics. The authors motivate it through difficulties they identify in Batch Normalization: changing parameters can make estimates of layer-input means and standard deviations inaccurate, especially early in training, and batch-size-one training is problematic.

Their method instead uses data-independent parametric estimates of each layer’s mean and standard deviation. It builds on the observation that inputs to rectified linear units follow a Gaussian distribution in deep networks. Once the dataset’s first- and second-order statistics have been normalized, the approach propagates that normalization through the network using the proposed parametric treatment.

The intended benefit is avoiding repeated estimation of approximate statistics for hidden layers. The authors describe the resulting method as non-adaptive and computationally faster than Batch Normalization. Its contribution is a specific alternative mechanism for normalization, grounded in the stated distributional observation, that addresses dependence on training batches while carrying normalization forward through successive layers of the network.
summary.tldr: Normalization Propagation uses parametric layer statistics to carry normalization through a network without batch-dependent estimates.

title: Normalization Propagation: A Parametric Technique for Removing Internal Covariate Shift in Deep Networks

abstract: Finite-sum optimization problems are ubiquitous in machine learning, and are commonly solved using first-order methods which rely on gradient computations. Recently, there has been growing interest in second-order methods, which rely on both gradients and Hessians. In principle, second-order methods can require much fewer iterations than first-order methods, and hold the promise for more efficient algorithms. Although computing and manipulating Hessians is prohibitive for high-dimensional problems in general, the Hessians of individual functions in finite-sum problems can often be efficiently computed, e.g. because they possess a low-rank structure. Can second-order information indeed be used to solve such problems more efficiently? In this paper, we provide evidence that the answer – perhaps surprisingly – is negative, at least in terms of worst-case guarantees. However, we also discuss what additional assumptions and algorithmic approaches might potentially circumvent this negative result.

However, we also discuss what additional assumptions and algorithmic approaches might potentially circumvent this negative result.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning objectives are sums of individual functions. First-order optimization methods use gradients, while second-order methods also use Hessians to describe curvature. Because curvature can reduce the number of iterations needed in principle, second-order information offers a possible route to more efficient optimization of these finite-sum problems.

Although full Hessian computations can be expensive in high dimensions, individual component Hessians may be much easier to compute or manipulate, for example when they have low-rank structure. The paper asks whether this apparent computational opportunity translates into better guarantees. It provides evidence that second-order information does not improve efficiency in the worst-case sense considered.

The negative conclusion is explicitly about worst-case guarantees, so it does not establish that curvature information is never useful. The authors also discuss additional assumptions and algorithmic approaches that might circumvent the result. The contribution clarifies a boundary between the promise of fewer iterations and guaranteed overall efficiency, while identifying the possibility of stronger results under further structure or different approaches.
summary.tldr: The paper gives worst-case evidence against an efficiency advantage from second-order information in finite-sum optimization while discussing possible ways around the result.

title: Oracle Complexity of Second-Order Methods for Finite-Sum Problems

abstract: We revisit semi-supervised learning on hypergraphs. Same as previous approaches, our method uses a convex program whose objective function is not everywhere differentiable. We exploit the non-uniqueness of the optimal solutions, and consider confidence intervals which give the exact ranges that unlabeled vertices take in any optimal solution. Moreover, we give a much simpler approach for solving the convex program based on the subgradient method. Our experiments on real-world datasets confirm that our confidence interval approach on hypergraphs outperforms existing methods, and our sub-gradient method gives faster running times when the number of vertices is much larger than the number of edges.

We exploit the non-uniqueness of the optimal solutions, and consider confidence intervals which give the exact ranges that unlabeled vertices take in any optimal solution. Moreover, we give a much simpler approach for solving the convex program based on the subgradient method. Our experiments on real-world datasets confirm that our confidence interval approach on hypergraphs outperforms existing methods, and our sub-gradient method gives faster running times when the number of vertices is much larger than the number of edges.

paragraphs: The paper revisits semi-supervised learning on hypergraphs, where some vertices are labeled and the remaining vertices must be inferred. Its formulation uses a convex objective that is not differentiable everywhere. An important feature of this optimization problem is that more than one solution may achieve the optimal value.

The authors use that non-uniqueness to construct confidence intervals for unlabeled vertices. Each interval gives the exact range of values that a vertex can take across all optimal solutions. These intervals describe ambiguity within the optimization problem itself, making variation among equally optimal answers part of the learning method.

The paper also presents a simpler solver based on the subgradient method, which accommodates the objective's lack of differentiability. Experiments on real-world datasets show that the confidence-interval approach outperforms existing methods. The solver runs faster when vertices greatly outnumber edges. The two contributions address different aspects of the same problem: interpreting multiple optimal answers and computing solutions efficiently in the stated graph-size regime.
summary.tldr: Exact ranges across optimal hypergraph solutions improve the reported learning results, while a simpler subgradient solver accelerates vertex-heavy cases.

title: Re-revisiting Learning on Hypergraphs: Confidence Interval and Subgradient Method

abstract: Standard methods for generating adversarial examples for neural networks do not consistently fool neural network classifiers in the physical world due to a combination of viewpoint shifts, camera noise, and other natural transformations, limiting their relevance to real-world systems. We demonstrate the existence of robust 3D adversarial objects, and we present the first algorithm for synthesizing examples that are adversarial over a chosen distribution of transformations. We synthesize two-dimensional adversarial images that are robust to noise, distortion, and affine transformation. We apply our algorithm to complex three-dimensional objects, using 3D-printing to manufacture the first physical adversarial objects. Our results demonstrate the existence of 3D adversarial objects in the physical world.

We demonstrate the existence of robust 3D adversarial objects, and we present the first algorithm for synthesizing examples that are adversarial over a chosen distribution of transformations. We synthesize two-dimensional adversarial images that are robust to noise, distortion, and affine transformation. We apply our algorithm to complex three-dimensional objects, using 3D-printing to manufacture the first physical adversarial objects. Our results demonstrate the existence of 3D adversarial objects in the physical world.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples produced by standard methods do not consistently fool classifiers after physical-world changes such as shifts in viewpoint or camera noise. This paper addresses that fragility by developing an algorithm to synthesize examples that remain adversarial across a chosen distribution of transformations. Robustness to those transformations becomes part of the generation objective.

The authors first synthesize two-dimensional adversarial images that withstand noise, distortion, and affine transformations. They then apply the algorithm to complex three-dimensional objects and manufacture physical examples using 3D printing. This carries the approach from transformed images into objects that can exist outside a purely digital image-processing pipeline.

The results demonstrate the existence of physical three-dimensional adversarial objects. The chosen transformation distribution is central to the claim: the method targets adversarial behavior across that distribution, rather than asserting success under every possible viewing condition. The contribution shows that natural transformations need not destroy an adversarial example when robustness to those changes is explicitly incorporated into its synthesis.
summary.tldr: Optimizing adversarial examples across a chosen transformation distribution produces robust images and physical 3D-printed adversarial objects.

title: Synthesizing Robust Adversarial Examples

abstract: An important class of non-convex objectives that has wide applications in machine learning consists of a sum of $n$ smooth functions and a non-smooth convex function. Tremendous studies have been devoted to conquering these problems by leveraging one of the two types of variance reduction techniques, i.e., SVRG-type that computes a full gradient occasionally and SAGA-type that maintains $n$ stochastic gradients at every iteration. In practice, SVRG-type is preferred to SAGA-type due to its potentially less memory costs. An interesting question that has been largely ignored is how to improve the complexity of variance reduction methods for problems with a large condition number that measures the degree to which the objective is close to a convex function. In this paper, we present a simple but non-trivial boosting of a state-of-the-art SVRG-type method for convex problems (namely Katyusha) to enjoy an improved complexity for solving non-convex problems with a large condition number (that is close to a convex function). To the best of our knowledge, its complexity has the best dependence on $n$ and the degree of non-convexity, and also matches that of a recent SAGA-type accelerated stochastic algorithm for a constrained non-convex smooth optimization problem.
originalAbstract: An important class of non-convex objectives that has wide applications in machine learning consists of a sum of $n$ smooth functions and a non-smooth convex function. Tremendous studies have been devoted to conquering these problems by leveraging one of the two types of variance reduction techniques, i.e., SVRG-type that computes a full gradient occasionally and SAGA-type that maintains $n$ stochastic gradients at every iteration. In practice, SVRG-type is preferred to SAGA-type due to its potentially less memory costs. An interesting question that has been largely ignored is how to improve the complexity of variance reduction methods for problems with a large condition number that measures the degree to which the objective is close to a convex function. In this paper, we present a simple but non-trivial boosting of a state-of-the-art SVRG-type method for convex problems (namely Katyusha) to enjoy an improved complexity for solving non-convex problems with a large condition number (that is close to a convex function). To the best of our knowledge, its complexity has the best dependence on $n$ and the degree of non-convexity, and also matches that of a recent SAGA-type accelerated stochastic algorithm for a constrained non-convex smooth optimization problem.

paragraphs: The paper considers objectives made from a sum of smooth functions plus a convex term that may be nonsmooth. The complete objective can still be nonconvex. Existing variance-reduction methods address these problems either by occasionally computing a full gradient or by keeping a collection of individual stochastic gradients in memory.

Katalyst builds on Katyusha, an SVRG-type method originally developed for convex optimization. Its target is the regime where the nonconvex objective is close to convex, expressed through a large condition number in the paper's formulation. The proposed adaptation improves the complexity of solving these problems while retaining the SVRG-type approach, which can require less memory than SAGA-type methods.

The authors state that, to their knowledge, the resulting complexity has the best dependence on both the number of component functions and the degree of nonconvexity. It also matches a recent accelerated SAGA-type result for a constrained smooth problem. The significance is a sharper computational guarantee in this particular near-convex regime, achieved through an adaptation of an existing convex optimizer.
summary.tldr: Katalyst adapts convex Katyusha to improve optimization complexity for nonconvex objectives that are close to convex.

title: Katalyst: Boosting Convex Katayusha for Non-Convex Problems with a Large Condition Number

abstract: Hypergraphs are used in machine learning to model higher-order relationships in data. While spectral methods for graphs are well-established, spectral theory for hypergraphs remains an active area of research. In this paper, we use random walks to develop a spectral theory for hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights: hypergraphs where every vertex v has a weight $\gamma_e(v)$ for each incident hyperedge e that describes the contribution of v to the hyperedge e. We derive a random walk-based hypergraph Laplacian, and bound the mixing time of random walks on such hypergraphs. Moreover, we give conditions under which random walks on such hypergraphs are equivalent to random walks on graphs. As a corollary, we show that current machine learning methods that rely on Laplacians derived from random walks on hypergraphs with edge-independent vertex weights do not utilize higher-order relationships in the data. Finally, we demonstrate the advantages of hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights on ranking applications using real-world datasets.

This paper studies hypergraphs in which a vertex can have a different weight in each hyperedge containing it. Those weights express how much the vertex contributes to each particular group relationship.

The authors use random walks to build a spectral theory for this setting. They derive a hypergraph Laplacian and bound the time required for the walks to mix. They also identify conditions under which these hypergraph walks are equivalent to walks on ordinary graphs, clarifying when a seemingly richer representation changes the underlying computation.

A consequence is that existing methods using random-walk Laplacians with edge-independent vertex weights do not exploit higher-order relationships. This conclusion concerns that specific class of methods. Experiments on real-world ranking applications demonstrate advantages of edge-dependent weights. The work therefore combines mathematical tools for richer hypergraph models with a diagnosis of when hypergraph-based methods effectively reduce to graph-based ones.
summary.tldr: Edge-dependent vertex weights support richer hypergraph random walks, while the analysis identifies cases where hypergraph methods reduce to ordinary graph walks.

title: Random Walks on Hypergraphs with Edge-Dependent Vertex Weights

abstract: We study the fundamental problem of learning an unknown, smooth probability function via point-wise Bernoulli tests. We provide a scalable algorithm for efficiently solving this problem with rigorous guarantees. In particular, we prove the convergence rate of our posterior update rule to the true probability function in L2-norm. Moreover, we allow the Bernoulli tests to depend on contextual features, and provide a modified inference engine with provable guarantees for this novel setting. Numerical results show that the empirical convergence rates match the theory, and illustrate the superiority of our approach in handling contextual features over the state-of-the-art.

Numerical results show that the empirical convergence rates match the theory, and illustrate the superiority of our approach in handling contextual features over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn an unknown smooth probability function when each observation is only a Bernoulli outcome at a selected point. Such a test supplies a binary result rather than the probability itself. The learning problem is to recover the underlying function from these noisy, pointwise observations.

The authors provide a scalable algorithm and analyze its posterior update rule. They prove a convergence rate toward the true probability function in L2 norm, which measures squared error across the function's domain. This gives a quantitative account of how estimation error decreases, connecting the inference procedure to a rigorous recovery guarantee.

The framework also allows test outcomes to depend on contextual features, and a modified inference engine comes with guarantees for that setting. Numerical experiments show convergence rates consistent with the theory and better handling of contextual features than the compared state-of-the-art approach. The contribution therefore extends beyond estimating a single smooth probability relationship: it also treats additional context as part of the inference problem and analyzes that extension.
summary.tldr: A scalable method learns smooth probability functions from binary tests, with convergence guarantees and an extension for contextual features.

title: Efficient learning of smooth probability functions from Bernoulli tests with guarantees

abstract: Machine learning (ML) systems often encounter Out-of-Distribution (OoD) errors when dealing with testing data coming from a distribution different from training data. It becomes important for ML systems in critical applications to accurately quantify its predictive uncertainty and screen out these anomalous inputs. However, existing OoD detection approaches are prone to errors and even sometimes assign higher likelihoods to OoD samples. Unlike standard learning tasks, there is currently no well established guiding principle for designing OoD detection architectures that can accurately quantify uncertainty. To address these problems, we first seek to identify guiding principles for designing uncertainty-aware architectures, by proposing Neural Architecture Distribution Search (NADS). NADS searches for a distribution of architectures that perform well on a given task, allowing us to identify common building blocks among all uncertainty-aware architectures. With this formulation, we are able to optimize a stochastic OoD detection objective and construct an ensemble of models to perform OoD detection. We perform multiple OoD detection experiments and observe that our NADS performs favorably, with up to 57% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods among 15 different testing configurations.

This paper investigates architecture design as a way to improve out-of-distribution detection.

That figure is the largest reported improvement among the configurations. The broader contribution is a search framework that connects architectural choices, ensemble construction, and uncertainty-oriented objectives in the same design process.
summary.tldr: NADS searches distributions of architectures to build uncertainty-aware ensembles, reporting improved out-of-distribution detection across multiple testing configurations.

title: NADS: Neural Architecture Distribution Search for Uncertainty Awareness

abstract: We study the problem of high-dimensional robust mean estimation in the presence of a constant fraction of adversarial outliers. A recent line of work has provided sophisticated polynomial-time algorithms for this problem with dimension-independent error guarantees for a range of natural distribution families. In this work, we show that a natural non-convex formulation of the problem can be solved directly by gradient descent. Our approach leverages a novel structural lemma, roughly showing that any approximate stationary point of our non-convex objective gives a near-optimal solution to the underlying robust estimation task. Our work establishes an intriguing connection between algorithmic high-dimensional robust statistics and non-convex optimization, which may have broader applications to other robust estimation tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a high-dimensional mean when a constant fraction of the observations are adversarial outliers. Earlier work had developed sophisticated polynomial-time algorithms with error guarantees independent of dimension for several natural distribution families. The question here is whether a more direct optimization approach can address this robust estimation problem.

The authors show that gradient descent can solve a natural nonconvex formulation. Their central structural result says, roughly, that any approximate stationary point of the objective yields a near-optimal robust estimate. A stationary point is a place where the optimization has little local direction for improvement, so connecting such points to estimation quality is crucial.

This connection explains why reaching approximate stationarity can be enough for the underlying statistical task in the analyzed formulation. It provides a bridge between high-dimensional robust statistics and nonconvex optimization, with gradient descent serving as the algorithmic link. The authors suggest that the connection may extend to other robust estimation problems, while presenting that broader applicability as a possibility.
summary.tldr: A structural result makes gradient descent sufficient to obtain near-optimal robust mean estimates from a natural nonconvex formulation.

title: High-dimensional Robust Mean Estimation via Gradient Descent

abstract: Robust optimization has been widely used in nowadays data science, especially in adversarial training. However, little research has been done to quantify how robust optimization changes the optimizers and the prediction losses comparing to standard training. In this paper, inspired by the influence function in robust statistics, we introduce the Adversarial Influence Function (AIF) as a tool to investigate the solution produced by robust optimization. The proposed AIF enjoys a closed-form and can be calculated efficiently. To illustrate the usage of AIF, we apply it to study model sensitivity — a quantity defined to capture the change of prediction losses on the natural data after implementing robust optimization. We use AIF to analyze how model complexity and randomized smoothing affect the model sensitivity with respect to specific models. We further derive AIF for kernel regressions, with a particular application to neural tangent kernels, and experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed AIF. Lastly, the theories of AIF will be extended to distributional robust optimization.

This paper asks how the resulting optimizer and prediction losses differ from those produced by standard training. Its contribution is an analytical tool for examining changes caused by robust optimization, with conclusions tied to the models analyzed.
summary.tldr: Adversarial Influence Functions efficiently characterize how robust optimization changes model solutions and prediction losses on natural data.

title: Interpreting Robust Optimization via Adversarial Influence Functions

abstract: We give a row sampling algorithm for the quantile loss function with sample complexity nearly linear in the dimensionality of the data, improving upon the previous best algorithm whose sampling complexity has at least cubic dependence on the dimensionality. Based upon our row sampling algorithm, we give the fastest known algorithm for quantile regression and a graph sparsification algorithm for balanced directed graphs. Our main technical contribution is to show that Lewis weights sampling, which has been used in row sampling algorithms for $\ell_p$ norms, can also be applied in row sampling algorithms for a variety of loss functions. We complement our theoretical results by experiments to demonstrate the practicality of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper develops a row-sampling algorithm for the quantile loss function. Row sampling reduces the data used in a computation by selecting a subset of rows, so the number of required samples is central to its usefulness. The proposed method needs a sample count nearly linear in data dimensionality, improving on a previous best bound with at least cubic dependence.

The main technical contribution extends the use of Lewis weights sampling. This sampling tool had been used for problems involving lp norms; the authors show that it also applies to a variety of loss functions. That extension supplies the foundation for their improved quantile-loss sampling result.

Using the sampling method, the paper derives what it reports as the fastest known quantile regression algorithm and also a graph sparsification algorithm for balanced directed graphs. Experiments complement the theory by demonstrating practicality. The contribution combines a sharper dimensional dependence with applications beyond quantile regression, showing that the sampling technique has a broader reach.
summary.tldr: Extending Lewis weights sampling to quantile loss yields nearly linear sample complexity in dimensionality and faster quantile regression.

title: Nearly Linear Row Sampling Algorithm for Quantile Regression

abstract: Reinforcement learning from large-scale offline datasets provides us with the ability to learn policies without potentially unsafe or impractical exploration. Significant progress has been made in the past few years in dealing with the challenge of correcting for differing behavior between the data collection and learned policies. However, little attention has been paid to potentially changing dynamics when transferring a policy to the online setting, where performance can be up to 90% reduced for existing methods. In this paper we address this problem with Augmented World Models (AugWM). We augment a learned dynamics model with simple transformations that seek to capture potential changes in physical properties of the robot, leading to more robust policies. We not only train our policy in this new setting, but also provide it with the sampled augmentation as a context, allowing it to adapt to changes in the environment. At test time we learn the context in a self-supervised fashion by approximating the augmentation which corresponds to the new environment. We rigorously evaluate our approach on over 100 different changed dynamics settings, and show that this simple approach can significantly improve the zero-shot generalization of a recent state-of-the-art baseline, often achieving successful policies where the baseline fails.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from previously collected data, avoiding potentially unsafe or impractical exploration. But a policy can encounter different physical dynamics when deployed. The paper highlights this transfer problem: existing methods can lose up to 90% of their performance when the environment’s dynamics change, even though training addressed differences between the data-collection policy and the learned policy.

Augmented World Models introduces simple transformations of a learned dynamics model to represent possible changes in a robot’s physical properties. The policy trains with these variations and receives the sampled transformation as context. This gives it information about which version of the dynamics it is currently facing, allowing its behavior to depend on that variation.

The approach often produces successful policies in settings where that baseline fails.
summary.tldr: Augmenting a learned world model and conditioning policies on those changes improves transfer to unfamiliar dynamics from a single offline environment.

title: Augmented World Models Facilitate Zero-Shot Dynamics Generalization From a Single Offline Environment

abstract: We give the first single-pass streaming algorithm for Column Subset Selection with respect to the entrywise $\ell_p$-norm with $1 \leq p < 2$. We study the $\ell_p$ norm loss since it is often considered more robust to noise than the standard Frobenius norm. Given an input matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$ ($n \gg d$), our algorithm achieves a multiplicative $k^{\frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{2}}\poly(\log nd)$-approximation to the error with respect to the \textit{best possible column subset} of size $k$. Furthermore, the space complexity of the streaming algorithm is optimal up to a logarithmic factor. Our streaming algorithm also extends naturally to a 1-round distributed protocol with nearly optimal communication cost. A key ingredient in our algorithms is a reduction to column subset selection in the $\ell_{p,2}$-norm, which corresponds to the $p$-norm of the vector of Euclidean norms of each of the columns of $A$. This enables us to leverage strong coreset constructions for the Euclidean norm, which previously had not been applied in this context. We also give the first provable guarantees for greedy column subset selection in the $\ell_{1, 2}$ norm, which can be used as an alternative, practical subroutine in our algorithms. Finally, we show that our algorithms give significant practical advantages on real-world data analysis tasks.

paragraphs: Column subset selection represents a matrix using a selection of its actual columns. This paper studies entrywise p-norm error for p from one up to, but excluding, two, a loss often regarded as more robust to noise than Frobenius error. The setting has many more columns than rows.

The authors provide a single-pass streaming algorithm with memory optimal up to a logarithmic factor. Its approximation factor relative to the best size-k column subset is k raised to 1/p−1/2, multiplied by polylogarithmic factors in matrix dimensions. The method also extends to a one-round distributed protocol with nearly optimal communication.

This enables existing Euclidean coreset constructions to serve the new objective. The paper also gives guarantees for greedy selection under the corresponding mixed norm with p equal to one, offering a practical subroutine. Experiments report significant advantages on real-world data-analysis tasks.
summary.tldr: Robust column selection gains single-pass and one-round distributed algorithms with approximation guarantees and nearly optimal resource use.

title: Streaming and Distributed Algorithms for Robust Column Subset Selection

abstract: We consider the problem of explainable $k$-medians and $k$-means introduced by Dasgupta, Frost, Moshkovitz, and Rashtchian (ICML 2020). In this problem, our goal is to find a \emph{threshold decision tree} that partitions data into $k$ clusters and minimizes the $k$-medians or $k$-means objective. The obtained clustering is easy to interpret because every decision node of a threshold tree splits data based on a single feature into two groups. We propose a new algorithm for this problem which is $\tilde O(\log k)$ competitive with $k$-medians with $\ell_1$ norm and $\tilde O(k)$ competitive with $k$-means. This is an improvement over the previous guarantees of $O(k)$ and $O(k^2)$ by Dasgupta et al (2020). We also provide a new algorithm which is $O(\log^{\nicefrac{3}{2}} k)$ competitive for $k$-medians with $\ell_2$ norm. Our first algorithm is near-optimal: Dasgupta et al (2020) showed a lower bound of $\Omega(\log k)$ for $k$-medians; in this work, we prove a lower bound of $\tilde\Omega(k)$ for $k$-means. We also provide a lower bound of $\Omega(\log k)$ for $k$-medians with $\ell_2$ norm.

paragraphs: The paper studies clustering whose assignments can be explained by a threshold decision tree. Each internal node tests one feature and splits the data into two groups, while the full tree produces k clusters. The challenge is to retain this readable decision structure while keeping the k-medians or k-means clustering objective small.

The proposed algorithm improves competitive guarantees from O(k) to approximately logarithmic in k for k-medians with the l1 norm, and from O(k²) to approximately linear in k for k-means. These approximate descriptions suppress the factors hidden by the paper's tilde notation. A separate algorithm achieves an O((log k)^(3/2)) guarantee for k-medians with the l2 norm.

Lower bounds clarify how much further these guarantees can improve. Together with an existing logarithmic lower bound for l1 k-medians, the paper's new approximately linear lower bound for k-means makes the first algorithm near-optimal. It also proves a logarithmic lower bound for l2 k-medians. The results quantify the clustering-cost tradeoff imposed by requiring simple, feature-by-feature explanations.
summary.tldr: New decision-tree clustering algorithms improve approximation guarantees, with lower bounds establishing near-optimality for l1 k-medians and k-means.

title: Near-Optimal Algorithms for Explainable k-Medians and k-Means

abstract: Hyperbolic ordinal embedding (HOE) represents entities as points in hyperbolic space so that they agree as well as possible with given constraints in the form of entity $i$ is more similar to entity $j$ than to entity $k$. It has been experimentally shown that HOE can obtain representations of hierarchical data such as a knowledge base and a citation network effectively, owing to hyperbolic space’s exponential growth property. However, its theoretical analysis has been limited to ideal noiseless settings, and its generalization error in compensation for hyperbolic space’s exponential representation ability has not been guaranteed. The difficulty is that existing generalization error bound derivations for ordinal embedding based on the Gramian matrix are not applicable in HOE, since hyperbolic space is not inner-product space. In this paper, through our novel characterization of HOE with decomposed Lorentz Gramian matrices, we provide a generalization error bound of HOE for the first time, which is at most exponential with respect to the embedding space’s radius. Our comparison between the bounds of HOE and Euclidean ordinal embedding shows that HOE’s generalization error comes at a reasonable cost considering its exponential representation ability.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic ordinal embedding represents objects using relative similarity judgments: one object should be closer to a second than to a third. Hyperbolic space is attractive for hierarchical data because its available space grows exponentially. Previous experiments showed useful representations, but theoretical analysis had largely focused on ideal settings without noise.

The paper asks what generalization cost accompanies this expressive geometry. Standard arguments based on Gramian matrices do not transfer directly because hyperbolic space is not an inner-product space. The authors develop a characterization using decomposed Lorentz Gramian matrices, providing a mathematical route around that obstacle and enabling an error analysis.

Their result gives a generalization error bound whose dependence on the embedding radius is at most exponential. This describes a bound on error, rather than asserting that actual error necessarily grows exponentially. Comparing it with bounds for Euclidean ordinal embedding, the authors conclude that the generalization cost is reasonable relative to hyperbolic space’s exponential representational capacity. The contribution supplies theoretical support for a previously demonstrated empirical advantage.
summary.tldr: A Lorentz-matrix characterization yields a generalization bound for hyperbolic ordinal embedding with at most exponential dependence on embedding radius.

title: Generalization Error Bound for Hyperbolic Ordinal Embedding

abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.
originalAbstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

The smaller networks learn partly by matching the supernet's predictions, making knowledge distillation important to their performance. This paper identifies a potential problem with the commonly used KL divergence: students may learn predictions that misrepresent the teacher's uncertainty in either direction.

The proposed training approach uses the more general alpha-divergence and chooses it adaptively. The authors describe this adaptation as preventing both overestimation and underestimation of teacher uncertainty. This makes the way knowledge is transferred a central design choice, rather than treating the standard distillation objective as fixed.

The approach improves both slimmable networks and weight-sharing architecture search in the reported experiments. The resulting AlphaNet model family outperforms BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS across a range of computation budgets. One reported model reaches 80.0% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 444 million FLOPs. The results show that changing supernet training can improve the smaller architectures obtained from it.
summary.tldr: AlphaNet improves supernet training through adaptive alpha-divergence distillation that better preserves teacher uncertainty in smaller networks.

title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence

abstract: Maximizing a monotone k-submodular function subject to cardinality constraints is a general model for several applications ranging from influence maximization with multiple products to sensor placement with multiple sensor types and online ad allocation. Due to the large problem scale in many applications and the online nature of ad allocation, a need arises for algorithms that process elements in a streaming fashion and possibly make online decisions. In this work, we develop a new streaming algorithm for maximizing a monotone k-submodular function subject to a per-coordinate cardinality constraint attaining an approximation guarantee close to the state of the art guarantee in the offline setting. Though not typical for streaming algorithms, our streaming algorithm also readily applies to the online setting with free disposal. Our algorithm is combinatorial and enjoys fast running time and small number of function evaluations. Furthermore, its guarantee improves as the cardinality constraints get larger, which is especially suited for the large scale applications. For the special case of maximizing a submodular function with large budgets, our combinatorial algorithm matches the guarantee of the state-of-the-art continuous algorithm, which requires significantly more time and function evaluations.

Monotone k-submodular maximization models such choices with separate limits on each category. Large inputs and arriving decisions motivate algorithms that process a stream instead of requiring the entire input in advance.

This paper introduces a combinatorial streaming algorithm whose approximation guarantee approaches the best offline guarantee for per-coordinate cardinality constraints. It also applies to an online setting with free disposal, where previously retained choices can be discarded. The algorithm requires little computation and relatively few evaluations of the objective function.

Its guarantee improves as the category budgets become larger, making the result particularly relevant to large-scale applications. For the special case of ordinary submodular maximization with large budgets, it matches the guarantee of the leading continuous algorithm, which requires substantially more time and function evaluations. The contribution combines a strong approximation guarantee with a discrete procedure usable under streaming and qualified online access.
summary.tldr: A fast combinatorial streaming algorithm approaches offline approximation guarantees for monotone k-submodular maximization and improves as category budgets grow.

title: Streaming Algorithm for Monotone k-Submodular Maximization with Cardinality Constraints

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a robust non-parametric density estimator combining the popular Kernel Density Estimation method and the Median-of-Means principle (MoM-KDE). This estimator is shown to achieve robustness for a large class of anomalous data, potentially adversarial. In particular, while previous works only prove consistency results under very specific contamination models, this work provides finite-sample high-probability error-bounds without any prior knowledge on the outliers. To highlight the robustness of our method, we introduce an influence function adapted to the considered OUI framework. Finally, we show that MoM-KDE achieves competitive results when compared with other robust kernel estimators, while having significantly lower computational complexity.

This paper introduces MoM-KDE, a nonparametric estimator combining kernel density estimation with the median-of-means principle. Its purpose is to retain useful density estimates in the presence of a broad class of anomalies, including potentially adversarial data.

The theoretical contribution is a set of finite-sample error bounds that hold with high probability without requiring prior knowledge of the outliers. These guarantees concern errors at a finite amount of data, going beyond consistency results available only under very specific contamination models. The robustness claim remains tied to the class of anomalous data covered by the analysis.

The authors also develop an influence function adapted to their OUI framework to examine robustness. In comparisons with other robust kernel estimators, MoM-KDE achieves competitive results with significantly lower computational complexity. Taken together, the analysis and comparisons present a method that combines explicit error guarantees under contamination with a computational advantage over the evaluated alternatives.
summary.tldr: MoM-KDE combines kernel density estimation with median-of-means robustness, providing finite-sample guarantees and competitive results at lower computational complexity.

title: Robust Kernel Density Estimation with Median-of-Means principle

abstract: We introduce a compositional physics-aware FInite volume Neural Network (FINN) for learning spatiotemporal advection-diffusion processes. FINN implements a new way of combining the learning abilities of artificial neural networks with physical and structural knowledge from numerical simulation by modeling the constituents of partial differential equations (PDEs) in a compositional manner. Results on both one- and two-dimensional PDEs (Burgers’, diffusion-sorption, diffusion-reaction, Allen{–}Cahn) demonstrate FINN’s superior modeling accuracy and excellent out-of-distribution generalization ability beyond initial and boundary conditions. With only one tenth of the number of parameters on average, FINN outperforms pure machine learning and other state-of-the-art physics-aware models in all cases{—}often even by multiple orders of magnitude. Moreover, FINN outperforms a calibrated physical model when approximating sparse real-world data in a diffusion-sorption scenario, confirming its generalization abilities and showing explanatory potential by revealing the unknown retardation factor of the observed process.

paragraphs: FINN learns physical processes that evolve over space and time by combining neural networks with structure from numerical simulation. It targets advection-diffusion processes and represents the constituent parts of their partial differential equations compositionally. This lets learned components operate within a model organized around the physical process.

The authors evaluate FINN on several one- and two-dimensional equations, including Burgers’, diffusion-sorption, diffusion-reaction, and Allen–Cahn equations. They report better modeling accuracy and strong generalization outside the training distribution, including across initial and boundary conditions. FINN outperforms a calibrated physical model and reveals an unknown retardation factor associated with the observed process. This result suggests explanatory potential alongside predictive accuracy: the compositional structure can help recover a meaningful physical quantity while learning from limited observations.
summary.tldr: FINN combines learned equation components with physical simulation structure, achieving strong accuracy and generalization across the reported physical modeling tasks.

title: Composing Partial Differential Equations with Physics-Aware Neural Networks

abstract: The great success of machine learning with massive amounts of data comes at a price of huge computation costs and storage for training and tuning. Recent studies on dataset condensation attempt to reduce the dependence on such massive data by synthesizing a compact training dataset. However, the existing approaches have fundamental limitations in optimization due to the limited representability of synthetic datasets without considering any data regularity characteristics. To this end, we propose a novel condensation framework that generates multiple synthetic data with a limited storage budget via efficient parameterization considering data regularity. We further analyze the shortcomings of the existing gradient matching-based condensation methods and develop an effective optimization technique for improving the condensation of training data information. We propose a unified algorithm that drastically improves the quality of condensed data against the current state-of-the-art on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and Speech Commands.
