paragraphs: Dataset condensation aims to replace a large training collection with a compact synthetic dataset that retains useful training information. This paper addresses a limitation of existing approaches: under a small storage budget, the way synthetic examples are represented can restrict what they express and make their optimization difficult.

The authors introduce a parameterization that takes regularities in data into account and generates multiple synthetic examples within a limited storage budget. The central idea is to improve how that budget represents training information. They also analyze shortcomings of gradient matching methods for condensation and develop an optimization technique intended to transfer training information into the synthetic dataset more effectively.

These representation and optimization changes are combined into one algorithm. The authors report substantial improvements in condensed-data quality over the state of the art on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and Speech Commands. The results support treating the representation of synthetic data and its optimization as connected design choices, with both contributing to more effective condensation.
summary.tldr: A data-aware synthetic representation and improved optimization produce higher-quality condensed datasets within a limited storage budget.

title: Dataset Condensation via Efficient Synthetic-Data Parameterization

abstract: In recent years, a growing number of deep model-based reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been introduced. The interest in deep model-based RL is not surprising, given its many potential benefits, such as higher sample efficiency and the potential for fast adaption to changes in the environment. However, we demonstrate, using an improved version of the recently introduced Local Change Adaptation (LoCA) setup, that well-known model-based methods such as PlaNet and DreamerV2 perform poorly in their ability to adapt to local environmental changes. Combined with prior work that made a similar observation about the other popular model-based method, MuZero, a trend appears to emerge, suggesting that current deep model-based methods have serious limitations. We dive deeper into the causes of this poor performance, by identifying elements that hurt adaptive behavior and linking these to underlying techniques frequently used in deep model-based RL. We empirically validate these insights in the case of linear function approximation by demonstrating that a modified version of linear Dyna achieves effective adaptation to local changes. Furthermore, we provide detailed insights into the challenges of building an adaptive nonlinear model-based method, by experimenting with a nonlinear version of Dyna.

paragraphs: Learning a model of an environment could help an agent adapt quickly when that environment changes. This paper tests whether prominent deep model-based reinforcement-learning methods deliver that potential. Using an improved Local Change Adaptation setup, the authors find that PlaNet and DreamerV2 adapt poorly to localized environmental changes.

Together with earlier observations about MuZero, these findings suggest a broader concern about current methods. The authors investigate elements that hinder adaptation and connect them to techniques commonly used in deep model-based learning. The study therefore examines why having a learned world model may fail to translate into effective behavioral adjustment.

Experiments with nonlinear Dyna then explore the challenges of extending adaptive behavior to nonlinear models. The results distinguish the potential benefits of model-based learning from the adaptation abilities of particular implementations and identify concrete directions for investigating that gap.
summary.tldr: Local-change tests reveal adaptation weaknesses in prominent model-based RL methods and show effective adaptation with a modified linear Dyna method.

title: Towards Evaluating Adaptivity of Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Methods

abstract: We consider solving equality-constrained nonlinear, nonconvex optimization problems. This class of problems appears widely in a variety of applications in machine learning and engineering, ranging from constrained deep neural networks, to optimal control, to PDE-constrained optimization. We develop an adaptive inexact Newton method for this problem class. In each iteration, we solve the Lagrangian Newton system inexactly via a randomized iterative sketching solver, and select a suitable stepsize by performing line search on an exact augmented Lagrangian merit function. The randomized solvers have advantages over deterministic linear system solvers by significantly reducing per-iteration flops complexity and storage cost, when equipped with suitable sketching matrices. Our method adaptively controls the accuracy of the randomized solver and the penalty parameters of the exact augmented Lagrangian, to ensure that the inexact Newton direction is a descent direction of the exact augmented Lagrangian. This allows us to establish a global almost sure convergence. We also show that a unit stepsize is admissible locally, so that our method exhibits a local linear convergence. Furthermore, we prove that the linear convergence can be strengthened to superlinear convergence if we gradually sharpen the adaptive accuracy condition on the randomized solver. We demonstrate the superior performance of our method on benchmark nonlinear problems in CUTEst test set, constrained logistic regression with data from LIBSVM, and a PDE-constrained problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies nonlinear, nonconvex optimization with equality constraints, where solutions must improve an objective while satisfying prescribed equations. The proposed method uses Newton-style updates but avoids solving each associated linear system exactly. Instead, it uses randomized iterative sketching, which can reduce arithmetic and storage costs when suitable sketching matrices are chosen.

Approximate updates require care because an inaccurate direction may fail to improve the optimization criterion. The method adaptively adjusts both the randomized solver’s accuracy and the penalty parameters in an exact augmented Lagrangian. This coordination ensures a descent direction for that merit function, while a line search selects an appropriate step length.

The authors establish global almost sure convergence and local linear convergence, with full steps becoming admissible locally. Tightening the adaptive solver-accuracy condition progressively can strengthen the local rate to superlinear convergence. These convergence results should not be read as a promise of finding a global optimum in a nonconvex problem. Experiments report superior performance on benchmark nonlinear problems, constrained logistic regression, and a PDE-constrained problem.
summary.tldr: An adaptive Newton method combines randomized approximate solves with an exact augmented Lagrangian to reduce costs while retaining convergence guarantees.

title: Constrained Optimization via Exact Augmented Lagrangian and Randomized Iterative Sketching

abstract: Gradient clipping is a popular modification to standard (stochastic) gradient descent, at every iteration limiting the gradient norm to a certain value $c >0$. It is widely used for example for stabilizing the training of deep learning models (Goodfellow et al., 2016), or for enforcing differential privacy (Abadi et al., 2016). Despite popularity and simplicity of the clipping mechanism, its convergence guarantees often require specific values of $c$ and strong noise assumptions. In this paper, we give convergence guarantees that show precise dependence on arbitrary clipping thresholds $c$ and show that our guarantees are tight with both deterministic and stochastic gradients. In particular, we show that (i) for deterministic gradient descent, the clipping threshold only affects the higher-order terms of convergence, (ii) in the stochastic setting convergence to the true optimum cannot be guaranteed under the standard noise assumption, even under arbitrary small step-sizes. We give matching upper and lower bounds for convergence of the gradient norm when running clipped SGD, and illustrate these results with experiments.

paragraphs: Gradient clipping caps the size of a gradient before an optimization update. It is widely used to stabilize training and in differential privacy, yet its simplicity can hide important effects on convergence. This paper analyzes those effects while allowing arbitrary positive clipping thresholds, rather than requiring a particular threshold choice.

The authors establish tight guarantees for both deterministic and stochastic gradients. With deterministic gradient descent, the clipping threshold affects only higher-order convergence terms. In the stochastic setting, however, clipping can create a more fundamental obstacle: under the standard noise assumption, convergence to the true optimum cannot be guaranteed, even when the step size is arbitrarily small.

This distinction means that making updates smaller does not by itself resolve the stochastic issue identified by the analysis. The paper provides matching upper and lower bounds on convergence of the gradient norm for clipped stochastic gradient descent and illustrates the results experimentally. Matching bounds show that the guarantees capture the difficulty tightly in the analyzed setting, clarifying how clipping thresholds and stochastic bias shape optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: Tight clipping bounds show mild threshold effects for deterministic gradients but no general guarantee of reaching the true optimum with stochastic gradients.

title: Revisiting Gradient Clipping: Stochastic bias and tight convergence guarantees

abstract: This work studies the estimation of many statistical quantiles under differential privacy. More precisely, given a distribution and access to i.i.d. samples from it, we study the estimation of the inverse of its cumulative distribution function (the quantile function) at specific points. For instance, this task is of key importance in private data generation. We present two different approaches. The first one consists in privately estimating the empirical quantiles of the samples and using this result as an estimator of the quantiles of the distribution. In particular, we study the statistical properties of the recently published algorithm introduced by (Kaplan et al., 2022) that privately estimates the quantiles recursively. The second approach is to use techniques of density estimation in order to uniformly estimate the quantile function on an interval. In particular, we show that there is a tradeoff between the two methods. When we want to estimate many quantiles, it is better to estimate the density rather than estimating the quantile function at specific points.

paragraphs: Quantiles describe values below which specified fractions of a distribution fall. This paper studies estimating many such values under differential privacy, given independent, identically distributed samples. The target is the underlying distribution's quantile function, a task relevant to applications such as private data generation.

The first approach privately estimates quantiles of the observed sample and uses them to estimate population quantiles. The authors examine the statistical properties of an existing recursive private-quantile algorithm in this setting. This distinction between sample and population quantiles matters because the desired answer concerns the distribution that generated the data, beyond the particular sample collected.

The second approach uses density estimation to estimate the quantile function uniformly over an interval. The paper identifies a tradeoff between these strategies: when many quantiles are needed, estimating the density is preferable to estimating the quantile function separately at specified points. The finding makes the number of requested quantiles an important consideration when choosing a private statistical estimation method.
summary.tldr: For estimating many quantiles under differential privacy, the paper finds advantages in estimating a density rather than individual quantile values.

title: Private Statistical Estimation of Many Quantiles

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a variant of Bayesian online change point detection with a reducedrank Student-t process (TP) and dependent Student-t noise, as a nonparametric time series model. Our method builds and improves upon the state-of-the-art Gaussian process (GP) change point model benchmark of Saatci et al. (2010). The Student-t process generalizes the concept of a GP and hence yields a more flexible alternative. Additionally, unlike a GP, the predictive variance explicitly depends on the training observations, while the use of an entangled Student-t noise model preserves analytical tractability. Our approach also uses a Hilbert space reduced-rank representation of the TP kernel, derived from an eigenfunction expansion of the Laplace operator (Solin & Sarkka, 2020), to alleviate its computational complexity. Improvements in prediction and training time are demonstrated with real-world data-sets

paragraphs: Online change point detection tracks a time series as observations arrive and looks for changes in its behavior. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that uses a Student-t process as its underlying time series model. It builds on an existing Gaussian process approach while seeking greater modeling flexibility and lower computational cost.

The Student-t process generalizes the Gaussian process, with a notable difference in how it represents uncertainty: its predictive variance explicitly depends on the observed training values. The authors combine this process with a dependent Student-t noise model. This coupled construction preserves analytical tractability, allowing the more flexible model to retain manageable mathematical calculations.

To reduce computational demands, the method approximates its kernel using a reduced-rank Hilbert space representation derived from Laplace-operator eigenfunctions. This provides a smaller representation for the calculations required by the process model. Experiments on real-world datasets report improvements in prediction and training time, supporting the combination of a more flexible uncertainty model with a computationally economical approximation.
summary.tldr: A reduced-rank Student-t process improves prediction and training time for Bayesian online change point detection in reported experiments.

title: Bayesian online change point detection with Hilbert space approximate Student-t process

abstract: Warm-Start reinforcement learning (RL), aided by a prior policy obtained from offline training, is emerging as a promising RL approach for practical applications. Recent empirical studies have demonstrated that the performance of Warm-Start RL can be improved quickly in some cases but become stagnant in other cases, especially when the function approximation is used. To this end, the primary objective of this work is to build a fundamental understanding on ”whether and when online learning can be significantly accelerated by a warm-start policy from offline RL?”. Specifically, we consider the widely used Actor-Critic (A-C) method with a prior policy. We first quantify the approximation errors in the Actor update and the Critic update, respectively. Next, we cast the Warm-Start A-C algorithm as Newton’s method with perturbation, and study the impact of the approximation errors on the finite-time learning performance with inaccurate Actor/Critic updates. Under some general technical conditions, we derive the upper bounds, which shed light on achieving the desired finite-learning performance in the Warm-Start A-C algorithm. In particular, our findings reveal that it is essential to reduce the algorithm bias in online learning. We also obtain lower bounds on the sub-optimality gap of the Warm-Start A-C algorithm to quantify the impact of the bias and error propagation.

paragraphs: Starting online reinforcement learning from an offline-trained policy can speed improvement, but sometimes learning stalls. This paper investigates when a warm start helps actor-critic learning, particularly when function approximation makes the updates imperfect. The central question is how errors in the actor and critic affect the benefit of the initial policy.

The authors first quantify approximation errors in the two updates separately. They then interpret warm-start actor-critic as a perturbed version of Newton’s method, providing a mathematical framework for tracing how inaccurate updates affect performance over a finite learning period. Under general technical conditions, they derive upper bounds that clarify requirements for achieving desired learning performance.

The analysis identifies reducing algorithmic bias during online learning as essential in the studied framework. Lower bounds on the remaining suboptimality gap also quantify the effects of bias and error propagation. Together, these results explain why a promising initial policy alone may not ensure continued rapid improvement: the quality and accumulated effects of subsequent updates also matter.
summary.tldr: A perturbed-Newton analysis explains how actor-critic approximation errors and bias can limit the benefits of an offline warm start.

title: Warm-Start Actor-Critic: From Approximation Error to Sub-optimality Gap

abstract: Privacy attacks and poisoning attacks are two of the thorniest problems in federation learning (FL). Homomorphic encryption (HE), which allows certain mathematical operations to be done in the ciphertext state, provides a way to solve these two problems simultaneously. However, existing Paillier-based and CKKS-based privacy-preserving byzantine-robust FL (PBFL) solutions not only suffer from low efficiency but also expose the final model to the server. Additionally, these methods are limited to one robust aggregation algorithm (AGR) and are therefore vulnerable to AGR-tailored poisoning attacks. In this paper, we present AegisFL, an efficient PBLF system that provides the flexibility to change the AGR. We first observe that the core of the existing advanced AGRs is to calculate the inner products, $L_2$ norms and mean values for vectors. Based on this observation, we tailor a packing scheme for PBFL, which fits perfectly with RLWE-based fully homomorphic encryption. Under this packing scheme, the server only needs to perform one ciphertext multiplication to construct any required AGR, while the global model only belongs to honest clients. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on different datasets and adversary settings, which also confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our scheme.

Homomorphic encryption (HE), which allows certain mathematical operations to be done in the ciphertext state, provides a way to solve these two problems simultaneously. However, existing Paillier-based and CKKS-based privacy-preserving byzantine-robust FL (PBFL) solutions not only suffer from low efficiency but also expose the final model to the server. Additionally, these methods are limited to one robust aggregation algorithm (AGR) and are therefore vulnerable to AGR-tailored poisoning attacks. In this paper, we present AegisFL, an efficient PBLF system that provides the flexibility to change the AGR. We first observe that the core of the existing advanced AGRs is to calculate the inner products, $L_2$ norms and mean values for vectors. Based on this observation, we tailor a packing scheme for PBFL, which fits perfectly with RLWE-based fully homomorphic encryption. Under this packing scheme, the server only needs to perform one ciphertext multiplication to construct any required AGR, while the global model only belongs to honest clients. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on different datasets and adversary settings, which also confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our scheme.

paragraphs: Federated learning must contend with both information leakage and participants that deliberately submit harmful updates. Combining encrypted computation with robust aggregation can address these concerns together, but the paper identifies shortcomings in existing systems: expensive computation, exposure of the final model to the server, and dependence on a single aggregation rule.

AegisFL builds its design around operations shared by advanced robust aggregation algorithms: vector inner products, lengths measured with the L2 norm, and averages. It packs the relevant values into ciphertexts in a way tailored to RLWE-based fully homomorphic encryption. Under this packing scheme, constructing the required aggregation computation needs only one ciphertext multiplication.

The system also permits changing the robust aggregation rule, addressing the rigidity that can leave a fixed rule vulnerable to attacks designed specifically for it. The global model remains available only to honest clients. Experiments across datasets and adversary settings support the system’s effectiveness and efficiency, connecting its encryption design to practical federated learning behavior.
summary.tldr: AegisFL makes encrypted, robust federated learning more efficient while supporting changes to the aggregation rule and protecting the final model from the server.

title: AegisFL: Efficient and Flexible Privacy-Preserving Byzantine-Robust Cross-silo Federated Learning

abstract: We study a variant of Collaborative PAC Learning, in which we aim to learn an accurate classifier for each of the $n$ data distributions, while minimizing the number of samples drawn from them in total. Unlike in the usual collaborative learning setup, it is not assumed that there exists a single classifier that is simultaneously accurate for all distributions. We show that, when the data distributions satisfy a weaker realizability assumption, which appeared in (Crammer & Mansour, 2012) in the context of multi-task learning, sample-efficient learning is still feasible. We give a learning algorithm based on Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) on a natural augmentation of the hypothesis class, and the analysis relies on an upper bound on the VC dimension of this augmented class. In terms of the computational efficiency, we show that ERM on the augmented hypothesis class is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, which gives evidence against the existence of computationally efficient learners in general. On the positive side, for two special cases, we give learners that are both sample- and computationally-efficient.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning seeks accurate classifiers for several data distributions while minimizing the total number of samples collected. A common assumption is that one classifier can work well for every distribution. This paper relaxes that requirement, allowing the distributions to have different labeling functions while retaining a weaker realizability assumption.

Under that weaker assumption, the authors show that learning can still be sample-efficient. Their algorithm minimizes empirical prediction error over an augmented hypothesis class. They analyze the complexity of this expanded class through its VC dimension, using that bound to establish how much data the learning procedure requires.

The computational picture is less favorable in general: empirical risk minimization over the augmented class is NP-hard. This supplies evidence against broadly efficient computation, rather than proving that every possible learner must be inefficient. For two special cases, however, the authors provide learners that are efficient in both samples and computation. The paper thus separates the possibility of learning with limited data from the difficulty of carrying out that learning.
summary.tldr: Collaborative learning remains sample-efficient under a weaker shared-structure assumption, although general computation is difficult and efficient learners are given for two special cases.

title: Collaborative Learning with Different Labeling Functions

abstract: Pretrained vision language models (VLMs) present an opportunity to caption unlabeled 3D objects at scale. The leading approach to summarize VLM descriptions from different views of an object (Luo et al., 2023) relies on a language model (GPT4) to produce the final output. This text-based aggregation is susceptible to hallucinations as it merges potentially contradictory descriptions. We propose an alternative algorithm to marginalize over factors such as the viewpoint that affect the VLM’s response. Instead of merging text-only responses, we utilize the VLM’s joint image-text likelihoods. We show our probabilistic aggregation is not only more reliable and efficient, but sets the SoTA on inferring object types with respect to human-verified labels. The aggregated annotations are also useful for conditional inference; they improve downstream predictions (e.g., of object material) when the object’s type is specified as an auxiliary text-based input. Such auxiliary inputs allow ablating the contribution of visual reasoning over visionless reasoning in an unsupervised setting. With these supervised and unsupervised evaluations, we show how a VLM-based pipeline can be leveraged to produce reliable annotations for 764K objects from the Objaverse dataset.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may describe the same three-dimensional object differently from different viewpoints. Combining those descriptions using a language model can introduce hallucinations when the descriptions conflict. This paper proposes combining probabilistic evidence from the views to make large-scale object annotation more reliable.

The method uses the vision-language model's joint image-text likelihoods and aggregates over factors such as viewpoint. This provides an alternative to merging independently generated text descriptions. The authors report improved reliability and efficiency, together with leading object-type inference performance measured against human-verified labels. The aggregation therefore addresses both inconsistent descriptions and the accuracy of the final annotation.

The annotations also help conditional prediction: supplying an object's type as auxiliary text improves downstream predictions such as material identification. Such inputs additionally let the authors investigate the contribution of visual information compared with reasoning from text alone in an unsupervised setting. Across supervised and unsupervised evaluations, the paper demonstrates a pipeline producing reliable annotations for 764,000 Objaverse objects, connecting its aggregation method to annotation at substantial scale.
summary.tldr: Aggregating image-text likelihoods across viewpoints improves the reliability and efficiency of large-scale 3D object annotation.

title: Leveraging VLM-Based Pipelines to Annotate 3D Objects

abstract: Among the widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, LoRA and its variants have gained considerable popularity because of avoiding additional inference costs. However, there still often exists an accuracy gap between these methods and full fine-tuning (FT). In this work, we first introduce a novel weight decomposition analysis to investigate the inherent differences between FT and LoRA. Aiming to resemble the learning capacity of FT from the findings, we propose Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA). DoRA decomposes the pre-trained weight into two components, magnitude and direction, for fine-tuning, specifically employing LoRA for directional updates to efficiently minimize the number of trainable parameters. By employing DoRA, we enhance both the learning capacity and training stability of LoRA while avoiding any additional inference overhead. DoRA consistently outperforms LoRA on fine-tuning LLaMA, LLaVA, and VL-BART on various downstream tasks, such as commonsense reasoning, visual instruction tuning, and image/video-text understanding. The code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/DoRA.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, reduces the number of parameters trained when adapting a pretrained model and avoids additional inference costs. Its accuracy nevertheless often trails full fine-tuning. This paper examines that gap by analyzing how weight changes differ between LoRA and full fine-tuning through a decomposition of the weights.

The resulting method, DoRA, separates a pretrained weight into magnitude and direction components for adaptation. It applies LoRA specifically to directional updates, keeping the number of trainable parameters small. This design aims to bring the learning capacity of the efficient adaptation method closer to that of full fine-tuning.

The authors report improvements in LoRA’s learning capacity and training stability without extra inference overhead. DoRA consistently outperforms LoRA in their fine-tuning experiments with LLaMA, LLaVA, and VL-BART, covering commonsense reasoning, visual instruction tuning, and image/video-text understanding. These findings support weight decomposition as a useful design choice for efficient adaptation; the stated comparison establishes gains over LoRA without claiming that DoRA universally matches full fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: DoRA adapts weight magnitude and direction separately, improving on LoRA in reported experiments without additional inference overhead.

title: DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation

abstract: In this paper we introduce the SCoRe (Submodular Combinatorial Representation Learning) framework, a novel approach in representation learning that addresses inter-class bias and intra-class variance. SCoRe provides a new combinatorial viewpoint to representation learning, by introducing a family of loss functions based on set-based submodular information measures. We develop two novel combinatorial formulations for loss functions, using the Total Information and Total Correlation, that naturally minimize intra-class variance and inter-class bias. Several commonly used metric/contrastive learning loss functions like supervised contrastive loss, orthogonal projection loss, and N-pairs loss, are all instances of SCoRe, thereby underlining the versatility and applicability of SCoRe in a broad spectrum of learning scenarios. Novel objectives in SCoRe naturally model class-imbalance with up to 7.6% improvement in classification on CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-100-LT, MedMNIST, 2.1% on ImageNet-LT, and 19.4% in object detection on IDD and LVIS (v1.0), demonstrating its effectiveness over existing approaches.

paragraphs: Representation learning must organize examples so that their learned features support useful distinctions between classes. SCoRe addresses inter-class bias and variation within classes through a combinatorial view of the training objective. It introduces losses built from submodular information measures defined over sets.

The framework develops two formulations based on Total Information and Total Correlation. These are designed to reduce both intra-class variance and inter-class bias. Several established objectives, including supervised contrastive loss, orthogonal projection loss, and N-pairs loss, emerge as instances of SCoRe. This unifies familiar losses while providing a basis for constructing new ones.

The new objectives also naturally model class imbalance. Reported classification improvements reach 7.6% across CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-100-LT, and MedMNIST, with a 2.1% improvement on ImageNet-LT. The abstract additionally reports object-detection improvements reaching 19.4% on IDD and LVIS. These empirical results support the value of treating class structure and imbalance through set-based objectives, alongside the framework's contribution in connecting previously separate loss formulations.
summary.tldr: SCoRe unifies familiar representation-learning losses and introduces set-based objectives that address class variation, bias, and imbalance.

title: SCoRe: Submodular Combinatorial Representation Learning

abstract: Pre-trained contrastive vision-language models have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks. However, they often struggle on fine-trained datasets with categories not adequately represented during pre-training, which makes adaptation necessary. Recent works have shown promising results by utilizing samples from web-scale databases for retrieval-augmented adaptation, especially in low-data regimes. Despite the empirical success, understanding how retrieval impacts the adaptation of vision-language models remains an open research question. In this work, we adopt a reflective perspective by presenting a systematic study to understand the roles of key components in retrieval-augmented adaptation. We unveil new insights on uni-modal and cross-modal retrieval and highlight the critical role of logit ensemble for effective adaptation. We further present theoretical underpinnings that directly support our empirical observations.

paragraphs: Pretrained contrastive vision-language models can struggle when a task contains categories poorly represented during pretraining. Retrieving examples from large databases has shown promise for adapting these models, especially when task-specific data are scarce. This paper asks which parts of that retrieval-augmented process account for its effectiveness.

The authors conduct a systematic study of the components involved in adaptation. They examine both unimodal retrieval, which stays within one modality, and cross-modal retrieval, which connects different modalities. They also highlight the critical role of logit ensembling: combining prediction scores as part of the adaptation procedure.

The paper adds theoretical support for its empirical observations, connecting observed component behavior with an explanatory account. Its contribution is therefore an analysis of how retrieval and prediction combination work together in adaptation. The findings direct attention to the design of the full adaptation process, including how retrieved information ultimately affects prediction scores, when interpreting the success of retrieval-augmented vision-language models.
summary.tldr: A systematic study explains components of retrieval-augmented vision-language adaptation and highlights logit ensembling, with theory supporting the empirical observations.

title: Understanding Retrieval-Augmented Task Adaptation for Vision-Language Models

abstract: The dynamical formulation of the optimal transport can be extended through various choices of the underlying geometry (kinetic energy), and the regularization of density paths (potential energy). These combinations yield different variational problems (Lagrangians), encompassing many variations of the optimal transport problem such as the Schrödinger bridge, unbalanced optimal transport, and optimal transport with physical constraints, among others. In general, the optimal density path is unknown, and solving these variational problems can be computationally challenging. We propose a novel deep learning based framework approaching all of these problems from a unified perspective. Leveraging the dual formulation of the Lagrangians, our method does not require simulating or backpropagating through the trajectories of the learned dynamics, and does not need access to optimal couplings. We showcase the versatility of the proposed framework by outperforming previous approaches for the single-cell trajectory inference, where incorporating prior knowledge into the dynamics is crucial for correct predictions.

paragraphs: Optimal transport can describe how a probability distribution changes over time. Different choices about the cost of motion and the cost of intermediate distributions produce different versions of this problem. The paper brings these variations into one computational framework, including Schrödinger bridges, unbalanced transport, and transport subject to physical constraints.

The central difficulty is that the best path of distributions is unknown and can be expensive to compute. The authors develop a deep learning approach based on a dual formulation of the underlying optimization problems. Their method does not require simulating the learned trajectories or propagating training derivatives through them. It also avoids requiring optimal couplings, the correspondences that specify how probability mass should be transported.

The framework is demonstrated on single-cell trajectory inference, where prior knowledge about the dynamics matters for correct predictions. The authors report better performance than previous approaches in that application. The contribution combines a common treatment of several transport problems with a computational strategy that removes specific trajectory-related requirements.
summary.tldr: A unified deep learning framework solves several optimal transport problems without simulating learned trajectories or needing optimal couplings.

title: A Computational Framework for Solving Wasserstein Lagrangian Flows

abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance in language modeling tasks. However, the reasons behind their tremendous success are still unclear. In this paper, towards a better understanding, we train a Transformer model on a simple next token prediction task, where sequences are generated as a first-order autoregressive process $s_{t+1} = W s_t$. We show how a trained Transformer predicts the next token by first learning $W$ in-context, then applying a prediction mapping. We call the resulting procedure in-context autoregressive learning. More precisely, focusing on commuting orthogonal matrices $W$, we first show that a trained one-layer linear Transformer implements one step of gradient descent for the minimization of an inner objective function, when considering augmented tokens. When the tokens are not augmented, we characterize the global minima of a one-layer diagonal linear multi-head Transformer. Importantly, we exhibit orthogonality between heads and show that positional encoding captures trigonometric relations in the data. On the experimental side, we consider the general case of non-commuting orthogonal matrices and generalize our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: The paper investigates transformer prediction in a controlled setting where each sequence element is produced by applying a matrix to the previous one. The authors show how a trained transformer uses the observed sequence to learn that transformation in context, then applies a prediction mapping. This separates extracting the sequence's rule from using it to predict.

The theoretical analysis focuses on commuting orthogonal matrices. With augmented tokens, a trained one-layer linear transformer implements one gradient-descent step on an internal objective. This provides a precise connection between the transformer's computation and an optimization procedure carried out using its input context.

Without token augmentation, the authors characterize the global minima of a one-layer diagonal linear multi-head transformer. They identify orthogonality between heads and show that positional encoding captures trigonometric relationships in the data. Experiments extend the investigation to non-commuting orthogonal matrices and generalize the theoretical findings empirically. The result offers a concrete mechanism for in-context learning within these studied autoregressive settings.
summary.tldr: In a controlled autoregressive task, transformers learn a sequence's transformation in context before using it to predict the next element.

title: How do Transformers Perform In-Context Autoregressive Learning ?

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a tremendous surge in capabilities thanks to the use of foundation models trained on internet-scale data. On the flip side, the uncurated nature of internet-scale data also poses significant privacy and legal risks, as they often contain personal information or copyrighted material that should not be trained on without permission. In this work, we propose as a mitigation measure a recipe to train foundation vision models via self-supervised learning with differential privacy (DP) guarantee. We identify masked autoencoders as a suitable learning algorithm that aligns well with DP-SGD, and train ViP—a Vision transformer with differential Privacy—under a strict privacy budget of $\epsilon=8$ on the LAION400M dataset. We evaluate the quality of representation learned by ViP using standard downstream vision tasks; in particular, ViP achieves a (non-private) linear probing accuracy of 55.7% on ImageNet, comparable to that of end-to-end trained AlexNet (trained and evaluated on ImageNet). Our result suggests that scaling to internet-scale data can be practical for private learning. Code and DP pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/ViP-MAE.

paragraphs: Internet-scale training data can contain personal information, motivating methods that provide formal privacy protection during learning. This paper presents a recipe for training vision foundation models through self-supervised learning with differential privacy. Its goal is to investigate whether private training remains practical at the scale used for broad visual representation learning.

The authors identify masked autoencoders as a suitable learning approach for differentially private stochastic gradient descent. Using that combination, they train ViP, a vision transformer, on LAION400M with a privacy budget of ε = 8. The resulting model supplies representations that are evaluated through standard downstream vision tasks.

On ImageNet, ViP reaches 55.7% accuracy in a non-private linear-probing evaluation, comparable to the cited result for AlexNet trained end to end on ImageNet. The privacy guarantee applies to the foundation-model training described in the paper; the reported probe is explicitly non-private. The findings suggest that scaling up data can be practical for private representation learning, with useful downstream performance under the stated training budget.
summary.tldr: ViP demonstrates internet-scale, differentially private vision pretraining with useful downstream representations under a privacy budget of ε = 8.

title: ViP: A Differentially Private Foundation Model for Computer Vision

abstract: Attention is a fundamental component behind the remarkable achievements of large language models (LLMs). However, our current understanding of the attention mechanism, especially regarding how attention distributions are established, remains limited. Inspired by recent studies that explore the presence of attention sink in the initial token, which receives disproportionately large attention scores despite their lack of semantic importance, this work delves deeper into this phenomenon. We aim to provide a more profound understanding of the existence of attention sinks within LLMs and to uncover ways to enhance the achievable accuracy of LLMs by directly optimizing the attention distributions, without the need for weight finetuning. Specifically, this work begins with comprehensive visualizations of the attention distributions in LLMs during inference across various inputs and tasks. Based on these visualizations, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to discover that (1) attention sinks occur not only at the start of sequences but also within later tokens of the input, and (2) not all attention sinks have a positive impact on the achievable accuracy of LLMs. Building upon our findings, we propose a training-free Attention Calibration Technique (ACT) that automatically optimizes the attention distributions on the fly during inference in an input-adaptive manner. Extensive experiments validate that ACT consistently enhances the accuracy of various LLMs across different applications. Specifically, ACT achieves an average improvement of up to $7.30%$ in accuracy across different datasets when applied to Llama-30B.

paragraphs: Attention sinks are tokens that receive unusually large attention scores despite limited semantic importance. Previous work had highlighted this behavior at the beginning of sequences. Through visualizations across inputs and tasks, this paper finds that sinks also appear later in the input and that some can negatively affect model accuracy.

The authors use these observations to develop Attention Calibration Technique, or ACT. It adjusts attention distributions during inference in a way that adapts to the current input. Because the intervention acts directly on attention distributions, it does not require weight fine-tuning. This makes the observed attention behavior a target for improving an already-trained model.

Experiments report consistent accuracy improvements across the evaluated language models and applications. For Llama-30B, the authors report average accuracy improvement reaching 7.30% across datasets. The findings connect an expanded account of where attention sinks occur with a practical inference-time intervention, showing that recalibrating attention can improve measured performance without an additional model-training stage.
summary.tldr: ACT adapts attention distributions during inference to address harmful attention sinks and improve accuracy without fine-tuning.

title: Unveiling and Harnessing Hidden Attention Sinks: Enhancing Large Language Models without Training through Attention Calibration

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the capability to perform in-context learning (ICL) for completely unseen tasks in classification or language completion. Sequence to sequence (seq2seq) is another popular task category with several applications seeking quick adaptation with ICL. We present a systematic analysis of the ICL capability of LLMs on Seq2Seq tasks using a formal structured language-pair. Our study reveals a critical limitation: except for very short input sequences, ICL fails to achieve consistent learning across all output positions. This exposes a fundamental weakness of modern LLMs — their inability to effectively uncover the alignment between input and output sequences. Consequently, this limitation results in incomplete induction heads, which are essential for in-context learning of new discrete mappings. To address these limitations, we propose ICA-Tune, a method for focused fine-tuning of an LLM using in-context examples. We present a mechanistic evaluation with two accuracy probes to show how input-output alignment emerges in middle layers of an LLM without direct supervision. This alignment leads to an abrupt jump in the completeness of the induction heads in higher layers. We show that, compared to standard fine-tuning, ICA-Tune enables more sample efficient learning and better generalization to OOD instances.

Consequently, this limitation results in incomplete induction heads, which are essential for in-context learning of new discrete mappings. To address these limitations, we propose ICA-Tune, a method for focused fine-tuning of an LLM using in-context examples. We present a mechanistic evaluation with two accuracy probes to show how input-output alignment emerges in middle layers of an LLM without direct supervision. This alignment leads to an abrupt jump in the completeness of the induction heads in higher layers. We show that, compared to standard fine-tuning, ICA-Tune enables more sample efficient learning and better generalization to OOD instances.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model adapt to a task from examples in its input. This paper examines that ability for sequence-to-sequence tasks using a formal structured language pair. Except for very short inputs, the studied models fail to learn consistently across all output positions, revealing difficulty in aligning input elements with their corresponding outputs.

The authors connect this alignment problem to incomplete induction heads, mechanisms important for learning new discrete mappings from context. They propose ICA-Tune, a focused fine-tuning procedure that uses in-context examples. Two accuracy probes track the mechanism: alignment emerges in middle layers without direct supervision, followed by an abrupt increase in induction-head completeness in higher layers.

Compared with standard fine-tuning, ICA-Tune produces more sample-efficient learning and better generalization to out-of-distribution instances. The findings connect a specific failure of sequence learning with an internal change accompanying improvement. The formal language-pair setting is central to the evidence, allowing the authors to study alignment and mapping behavior systematically and to test whether targeted fine-tuning addresses the observed weakness.
summary.tldr: ICA-Tune improves studied sequence-to-sequence learning by encouraging input-output alignment and more complete induction heads.

title: The Missing Alignment Link of In-context Learning on Sequences

abstract: Despite significant advancements in post-hoc explainability techniques for neural networks, many current methods rely on heuristics and do not provide formally provable guarantees over the explanations provided. Recent work has shown that it is possible to obtain explanations with formal guarantees by identifying subsets of input features that are sufficient to determine that predictions remain unchanged using neural network verification techniques. Despite the appeal of these explanations, their computation faces significant scalability challenges. In this work, we address this gap by proposing a novel abstraction-refinement technique for efficiently computing provably sufficient explanations of neural network predictions. Our method abstracts the original large neural network by constructing a substantially reduced network, where a sufficient explanation of the reduced network is also provably sufficient for the original network, hence significantly speeding up the verification process. If the explanation is insufficient on the reduced network, we iteratively refine the network size by gradually increasing it until convergence. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach enhances the efficiency of obtaining provably sufficient explanations for neural network predictions while additionally providing a fine-grained interpretation of the network’s predictions across different abstraction levels.

paragraphs: A formally sufficient explanation identifies input features that guarantee a neural network’s prediction remains unchanged. Computing such explanations can require expensive neural network verification. This paper addresses that computational bottleneck with an abstraction-and-refinement method designed to make the verification problem smaller while retaining a guarantee about the original network.

The method constructs a substantially reduced network with a crucial property: an explanation proved sufficient for the reduced model is also sufficient for the original model. Verification can therefore succeed on a smaller object and still establish the desired claim. If the explanation is insufficient for that reduced network, the method gradually increases the network’s size and repeats the process until convergence.

Experiments show improved efficiency in obtaining provably sufficient explanations. The different abstraction levels also provide a finer-grained view of the network’s predictions. The main contribution is the connection between computational simplification and preserved sufficiency: reducing the network creates a faster verification route, and refinement provides a way to add detail when the initial abstraction does not establish the explanation.
summary.tldr: Reduced network abstractions speed up formally sufficient explanations, with refinement adding detail when the smaller network cannot verify them.

title: Explaining, Fast and Slow: Abstraction and Refinement of Provable Explanations

abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis claims that recent foundation models are converging to a shared representation space as a function of their downstream task performance, irrespective of the objectives and data modalities used to train these models (Huh et al., 2024). Representational similarity is generally measured for individual datasets and is not necessarily consistent across datasets. Thus, one may wonder whether this convergence of model representations is confounded by the datasets commonly used in machine learning. Here, we propose a systematic way to measure how representational similarity between models varies with the set of stimuli used to construct the representations. We find that the objective function is a crucial factor in determining the consistency of representational similarities across datasets. Specifically, self-supervised vision models learn representations whose relative pairwise similarities generalize better from one dataset to another compared to those of image classification or image-text models. Moreover, the correspondence between representational similarities and the models’ task behavior is dataset-dependent, being most strongly pronounced for single-domain datasets. Our work provides a framework for analyzing similarities of model representations across datasets and linking those similarities to differences in task behavior.

paragraphs: Claims that foundation models are approaching a shared representation space depend on how similarity between models is measured. Usually, that measurement uses representations of examples from a particular dataset. This paper asks whether the apparent relationships between models remain consistent when the examples used for comparison change.

The authors propose a systematic framework for measuring this variation across stimulus sets. They find that the training objective strongly influences consistency. In particular, self-supervised vision models show relative pairwise similarities that transfer better across datasets than those of image-classification or image-text models. The finding concerns stability of relationships between representations across datasets, rather than simply how similar two models look on one collection of examples.

The connection between representational similarity and task behavior also depends on the dataset, appearing most strongly for single-domain datasets. These results make the choice of evaluation stimuli part of the interpretation of representation comparisons. The framework helps assess whether an observed similarity pattern generalizes across datasets and how it relates to differences in model behavior.
summary.tldr: Training objectives influence how consistently model-representation similarities transfer across datasets, and their relationship to task behavior is also dataset-dependent.

title: Objective drives the consistency of representational similarity across datasets

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated outstanding performance in industrial anomaly detection. However, their iterative denoising nature results in slow inference speed, limiting their practicality for real-time industrial deployment. To address this challenge, we propose OmiAD, a one-step masked diffusion model for multi-class anomaly detection, derived from a well-designed multi-step Adaptive Masked Diffusion Model (AMDM) and compressed using Adversarial Score Distillation (ASD). OmiAD first introduces AMDM, equipped with an adaptive masking strategy that dynamically adjusts masking patterns based on noise levels and encourages the model to reconstruct anomalies as normal counterparts by leveraging broader context, to reduce the pixel-level shortcut reliance. Then, ASD is developed to compress the multi-step diffusion process into a single-step generator by score distillation and incorporating a shared-weight discriminator effectively reusing parameters while significantly improving both inference efficiency and detection performance. The effectiveness of OmiAD is validated on four diverse datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance across seven metrics while delivering a remarkable inference speedup.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can detect industrial anomalies effectively, but repeated denoising steps make inference slow. OmiAD targets this obstacle by turning a multi-step diffusion model into a single-step generator for multiclass anomaly detection. Its approach combines a reconstruction strategy designed for anomalies with a compression procedure designed to preserve useful detection behavior.

The starting model adjusts masking patterns according to noise levels. Masking encourages it to use broader context when reconstructing abnormal regions as normal counterparts, reducing reliance on pixel-level shortcuts. The authors then apply Adversarial Score Distillation to compress the denoising process. This combines score distillation with a discriminator that shares weights, reusing parameters while improving efficiency and detection performance.

Evaluation on four diverse datasets reports state-of-the-art results across seven metrics and a substantial inference speedup. The stated result is therefore more than reducing the number of generation steps: the compressed system also performs strongly at detecting anomalies. This supports the combination of context-sensitive reconstruction and adversarial distillation for the industrial deployment problem motivating the work.
summary.tldr: OmiAD distills an adaptively masked diffusion model into one-step anomaly detection, reporting faster inference and state-of-the-art detection results.

title: OmiAD: One-Step Adaptive Masked Diffusion Model for Multi-class Anomaly Detection via Adversarial Distillation

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) with low-rank adaptations (LoRAs) has become common practice, often yielding numerous copies of the same LLM differing only in their LoRA updates. This paradigm presents challenges for systems that serve real-time responses to queries that each involve a different LoRA. Prior works optimize the design of such systems but still require continuous loading and offloading of LoRAs, as it is infeasible to store thousands of LoRAs in GPU memory. To mitigate this issue, we investigate the efficacy of compression when serving LoRAs. We propose a method for the joint compression of LoRAs into a shared basis paired with LoRA-specific scaling matrices. We extend our algorithm to learn clusters of LoRAs that are amenable to joint compression, allowing it to scale gracefully to large LoRA collections. Our experiments with up to 1000 LoRAs demonstrate that compressed LoRAs preserve performance while offering major throughput gains in realistic serving scenarios with over a thousand LoRAs, maintaining 80% of the throughput of serving a single LoRA.

paragraphs: LoRA fine-tuning creates specialized versions of a language model through relatively small parameter updates. Serving a large collection still presents a memory problem: requests may require different updates, and thousands of adapters cannot all fit in GPU memory. Continually moving adapters into and out of memory therefore remains a bottleneck even in optimized serving systems.

This paper addresses the bottleneck by compressing adapters jointly. It represents them using a shared basis together with scaling matrices specific to each adapter. The method also learns clusters of adapters that can be compressed effectively together. Clustering allows the approach to handle large collections without requiring every adapter to share the same compression structure.

The authors report experiments with up to 1,000 adapters in which compression preserves performance. They also report substantial throughput improvements in realistic serving scenarios involving more than a thousand adapters, reaching 80% of single-adapter serving throughput. The result shows how exploiting shared structure across adaptations can reduce the serving overhead associated with supporting many specialized versions of one model.
summary.tldr: Jointly compressing LoRA adapters into shared bases reduces serving overhead while preserving performance in the reported experiments.

title: Compress then Serve: Serving Thousands of LoRA Adapters with Little Overhead

abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving distributed machine learning by sharing gradients instead of raw data. However, FL remains vulnerable to gradient inversion attacks, in which shared gradients can reveal sensitive training data. Prior research has mainly concentrated on unimodal tasks, particularly image classification, examining the reconstruction of single-modality data, and analyzing privacy vulnerabilities in these relatively simple scenarios. As multimodal models are increasingly used to address complex vision-language tasks, it becomes essential to assess the privacy risks inherent in these architectures. In this paper, we explore gradient inversion attacks targeting multimodal vision-language Document Visual Question Answering (DQA) models and propose GI-DQA, a novel method that reconstructs private document content from gradients. Through extensive evaluation on state-of-the-art DQA models, our approach exposes critical privacy vulnerabilities and highlights the urgent need for robust defenses to secure multimodal FL systems.

paragraphs: Federated learning shares training gradients instead of raw examples, but those gradients can still reveal information about the data. Gradient inversion attacks exploit this exposure to reconstruct private content. This paper asks how that risk extends to multimodal models, where earlier work had largely examined simpler, single-modality tasks such as image classification.

The authors focus on document visual question answering, a vision-language task involving document content. They introduce GI-DQA, a method that reconstructs private document information from gradients. By studying this setting, the work moves the privacy investigation beyond reconstructing a single type of input in a relatively simple prediction task.

Extensive evaluations on state-of-the-art document question-answering models reveal substantial privacy vulnerabilities. The findings show that exchanging gradients can expose sensitive document content even in these more complex multimodal systems. The paper's contribution is both an attack method and evidence that privacy assessments of federated learning need to cover vision-language architectures. It motivates stronger defenses for such systems without presenting gradient sharing itself as a sufficient privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: GI-DQA reconstructs private document content from multimodal model gradients, exposing privacy risks in federated document question answering.

title: Gradient Inversion of Multimodal Models

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has emerged as a powerful technology for bridging histology imaging with gene expression profiling. However, its application has been limited by low throughput and the need for specialized experimental facilities. Prior works sought to predict ST from whole-slide histology images to accelerate this process, but they suffer from two major limitations. First, they do not explicitly model cell-cell interaction as they factorize the joint distribution of whole-slide ST data and predict the gene expression of each spot independently. Second, their encoders struggle with memory constraints due to the large number of spots (often exceeding 10,000) in typical ST datasets. Herein, we propose STFlow, a flow matching generative model that considers cell-cell interaction by modeling the joint distribution of gene expression of an entire slide. It also employs an efficient slide-level encoder with local spatial attention, enabling whole-slide processing without excessive memory overhead. On the recently curated HEST-1k and STImage-1K4M benchmarks, STFlow substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves over 18% relative improvements over the pathology foundation models.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics connects tissue structure with gene expression, but collecting it requires specialized facilities and has limited throughput. Predicting it from histology images offers a way to accelerate the process. The paper identifies two obstacles in earlier approaches: predicting each spatial spot independently and handling slides with more than 10,000 spots without excessive memory use.

STFlow models the joint distribution of gene expression across an entire slide using flow matching. This allows the model to account for cell-cell interactions instead of factorizing predictions into independent spots. An efficient slide-level encoder uses local spatial attention to process the large collection of locations while controlling memory overhead.

On HEST-1k and STImage-1K4M, STFlow substantially outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches and reports more than 18% relative improvement over pathology foundation models. The results support treating whole-slide expression as a connected prediction problem. The architecture combines that modeling choice with an encoder designed to make whole-slide processing computationally feasible.
summary.tldr: STFlow generates whole-slide gene expression jointly from histology images while using local attention to manage memory costs.

title: Scalable Generation of Spatial Transcriptomics from Histology Images via Whole-Slide Flow Matching

abstract: We examine the problem of learning sequential tasks from a single visual demonstration. A key challenge arises when demonstrations are temporally misaligned due to variations in timing, differences in embodiment, or inconsistencies in execution. Existing approaches treat imitation as a distribution-matching problem, aligning individual frames between the agent and the demonstration. However, we show that such frame-level matching fails to enforce temporal ordering or ensure consistent progress. Our key insight is that matching should instead be defined at the level of sequences. We propose that perfect matching occurs when one sequence successfully covers all the subgoals in the same order as the other sequence. We present ORCA (ORdered Coverage Alignment), a dense per-timestep reward function that measures the probability of the agent covering demonstration frames in the correct order. On temporally misaligned demonstrations, we show that agents trained with the ORCA reward achieve $4.5$x improvement ($0.11 \rightarrow 0.50$ average normalized returns) for Meta-world tasks and $6.6$x improvement ($6.55 \rightarrow 43.3$ average returns) for Humanoid-v4 tasks compared to the best frame-level matching algorithms. We also provide empirical analysis showing that ORCA is robust to varying levels of temporal misalignment. The project website is at https://portal-cornell.github.io/orca/

paragraphs: Learning a sequential task from one video becomes difficult when the demonstrator and learner move at different speeds or have different bodies. Matching individual frames can identify visually similar states without ensuring that the learner completes the task’s stages in order. The paper shows that such matching also fails to ensure consistent progress.

ORCA moves the comparison from individual frames to whole sequences. Its definition of perfect matching requires one sequence to cover the other’s subgoals in the same order. It turns this idea into a dense reward at every timestep, measuring the probability that the agent covers demonstration frames in the correct sequence.

On temporally misaligned demonstrations, ORCA-trained agents achieve 4.5 times the average normalized return on Meta-world and 6.6 times the average return on Humanoid-v4 compared with the best frame-level matching algorithms. Additional empirical analysis shows robustness across different amounts of timing mismatch. These results support using ordered progress as the learning signal when successful imitation should preserve task structure despite differences in execution timing.
summary.tldr: ORCA learns from a single video by rewarding ordered coverage of demonstrated subgoals, improving imitation when execution timing differs.

title: Imitation Learning from a Single Temporally Misaligned Video

abstract: Recent explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods for time series primarily estimate point-wise attribution magnitudes, while overlooking the directional impact on predictions, leading to suboptimal identification of significant points. Our analysis shows that conventional Integrated Gradients (IG) effectively capture critical points with both positive and negative impacts on predictions. However, current evaluation metrics fail to assess this capability, as they inadvertently cancel out opposing feature contributions. To address this limitation, we propose novel evaluation metrics—Cumulative Prediction Difference (CPD) and Cumulative Prediction Preservation (CPP)—to systematically assess whether attribution methods accurately identify significant positive and negative points in time series XAI. Under these metrics, conventional IG outperforms recent counterparts. However, directly applying IG to time series data may lead to suboptimal outcomes, as generated paths ignore temporal relationships and introduce out-of-distribution samples. To overcome these challenges, we introduce TIMING, which enhances IG by incorporating temporal awareness while maintaining its theoretical properties. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world time series benchmarks demonstrate that TIMING outperforms existing time series XAI baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/drumpt/TIMING.

paragraphs: Explaining a time-series prediction requires identifying both which points matter and whether they push the prediction upward or downward. The paper finds that conventional Integrated Gradients can capture both directions, but existing evaluation metrics can hide this ability by allowing opposing contributions to cancel.

The authors introduce Cumulative Prediction Difference and Cumulative Prediction Preservation to assess identification of significant positive and negative points. Under these metrics, conventional Integrated Gradients outperforms recent alternatives. This changes the assessment of existing methods by making the evaluation sensitive to an aspect of attribution that magnitude-focused comparisons can overlook.

The paper then addresses a separate weakness of applying Integrated Gradients directly to time series. Its generated paths can ignore temporal relationships and create out-of-distribution samples. TIMING adds temporal awareness while retaining the method's theoretical properties. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show improvements over existing explanation baselines. Together, the evaluation metrics and algorithm address both how explanations are judged and how they are constructed.
summary.tldr: TIMING makes Integrated Gradients sensitive to temporal structure, while new evaluation metrics preserve the distinction between positive and negative contributions.

title: TIMING: Temporality-Aware Integrated Gradients for Time Series Explanation

abstract: Federated learning (FL) often struggles with generalization due to heterogeneous client data. Local models are prone to overfitting their local data distributions, and even transferable features can be distorted during aggregation. To address these challenges, we propose FedCONST, an approach that adaptively modulates update magnitudes based on the global model’s parameter strength. This prevents over-emphasizing well-learned parameters while reinforcing underdeveloped ones. Specifically, FedCONST employs linear convex constraints to ensure training stability and preserve locally learned generalization capabilities during aggregation. A Gradient Signal-to-Noise Ratio (GSNR) analysis further validates FedCONST’s effectiveness in enhancing feature transferability and robustness. As a result, FedCONST effectively aligns local and global objectives, mitigating overfitting and promoting stronger generalization across diverse FL environments, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from clients whose data may have very different distributions. Local training can become too specialized to a client, and combining updates can distort features that would otherwise transfer well. FedCONST addresses both problems by controlling how strongly different parts of the model are updated.

The method adapts update magnitudes according to the global model’s parameter strength. It reduces emphasis on parameters that are already well learned and reinforces those that remain underdeveloped. Linear convex constraints provide the mechanism for stabilizing training and preserving the generalization capabilities acquired locally when client contributions are aggregated.

The authors use Gradient Signal-to-Noise Ratio analysis to support the method’s effect on feature transferability and robustness. They also report state-of-the-art performance across diverse federated learning environments. Together, these findings connect the update rule to the central coordination problem: local learning should contribute useful features to the shared model without allowing differences between client distributions to drive excessive specialization or erase transferable information during aggregation.
summary.tldr: FedCONST constrains and scales client updates to preserve transferable features and improve generalization in federated learning.

title: Federated Learning for Feature Generalization with Convex Constraints

abstract: In this paper, we aim to establish a simple, effective, and theoretically grounded benchmark for rigorously probing abstract reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). To achieve this, we first develop a mathematic framework that defines abstract reasoning as the ability to: (i) extract essential patterns independent of surface representations, and (ii) apply consistent rules to these abstract patterns. Based on this framework, we introduce two novel complementary metrics: $\Gamma$ measures basic reasoning accuracy, while $\Delta$ quantifies a model’s reliance on specific symbols rather than underlying patterns - a key indicator of true abstraction versus mere memorization. To implement this measurement, we design a benchmark: systematic symbol remapping in rule-based tasks, which forces models to demonstrate genuine pattern recognition beyond superficial token matching. Extensive LLM evaluations using this benchmark (commercial API models, 7B-70B, multi-agent) reveal:1) critical limitations in non-decimal arithmetic and symbolic reasoning; 2) persistent abstraction gaps despite chain-of-thought prompting; and 3) $\Delta$’s effectiveness in robustly measuring memory dependence by quantifying performance degradation under symbol remapping, particularly highlighting operand-specific memorization. These findings underscore that current LLMs, despite domain-specific strengths, still lack robust abstract reasoning, highlighting key areas for future improvement.

paragraphs: A model can answer a familiar symbolic problem correctly while depending heavily on the particular symbols it has seen before. This paper builds an evaluation framework that separates extracting an underlying pattern from applying rules to that pattern. Both abilities are needed for the paper’s definition of abstract reasoning.

The benchmark systematically changes the symbols used in rule-based tasks while preserving the structure being tested. It introduces two complementary measurements: Gamma tracks basic reasoning accuracy, and Delta measures dependence on particular symbols. Comparing performance under remapping gives the authors a way to assess whether success survives changes in surface representation.

Evaluations span commercial models, models with 7B–70B parameters, and multi-agent settings. They reveal weaknesses in non-decimal arithmetic and symbolic reasoning, with abstraction gaps persisting under chain-of-thought prompting. Delta also exposes performance degradation associated with operand-specific memorization. The findings suggest that strong results in familiar domains can coexist with fragile abstraction, and that testing invariance under symbol changes provides information beyond ordinary accuracy.
summary.tldr: A symbol-remapping benchmark separates reasoning accuracy from dependence on familiar symbols, revealing persistent abstraction gaps in evaluated language models.

title: Benchmarking Abstract and Reasoning Abilities Through A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: One of the core pillars of efficient deep learning methods are architectural improvements, such as residual/skip connections, which have led to significantly better model convergence and quality. Since their introduction, residual connections have become ubiquitous not only in convolutional neural networks but also in transformer-based architectures, the backbone of LLMs. In this paper, we introduce the Learned Augmented Residual Layer (LAuReL) — a novel generalization of the canonical residual connection — designed to serve as an in-situ replacement while outperforming it in both model quality and footprint metrics. Our experiments show that LAuReL can enhance quality for both vision and language models while adding fewer parameters and incurring less latency and memory overhead than naively increasing parameter count. For example, on the ImageNet-1K task, LAuReL achieves the same model quality improvements as naively adding an extra layer while using $2.6 \times$ fewer parameters. Similarly, when pre-training 1B and 4B parameter LLMs, LAuReL improves performance on a variety of challenging downstream evaluation tasks by 2.54% to 20.05%, while adding only 0.012% and 0.1% additional parameters, respectively.
