paragraphs: Residual connections are central architectural components in both vision networks and transformer language models. The paper introduces the Learned Augmented Residual Layer, or LAuReL, as a generalization that can replace the conventional residual connection in place. Its aim is to improve model quality with a small increase in model footprint.

Experiments cover both vision and language tasks. The authors find that LAuReL can improve quality while requiring fewer additional parameters and less latency and memory overhead than simply increasing parameter count. On ImageNet-1K, it matches the quality improvement from adding another layer while using 2.6 times fewer parameters for that improvement.

In pretraining experiments with 1-billion- and 4-billion-parameter language models, LAuReL improves performance on various challenging downstream tasks by 2.54% to 20.05%. The respective parameter additions are only 0.012% and 0.1%. These results support modifying residual connections as an efficient architectural route to better performance, with the reported improvements tied to the tested models and evaluations.
summary.tldr: LAuReL replaces standard residual connections with a learned generalization that improves tested vision and language models with very small parameter overhead.

title: LAuReL: Learned Augmented Residual Layer

abstract: A maximal ancestral graph (MAG) is widely used to characterize the causal relations among observable variables in the presence of latent variables. However, given observational data, only a partial ancestral graph representing a Markov equivalence class (MEC) of MAGs is identifiable, which generally contains uncertain causal relations. Due to the uncertainties, MAG listing, i.e., listing all the MAGs in the MEC, is critical for many downstream tasks. In this paper, we present the first polynomial-delay MAG listing method, where delay refers to the time for outputting each MAG, through introducing enumerated structural knowledge in the form of singleton background knowledge (BK). To incorporate such knowledge, we propose the sound and locally complete orientation rules. By recursively introducing singleton BK and applying the rules, our method can output all and only MAGs in the MEC with polynomial delay. Additionally, while the proposed novel rules enable more efficient MAG listing, for the goal of incorporating general BK, we present two counterexamples to imply that existing rules including ours, are not yet complete, which motivate two more rules. Experimental results validate the efficiency of the proposed MAG listing method.

paragraphs: Maximal ancestral graphs represent causal relationships among observed variables when some variables are hidden. Observational data generally identifies an equivalence class of such graphs, represented by a partial ancestral graph, leaving some relationships uncertain. Listing the compatible graphs allows downstream analyses to work with these unresolved possibilities.

The paper introduces a listing method with polynomial delay: the time required to produce each successive graph is polynomial. It recursively introduces individual pieces of structural background knowledge and applies new orientation rules. These rules are sound and locally complete for the relevant knowledge, enabling the method to output every graph in the equivalence class and exclude graphs outside it.

The authors also examine the broader problem of incorporating general background knowledge. Two counterexamples show that existing rules, including their new ones, are not complete for that broader purpose, motivating two additional rules. Experiments validate the listing method’s efficiency. The computational guarantee applies to the delay between outputs, which matters when the set of compatible causal graphs itself may be large.
summary.tldr: New orientation rules enable exhaustive listing of compatible maximal ancestral graphs with polynomial delay between outputs.

title: Polynomial-Delay MAG Listing with Novel Locally Complete Orientation Rules

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for long-content generation (e.g., long Chain-of-Thought reasoning) where decoding efficiency becomes a critical bottleneck: Autoregressive decoding is inherently limited by its sequential token generation process, where each token must be generated before the next can be processed. This sequential dependency restricts the ability to fully leverage modern hardware’s parallel processing capabilities. Existing methods like speculative decoding and layer skipping offer potential speedups but have notable drawbacks: speculative decoding relies on an auxiliary “drafter” model, which can be challenging to acquire and increases memory overhead, while layer skipping may introduce discrepancies in the generated outputs due to the missing key-value cache at skipped layers. In this work, we propose AdaDecode, which accelerates LLM decoding without requiring auxiliary models or changes to the original model parameters, while ensuring output consistency. AdaDecode leverages the insight that many tokens—particularly simple or highly-predictable ones—can accurately be generated at intermediate layers, as further layers often do not significantly alter predictions once the model reaches a certain confidence. By adaptively generating tokens at intermediate layers when confidence is high, AdaDecode enables the next token’s computation to begin immediately. The remaining layer computations for early-predicted tokens are deferred and executed in parallel with subsequent tokens when needed, maximizing hardware utilization and reducing decoding latency. A final verification step ensures that early predictions match the results of standard autoregressive decoding, preserving output parity. Experiments across diverse generation tasks shows that AdaDecode consistently achieves superior decoding throughput compared to baselines with up to 1.73$\times$ speedup, while guaranteeing output parity with standard autoregressive decoding.

paragraphs: Generating long passages is slow partly because a language model normally finishes processing one token before starting the next. AdaDecode targets this dependency by using an observation about intermediate layers: for many simple or predictable tokens, later layers do not substantially change the predicted answer once confidence is sufficiently high.

When that happens, AdaDecode predicts the token early and immediately begins computing the next one. It defers the unfinished layer computations and runs them alongside subsequent token processing when needed. This preserves a role for the remaining layers while creating opportunities for parallel execution. The method requires neither an auxiliary drafting model nor changes to the original model parameters.

A final verification step checks early predictions against standard autoregressive decoding, preserving output parity. Across the reported generation tasks, AdaDecode improves throughput relative to the evaluated baselines, with speedups reaching 1.73 times. The result shows that overlapping layer computations can accelerate decoding while retaining the outputs of the original decoding procedure.
summary.tldr: AdaDecode overlaps unfinished layer computations across tokens to accelerate generation while verifying that outputs match standard decoding.

title: AdaDecode: Accelerating LLM Decoding with Adaptive Layer Parallelism

abstract: Distribution matching is a key technique in machine learning, with applications in generative models, domain adaptation, and algorithmic fairness. A related but less explored challenge is generating a distribution that aligns with multiple underlying distributions, often with conflicting objectives, known as a Pareto optimal distribution. In this paper, we develop a general theory based on information geometry to construct the Pareto set and front for the entire exponential family under KL and inverse KL divergences. This formulation allows explicit derivation of the Pareto set and front for multivariate normal distributions, enabling applications like multiobjective variational autoencoders (MOVAEs) to generate interpolated image distributions. Experimental results on real-world images demonstrate that both algorithms can generate high-quality interpolated images across multiple distributions.

This formulation allows explicit derivation of the Pareto set and front for multivariate normal distributions, enabling applications like multiobjective variational autoencoders (MOVAEs) to generate interpolated image distributions. paragraphs: Distribution matching usually asks a model to align with a target distribution. This paper considers several targets whose requirements may conflict. Its objective is to characterize Pareto-optimal distributions: tradeoffs for which improving alignment with one target would require sacrificing alignment with another. This turns matching into a problem with several objectives.

The authors develop an information-geometric theory for constructing the Pareto set and its corresponding objective-value front across the exponential family. The analysis covers both KL divergence and its reverse direction. Within that framework, they explicitly derive the set and front for multivariate normal distributions, making the general theory concrete for an important distribution family.

The resulting formulation supports applications such as multiobjective variational autoencoders, which generate image distributions interpolating among multiple targets. Experiments on real-world images show that both proposed algorithms produce high-quality interpolated images. The work connects a mathematical account of competing distribution objectives with generative modeling, providing a structured way to describe and explore compromises among several desired distributions.
summary.tldr: An information-geometric framework characterizes Pareto-optimal distribution matching and supports generating images that interpolate across multiple target distributions.

title: Multiobjective distribution matching

abstract: Recent advancements have integrated various deep-learning methodologies into physical design, aiming for workflows acceleration and surpasses human-devised solutions. However, prior research has primarily concentrated on developing task-specific networks, which necessitate a significant investment of time to construct large, specialized datasets, and the unintended isolation of models across different tasks. In this paper, we introduce DeepLayout, the first general representation learning framework specifically designed for backend circuit design. To address the distinct characteristics of post-placement circuits, including topological connectivity and geometric distribution, we propose a hybrid encoding architecture that integrates GNN with spatial transformers. Additionally, the framework includes a flexible decoder module that accommodates a variety of task types, supporting multiple hierarchical outputs such as nets and layouts. To mitigate the high annotation costs associated with layout data, we introduce a mask-based self-supervised learning approach designed explicitly for layout representation. This strategy involves a carefully devised masking approach tailored to layout features, precise reconstruction guidance, and most critically—two key supervised learning tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on large-scale industrial datasets, demonstrating that DeepLayout surpasses state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods specialized for individual tasks on two crucial layout quality assessment benchmarks. The experiment results underscore the framework’s robust capability to learn the intrinsic properties of circuits.

paragraphs: Learning systems for circuit design often target individual tasks, requiring specialized datasets and leaving representations isolated across applications. DeepLayout instead develops a general representation framework for backend circuit design. Its focus is on placed circuits, where understanding a layout requires both its connectivity structure and the physical arrangement of its components.

The encoder combines a graph neural network with spatial transformers to capture these two forms of information. A flexible decoder supports different tasks and output levels, including nets and complete layouts. This architecture gives the framework a way to reuse circuit representations while adapting its outputs to the particular assessment being performed.

To address annotation costs, the authors introduce layout-specific masked self-supervised learning with reconstruction guidance, alongside two supervised learning tasks. Experiments on large industrial datasets show performance above state-of-the-art task-specific methods on two layout quality assessment benchmarks. The results support the value of learning shared circuit properties, with the reported evidence centered on those assessment tasks rather than every stage of circuit design.
summary.tldr: DeepLayout combines circuit connectivity and geometry in a reusable representation framework that outperforms specialized methods on two layout assessment benchmarks.

title: DeepLayout: Learning Neural Representations of Circuit Placement Layout

abstract: Recent advances in hierarchical policy learning highlight the advantages of decomposing systems into high-level and low-level agents, enabling efficient long-horizon reasoning and precise fine-grained control. However, the interface between these hierarchy levels remains underexplored, and existing hierarchical methods often ignore domain symmetry, resulting in the need for extensive demonstrations to achieve robust performance. To address these issues, we propose Hierarchical Equivariant Policy (HEP), a novel hierarchical policy framework. We propose a frame transfer interface for hierarchical policy learning, which uses the high-level agent’s output as a coordinate frame for the low-level agent, providing a strong inductive bias while retaining flexibility. Additionally, we integrate domain symmetries into both levels and theoretically demonstrate the system’s overall equivariance. HEP achieves state-of-the-art performance in complex robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating significant improvements in both simulation and real-world settings.

paragraphs: Hierarchical robot policies divide work between a high-level agent that handles longer-horizon reasoning and a low-level agent that performs precise control. This paper focuses on the interface connecting those agents. It also addresses the tendency of existing hierarchical methods to overlook domain symmetries, which the abstract links to needing extensive demonstrations for robust behavior.

The proposed Hierarchical Equivariant Policy uses frame transfer: the high-level agent produces a coordinate frame that the low-level agent uses to interpret its control problem. That interface supplies a strong structural bias while preserving flexibility. The framework additionally incorporates domain symmetries at both levels, and the authors theoretically establish equivariance of the overall system.

Equivariance means that the policy's behavior transforms consistently with the symmetries incorporated into its design. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on complex manipulation tasks, with significant gains in simulation and real-world settings. The contribution connects a concrete communication mechanism between hierarchy levels with a system-wide symmetry property, and evaluates that combination in robotic control.
summary.tldr: HEP passes coordinate frames between policy levels and incorporates symmetry to improve hierarchical robotic manipulation.

title: Hierarchical Equivariant Policy via Frame Transfer

abstract: Large-scale physical systems defined on irregular grids pose significant scalability challenges for deep learning methods, especially in the presence of long-range interactions and multi-scale coupling. Traditional approaches that compute all pairwise interactions, such as attention, become computationally prohibitive as they scale quadratically with the number of nodes. We present Erwin, a hierarchical transformer inspired by methods from computational many-body physics, which combines the efficiency of tree-based algorithms with the expressivity of attention mechanisms. Erwin employs ball tree partitioning to organize computation, which enables linear-time attention by processing nodes in parallel within local neighborhoods of fixed size. Through progressive coarsening and refinement of the ball tree structure, complemented by a novel cross-ball interaction mechanism, it captures both fine-grained local details and global features. We demonstrate Erwin’s effectiveness across multiple domains, including cosmology, molecular dynamics, and particle fluid dynamics, where it consistently outperforms baseline methods both in accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Physical systems on irregular grids can contain both detailed local interactions and effects spanning large distances. Computing attention between every pair of nodes becomes expensive because the number of pairs grows quadratically. Erwin addresses this scaling problem with a hierarchical transformer inspired by tree-based methods from computational many-body physics.

The model organizes nodes using a ball tree and computes attention in parallel inside fixed-size local neighborhoods. This arrangement enables linear-time attention. To connect information across scales, Erwin progressively coarsens and refines the tree representation. A cross-ball interaction mechanism also exchanges information between neighborhoods, helping the model capture global features alongside fine local detail.

Experiments cover cosmology, molecular dynamics, and particle fluid dynamics. Across these evaluated domains, Erwin consistently exceeds the compared baselines in both accuracy and computational efficiency. The significance is that its efficiency mechanism also organizes how information moves through the system: local attention handles nearby structure, while the hierarchy and cross-ball exchanges support broader interactions. The reported results support this combination for large physical learning problems.
summary.tldr: Erwin combines local attention with a tree hierarchy to model large physical systems efficiently while capturing interactions across scales.

title: Erwin: A Tree-based Hierarchical Transformer for Large-scale Physical Systems

abstract: Our paper argues that the majority of theory of mind benchmarks are broken because of their inability to directly test how large language models (LLMs) adapt to new partners. This problem stems from the fact that theory of mind benchmarks for LLMs are overwhelmingly inspired by the methods used to test theory of mind in humans and fall victim to a fallacy of attributing human-like qualities to AI agents. We expect that humans will engage in a consistent reasoning process across various questions about a situation, but this is known to not be the case for current LLMs. Most theory of mind benchmarks only measure what we call *literal theory of mind*: the ability to predict the behavior of others. However, this type of metric is only informative when agents exhibit self-consistent reasoning. Thus, we introduce the concept of *functional theory of mind*: the ability to adapt to agents in-context following a rational response to their behavior. We find that many open source LLMs are capable of displaying strong literal theory of mind capabilities, but seem to struggle with functional theory of mind -- even with exceedingly simple partner policies. Simply put, strong literal theory of mind performance does not necessarily imply strong functional theory of mind performance or vice versa. Achieving functional theory of mind, particularly over long interaction horizons with a partner, is a significant challenge deserving a prominent role in any meaningful LLM theory of mind evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper argues that most language model theory-of-mind benchmarks fail to directly test adaptation to new interaction partners. Many borrow methods from human studies, where researchers expect reasonably consistent reasoning across questions about a situation. The authors argue that current language models do not reliably satisfy that expectation, weakening the interpretation of these tests.

They distinguish literal theory of mind, meaning prediction of another agent’s behavior, from functional theory of mind, meaning adaptation in context through rational responses to that behavior. The distinction shifts attention toward what a model does during interaction. Predicting a partner accurately and adjusting one’s own behavior appropriately are separate capabilities.

The authors find that many open source models show strong literal performance but appear to struggle with functional performance, even with very simple partner policies. They conclude that strength in either capability does not necessarily imply strength in the other. The paper calls for functional adaptation, particularly over long interactions, to play a central role in meaningful theory-of-mind evaluation.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that predicting others’ behavior does not establish an LLM’s ability to adapt to them during interaction.

title: Position: Theory of Mind Benchmarks are Broken for Large Language Models

abstract: Agentic language models operate in a fundamentally different safety regime than chat models: they must plan, call tools, and execute long-horizon actions where a single misstep, such as accessing files or entering credentials, can cause irreversible harm. Existing alignment methods, largely optimized for static generation and task completion, break down in these settings due to sequential decision-making, adversarial tool feedback, and overconfident intermediate reasoning. We introduce MOSAIC, a post-training framework that aligns agents for safe multi-step tool use by making safety decisions explicit and learnable. MOSAIC structures inference as a plan, check, then act or refuse loop, with explicit safety reasoning and refusal as first-class actions. To train without trajectory-level labels, we use preference-based reinforcement learning with pairwise trajectory comparisons, which captures safety distinctions often missed by scalar rewards. We evaluate MOSAIC zero-shot across three model families, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-4B-Thinking, Phi-4 and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking, and across out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning harmful tasks, prompt injection, benign tool use, and cross-domain privacy leakage. MOSAIC reduces harmful behavior by up to 50%, increases harmful-task refusal by over 20% on injection attacks, cuts privacy leakage, and preserves or improves benign task performance, demonstrating robust generalization across models, domains, and agentic settings.

paragraphs: Tool-using agents face safety decisions throughout an action sequence, including when tool feedback is adversarial. This paper introduces MOSAIC, a post-training framework that makes those decisions explicit. Its inference loop asks the agent to plan, check safety, and then either act or refuse, treating refusal as an action the model can learn.

Training uses preference-based reinforcement learning with comparisons between pairs of trajectories, avoiding the need for trajectory-level labels. The authors argue that these comparisons capture safety distinctions that scalar rewards can miss. Evaluation covers multiple model families and out-of-distribution benchmarks involving harmful requests, prompt injection, benign tool use, and privacy leakage across domains.

The reported results include reductions in harmful behavior of up to 50% and increases in harmful-task refusal of over 20% on injection attacks. MOSAIC also reduces privacy leakage while preserving or improving benign-task performance. These findings support the framework’s generalization across the evaluated models and settings, connecting explicit safety checks to safer multi-step execution.
summary.tldr: MOSAIC trains tool-using agents to plan, check safety, and act or refuse, reducing harmful behavior while maintaining useful task performance in evaluations.

title: Learning When to Act or Refuse: Guarding Agentic Reasoning Models for Safe Multi-Step Tool Use

abstract: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically take 2D images as visual input, which limits their spatial understanding in complex scenes. How can we incorporate 3D information to enhance VLA capabilities? We conduct a pilot study across different observation spaces and visual representations. The results show that explicitly lifting visual input into point clouds yields representations that better complement their corresponding 2D representations. To address the challenges of (1) scarce 3D data and (2) the domain gap induced by cross-environment differences and depth-scale biases, we propose Any3D-VLA. It unifies the simulator, sensor, and model-estimated point clouds within a training pipeline, constructs diverse inputs, and learns domain-agnostic 3D representations that are fused with the corresponding 2D representations. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate Any3D-VLA’s advantages in improving performance and mitigating the domain gap. Our project homepage is available at https://xianzhefan.github.io/Any3D-VLA.github.io.

paragraphs: Any3D-VLA investigates how three-dimensional visual information can improve models that translate images and language into robot actions. Images alone can make spatial relationships difficult to interpret in complex scenes. The authors first compare observation spaces and visual representations, finding that explicitly converting visual input into point clouds produces information that complements the corresponding two-dimensional representations.

The proposed training pipeline brings together point clouds from simulators, physical sensors, and model-based estimates. This diversity addresses two related problems: limited availability of 3D training data and differences between environments or depth scales. The model learns 3D representations intended to remain useful across those differences, then combines them with matching 2D representations.

Experiments in simulation and the real world report improved performance and a smaller domain gap. The contribution therefore concerns both adding spatial information and making that information usable across varied sources. The findings support training with diverse point clouds as a way to strengthen VLA robustness while retaining complementary information from ordinary images.
summary.tldr: Any3D-VLA combines images with diverse point clouds to improve robot performance and reduce differences across environments.

title: Any3D-VLA: Enhancing VLA Robustness via Diverse Point Clouds

abstract: Bottleneck states, which connect distinct regions of the state space, provide a principled and interpretable basis for constructing temporal abstractions in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL). However, existing bottleneck identification methods primarily rely on topological analysis of the state-transition graph, limiting their scalability to high-dimensional or continuous domains. To address this challenge, we introduce Value Power Strength (VPS), a value function-based metric inspired by the analogy between the Bellman equation and Kirchhoff’s current law, to quantify bottleneck property via the diffusion of reward in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). VPS is estimated efficiently using value functions learned from random reward signals and captures reward diffusion bottlenecks in both discrete and continuous state spaces. Leveraging VPS, we design options that guide agents toward or away from bottleneck regions. Experiments on tabular domains, continuous-control, and Atari 2600 games show that VPS identifies semantically meaningful bottlenecks, while the learned options improve exploration.
originalAbstract: Bottleneck states, which connect distinct regions of the state space, provide a principled and interpretable basis for constructing temporal abstractions in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL). However, existing bottleneck identification methods primarily rely on topological analysis of the state-transition graph, limiting their scalability to high-dimensional or continuous domains. To address this challenge, we introduce Value Power Strength (VPS), a value function-based metric inspired by the analogy between the Bellman equation and Kirchhoff’s current law, to quantify bottleneck property via the diffusion of reward in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). VPS is estimated efficiently using value functions learned from random reward signals and captures reward diffusion bottlenecks in both discrete and continuous state spaces. Leveraging VPS, we design options that guide agents toward or away from bottleneck regions. Experiments on tabular domains, continuous-control, and Atari 2600 games show that VPS identifies semantically meaningful bottlenecks, while the learned options improve exploration.

paragraphs: Bottleneck states connect otherwise distinct regions of an agent’s state space, making them useful landmarks for longer-duration behaviors. Existing methods often locate these states by analyzing the structure of a state-transition graph. That dependence makes them difficult to scale to high-dimensional or continuous environments, where an explicit graph is less convenient.

This paper introduces Value Power Strength, or VPS, which measures bottleneck properties through value functions. Its motivation comes from an analogy between the Bellman equation and Kirchhoff’s current law: the method examines how reward diffuses through a decision process. VPS can be estimated efficiently from value functions learned using random reward signals, and it applies to both discrete and continuous state spaces.

The authors use the resulting measurements to construct options that move agents toward or away from bottleneck regions. The approach connects interpretable temporal abstractions to value-function learning, offering an alternative to relying primarily on explicit transition-graph topology.

title: Learning Interpretable Options by Identifying Reward Diffusion Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: VideoQA models can be accurate yet often fail to align answers with the correct video segments (the grounding gap). We introduce LINGUA (Language-based INference for Grounded Video Understanding Agent), a memory-based agent that performs grounded VideoQA by reasoning in an explicit linguistic belief state. LINGUA uses five mechanisms: (1) event-driven perception (retains 8–12% of frames while preserving 94% of question-relevant events); (2) typed memory for episodic narratives, semantic affordances, and procedural scripts; (3) Belief-Action-Verification loops with postcondition and temporal checks; (4) meta reflection with contrastive refinement; and (5) Bayesian reliability tracking for continual learning without gradient updates. Built with Gemma3-4B (Ollama, 4-bit), LINGUA outperforms strong baselines on five VideoQA benchmarks, reaching 82.4% on NExT-QA and 42.3% Acc@GQA on NExT-GQA (answer + IoU$\geq$0.5 temporal localization), while running 2.6$\times$ faster than dense-frame methods. In continual learning over 100 videos, accuracy rises from 45.2% (first 10) to 61.8% (last 10) without catastrophic forgetting, indicating online adaptation via memory refinement.

title: LINGUA: Bridging the Grounding Gap in VideoQA via Typed Memory and Belief-State Reasoning

abstract: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are central to scientific modelling, but inferring their vector fields from noisy trajectories remains challenging. Current approaches such as symbolic regression, Gaussian process (GP) regression, and Neural ODEs often require complex training pipelines and substantial machine learning expertise, or they depend strongly on system-specific prior knowledge. We propose FIM-ODE, a pretrained Foundation Inference Model that amortises ODE inference by predicting the vector field directly from noisy trajectory data in a single forward pass. We pretrain FIM-ODE on a prior distribution over ODEs with low-degree polynomial vector fields and represent the target field with neural operators. FIM-ODE achieves strong zero-shot performance, matching and often improving upon ODEFormer, a recent pretrained symbolic baseline, across a range of regimes despite using a simpler training prior. Pretraining also provides a strong initialisation for finetuning, enabling fast and stable adaptation that outperforms modern neural and GP baselines without requiring machine learning expertise. Our pretrained model, code repository, and tutorials are available online.

paragraphs: An ordinary differential equation describes how a system changes through a vector field that assigns a direction and rate of motion to each state. Recovering that field from noisy trajectories is difficult. Existing approaches can require substantial training effort, specialist knowledge, or assumptions tailored to the particular system.

FIM-ODE moves much of this effort into pretraining. It learns from a distribution of equations with low-degree polynomial vector fields and represents target fields using neural operators. Once pretrained, it predicts a vector field from noisy observations in a single forward pass. This amortizes inference by reusing learned capabilities across new systems.

The model shows strong zero-shot performance, matching and often exceeding ODEFormer across the evaluated regimes despite a simpler training prior. Pretraining also supplies an initialization for fast, stable fine-tuning, which outperforms the evaluated neural and Gaussian Process baselines. The results support both immediate inference on new trajectory data and adaptation when further training is appropriate, with a workflow intended to reduce the machine learning expertise required.
summary.tldr: FIM-ODE infers differential-equation vector fields from noisy trajectories in one forward pass and provides a strong starting point for fine-tuning.

title: Foundation Inference Models for Ordinary Differential Equations

abstract: Recent analyses of multi-pathway Deep Linear Networks use Gradient Flow to predict a "winner-takes-all" specialization in which path symmetry breaks and each feature concentrates in a single pathway. In this work, we show that discrete Gradient Descent (GD) with a large step size tells a different story. We prove that single-path solutions are sharp minima, whereas distributing signals across pathways reduces sharpness by a factor that decreases with both the number of pathways and depth. Consequently, while early training reproduces the depth-driven symmetry breaking predicted by GF, oscillations at the Edge of Stability subsequently override this tendency and drive the network into a re-balancing phase, where signals redistribute across pathways. Together, these results clarify how depth shapes pathway competition and explain why large-step GD favors shared representations rather than persistent single-pathway dominance.

paragraphs: Multi-pathway deep linear networks provide a setting for studying how different computational routes divide learned features. Analyses based on gradient flow predict that symmetry breaks and a feature becomes concentrated in one pathway. This paper shows that discrete gradient descent with a large step size can produce a different long-term outcome.

The authors prove that solutions concentrating a signal in one pathway are sharp minima. Distributing the signal across pathways reduces sharpness, with a reduction factor that decreases as pathway count and depth increase. This establishes a connection between how the network distributes information and the local geometry of its training objective.

Early training still exhibits the depth-driven specialization predicted by gradient flow. Later, oscillations at the edge of stability override that tendency and trigger a rebalancing phase, redistributing signals among pathways. The result explains why large-step gradient descent favors shared representations in the studied deep linear networks. It also shows that the continuous-time view can miss a training phase driven by discrete optimization dynamics.
summary.tldr: Large-step gradient descent can reverse early pathway specialization in deep linear networks by driving signals toward less-sharp shared solutions.

title: Gradient Descent with Large Step Size Restores Symmetry in Deep Linear Networks with Multi-Pathway

abstract: We present a general framework for synthesizing search spaces of parametric functions, along with strategies for traversing these spaces to find optima. We formalize an algebraic theory for the categorical model of parametric functions in finite combinatory logic with predicates (FCLP). Based on a component-oriented synthesis framework for FCLP we automate composition from given components and search for parametric functions. Components are language-agnostic and may be instantiated as any implementation of parametric functions, e.g., as PyTorch modules. A proof-of-concept implementation demonstrates how to represent more specific concepts, such as neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization, within the framework.

paragraphs: Searching for a useful parametric function involves deciding both which functions are available and how to explore them. This paper presents a general framework for constructing those search spaces from components, together with strategies for traversing the resulting spaces to find optima. The space of candidates is itself part of what the framework synthesizes.

The theoretical foundation is an algebraic account of a categorical model of parametric functions, expressed in finite combinatory logic with predicates. A component-oriented synthesis framework then automates composition from the supplied pieces. This connects a formal description of allowable combinations with the practical task of searching over composed functions.

The components are language-agnostic and can be implemented as parametric functions in different programming environments, including PyTorch modules. A proof-of-concept implementation shows how neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization can be represented within the framework. The demonstrated contribution is a common formal and implementation structure for expressing these search problems, with automated composition linking reusable components to candidate solutions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a formal framework for composing parametric-function search spaces and representing architecture and hyperparameter search within them.

title: Search Space Synthesis for Parametric Functions

abstract: We propose Euler Mean Flows (EMF), a flow-based generative framework for one-step and few-step generation that enforces long-range trajectory consistency with minimal sampling cost. The key idea of EMF is to replace the trajectory consistency constraint, which is difficult to supervise and optimize over long time scales, with a principled linear surrogate that enables direct data supervision for long-horizon flow-map compositions. We derive this approximation from the semigroup formulation of flow-based models and show that, under mild regularity assumptions, it faithfully approximates the original consistency objective while being substantially easier to optimize. This formulation leads to a unified, JVP-free training framework that supports both $u$-prediction and $x_1$-prediction variants, avoiding explicit Jacobian computations and significantly reducing memory and computational overhead. Experiments on image synthesis, particle-based geometry generation, and functional generation demonstrate improved optimization stability and sample quality under fixed sampling budgets, together with approximately $50%$ reductions in training time and memory consumption compared to existing one-step methods for image generation.

paragraphs: Flow-based generation can reduce sampling cost by producing outputs in one or a few steps, but learning consistent transformations over long time intervals is difficult. Euler Mean Flows, or EMF, addresses this training problem by replacing a difficult trajectory-consistency constraint with a linear surrogate that allows direct supervision from data.

The surrogate is derived from the semigroup formulation of flows, which relates a transformation over a whole interval to compositions over shorter intervals. Under mild regularity assumptions, the authors show that the surrogate faithfully approximates the original consistency objective while being easier to optimize. The resulting framework supports both u-prediction and x1-prediction variants without explicit Jacobian computations or Jacobian-vector products.

Experiments cover image synthesis, particle-based geometry generation, and functional generation. They show improved optimization stability and sample quality at fixed sampling budgets. For image generation, the authors also report approximately 50% reductions in training time and memory compared with existing one-step methods. The contribution connects a conditionally justified approximation to practical reductions in the cost of training fast generators.
summary.tldr: Euler Mean Flows replaces difficult long-range consistency training with a tractable linear surrogate, improving fast generation while reducing training costs.

title: Trajectory Consistency for One-Step Generation on Euler Mean Flows

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffers from training collapse in long-horizon tasks due to exploding gradient variance. To mitigate this, a baseline is commonly introduced for advantage computation; however, traditional value models remain difficult to optimize, and standard group-based baselines overlook sequence heterogeneity. Although classic optimal baseline theory can achieve global variance reduction, it neglects token heterogeneity and requires prohibitive gradient-based computation. In this work, we derive the Optimal Token Baseline (OTB) from first principles, proving that gradient updates should be weighted inversely to their cumulative gradient norm. To ensure efficiency, we propose the Logit-Gradient Proxy that approximates the gradient norm using only forward-pass probabilities. Our method achieves training stability and matches the performance of large group sizes ($N=32$) with only $N=4$, reducing token consumption by over 65% across single-turn and tool-integrated reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning over long language-model responses can become unstable when gradient variance grows sharply. Baselines used to compute advantages can reduce this noise, but value models are difficult to optimize and standard group-based baselines overlook differences among sequences. Classical optimal-baseline theory also misses token-level differences and requires expensive gradient calculations.

The paper derives an Optimal Token Baseline from first principles, showing that gradient updates should receive weights inversely related to their cumulative gradient norm. To make this practical, it introduces a Logit-Gradient Proxy that estimates the needed norm using probabilities available from forward passes. This provides a cheaper way to apply the token-sensitive weighting derived by the theory.

Across single-turn reasoning and reasoning with tools, the method stabilizes training and matches performance obtained with groups of 32 using groups of only four. It also reduces token consumption by more than 65% in the reported evaluations. The findings connect better variance control with more efficient learning: smaller groups can suffice when baseline construction accounts for heterogeneity at the token level.
summary.tldr: The Optimal Token Baseline reduces reinforcement-learning variance, matching larger-group performance with fewer samples and substantially lower token consumption.

title: The Optimal Token Baseline: Variance Reduction for Long-Horizon LLM-RL

abstract: Common deep learning approaches for antibody engineering focus on modeling the marginal distribution of sequences. By treating sequences as independent samples, however, these methods overlook affinity maturation as a rich and largely untapped source of information about the evolutionary process by which antibodies explore the underlying fitness landscape. In contrast, classical phylogenetic models explicitly represent evolutionary dynamics but lack the expressivity to capture complex epistatic interactions. We bridge this gap with CoSiNE, a continuous-time Markov chain parameterized by a deep neural network. Mathematically, we prove that CoSiNE provides a first-order approximation to the intractable sequential point mutation process, capturing epistatic effects with an error bound that is quadratic in branch length. Empirically, CoSiNE outperforms state-of-the-art language models in zero-shot variant effect prediction by explicitly disentangling selection from context-dependent somatic hypermutation. Finally, we introduce Guided Gillespie, a classifier-guided sampling scheme that steers CoSiNE at inference time, enabling efficient optimization of antibody binding affinity toward specific antigens.

paragraphs: Antibody sequences contain information about the evolutionary process that produced them. Models that treat sequences as independent examples can miss this information, while classical evolutionary models have limited ability to represent interactions between mutations. CoSiNE combines explicit evolutionary dynamics with the flexibility of a neural network.

The method uses a continuous-time Markov chain whose behavior is parameterized by a deep network. The authors prove that it approximates sequential point mutation to first order, with an error bound that grows quadratically with evolutionary branch length. This gives a precise qualification to the approximation while allowing it to capture epistasis, where a mutation’s effect depends on other sequence positions.

Empirically, CoSiNE outperforms leading language models at zero-shot variant effect prediction by separating selection from context-dependent somatic hypermutation. The paper also introduces Guided Gillespie, which uses classifier guidance to steer sampling at inference time toward antibody binding affinity for particular antigens. Together, the contributions connect modeling how antibodies evolve with directing that modeled process toward an engineering objective.
summary.tldr: CoSiNE models antibody evolution with a neural continuous-time process and uses guided sampling to optimize binding affinity toward specific antigens.

title: Conditionally Site-Independent Neural Evolution of Antibody Sequences

abstract: In real-world scenarios, data collection for reinforcement learning (RL) is often constrained by safety concerns and high costs, resulting in limited data availability. Diffusion models (DMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in capturing complex distributions, making data augmentation a promising approach. However, existing DM-based data augmentation methods still suffer from the limited quality of synthesized data for downstream RL tasks. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method called episodic memory-guided controllable experience synthesizer (EMCES). EMCES incorporates an episodic memory-based controllable DM with informative yet concise conditions constructed by episodic memory (EM). To guide the synthesis toward high-quality data, we propose an EM-prioritized condition sampling strategy that leverages EM-based temporal-difference errors to focus generation on data most helpful for RL. Furthermore, we introduce a hashing-based state representation for EM to improve its efficiency and further boost the quality of synthetic data. To the best of our knowledge, EMCES is the first work to incorporate EM into controllable DMs and to leverage EM for guiding data synthesis in RL. Experimental results across multiple environments demonstrate that EMCES significantly improves the quality of the synthetic data, thereby improving the performance of several state-of-the-art RL algorithms. In particular, the hashing-based state representation can reduce storage cost by about 8000-fold and reduce time cost by 25.5-fold, without degrading the normalized score.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can be limited by expensive or safety-constrained data collection. Generating extra experience with diffusion models offers a way to expand the available data, but synthetic transitions must be useful for learning. EMCES addresses this quality problem by using episodic memory to control what the diffusion model generates.

The memory supplies concise, informative conditioning signals. A prioritized sampling strategy uses temporal-difference errors derived from that memory to focus generation on experience expected to help the reinforcement learner. This connects the choice of synthetic data to learning needs. The method also uses a hashing-based state representation to make the memory more efficient and further improve synthesis quality.

Across multiple environments, the authors report better synthetic data and improved performance for several state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms. The hashing-based representation reduces storage cost by about 8,000 times and time cost by 25.5 times without lowering the normalized score in the reported evaluation. These findings suggest that memory can guide useful experience generation while remaining practical enough to avoid overwhelming its computational benefits.
summary.tldr: EMCES uses episodic memory to guide diffusion-based experience generation, improving reinforcement learning while sharply reducing memory costs through hashing.

title: Episodic Memory-Guided Controllable Experience Synthesis for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) significantly enhances large language models (LLMs) reasoning but severely suffers from calibration degeneration, where models become excessively over-confident in incorrect answers. Previous studies devote to directly incorporating calibration objective into existing optimization target. However, our theoretical analysis demonstrates that there exists a fundamental gradient conflict between the optimization for maximizing policy accuracy and minimizing calibration error. Building on this insight, we propose DCPO, a simple yet effective framework that systematically decouples reasoning and calibration objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our DCPO not only preserves accuracy on par with GRPO but also achieves the best calibration performance and substantially mitigates the over-confidence issue. Our study provides valuable insights and practical solution for more reliable LLM deployment.

Previous studies devote to directly incorporating calibration objective into existing optimization target. However, our theoretical analysis demonstrates that there exists a fundamental gradient conflict between the optimization for maximizing policy accuracy and minimizing calibration error. Our study provides valuable insights and practical solution for more reliable LLM deployment.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards can improve a language model’s reasoning while making its confidence less trustworthy. The problem studied here is calibration degeneration: a model becomes excessively confident even when its answers are wrong. Better answer accuracy and better confidence estimates therefore need to be considered together.

Earlier approaches incorporate a calibration objective directly into the existing training objective. The authors provide theoretical analysis showing a fundamental gradient conflict between maximizing policy accuracy and minimizing calibration error. This means the two objectives can push learning in conflicting directions. Their proposed framework, DCPO, responds by systematically separating reasoning optimization from calibration optimization.

In the reported experiments, DCPO maintains accuracy comparable to GRPO while achieving the best calibration performance among the evaluated approaches and substantially reducing overconfidence. These findings support decoupling as a way to preserve reasoning gains while improving the reliability of confidence estimates. The contribution combines an explanation of the optimization conflict with a training framework designed around it, addressing a reliability problem that accuracy alone does not capture.
summary.tldr: DCPO separates reasoning and calibration objectives to reduce overconfidence while preserving accuracy comparable to GRPO.

title: Decoupling Reasoning and Confidence: Resurrecting Calibration in Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards

abstract: Macrocycles are ring-shaped molecules that offer a promising alternative to small-molecule drugs due to their enhanced selectivity and binding affinity against difficult targets. Despite their chemical value, they remain underexplored in generative modeling, likely owing to their scarcity in public datasets and the challenges of enforcing topological constraints in standard deep generative models. We introduce MacroGuide: Topological Guidance for Macrocycle Generation, a diffusion guidance mechanism that uses Persistent Homology to steer the sampling of pretrained molecular generative models toward the generation of macrocycles, in both unconditional and conditional (protein pocket) settings. At each denoising step, MacroGuide constructs a Vietoris-Rips complex from atomic positions and promotes ring formation by optimizing persistent homology features. Empirically, applying MacroGuide to pretrained diffusion models increases macrocycle generation rates from 1% to 99%, while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art performance on key quality metrics such as chemical validity, diversity, and PoseBusters checks. The implementation can be found at https://github.com/ala1705/MacroGuide.

paragraphs: Macrocycles are ring-shaped molecules with promising selectivity and binding affinity against difficult targets. Generating them is challenging because they are scarce in public datasets and their ring structure is difficult to enforce in standard generative models. MacroGuide addresses this structural requirement by guiding pretrained molecular diffusion models during sampling.

At each denoising step, the method constructs a Vietoris-Rips complex from atomic positions and optimizes persistent homology features to encourage rings. These mathematical objects provide a way to describe ring-like structure in the developing arrangement of atoms. The guidance works both for unconditional generation and for generation conditioned on a protein pocket.

In the reported experiments, adding MacroGuide increases macrocycle generation rates from 1% to 99%. It also matches or exceeds leading performance on chemical validity, diversity, and PoseBusters checks. This combination matters because increasing ring production alone would not establish molecule quality. The findings show that topological guidance can strongly redirect pretrained generators toward macrocycles while maintaining the assessed quality properties.
summary.tldr: MacroGuide steers pretrained molecular diffusion models toward macrocycles, raising reported generation rates from 1% to 99%.

title: MacroGuide: Topological Guidance for Macrocycle Generation

abstract: Recent studies have attempted to fine-tune time-series foundation models to enhance a target dataset’s forecasting performance. However, these approaches proceed without a clear criterion for identifying complex datasets that require fine-tuning due to performance degradation in zero-shot forecasting. To distinguish datasets that are more challenging than standard benchmarks, we introduce data-driven temporal complexity and multichannel complexity. Temporal complexity captures the difficulty of identifying distinct patterns by quantifying spectral entropy in the frequency domain, while multichannel complexity captures cross-channel information flow that can impact predictive uncertainty. These metrics serve as effective proxies for performance gains achievable through fine-tuning. Based on the two metrics, we develop Time-PEFT, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that incorporates a frequency adapter for top-$k$ filtering and a channel adapter for multichannel modeling. With the base variant of MOMENT as a backbone, Time-PEFT improves performance by up to 38% over LoRA on complex datasets.
originalAbstract: Recent studies have attempted to fine-tune time-series foundation models to enhance a target dataset’s forecasting performance. However, these approaches proceed without a clear criterion for identifying complex datasets that require fine-tuning due to performance degradation in zero-shot forecasting. To distinguish datasets that are more challenging than standard benchmarks, we introduce data-driven temporal complexity and multichannel complexity. Temporal complexity captures the difficulty of identifying distinct patterns by quantifying spectral entropy in the frequency domain, while multichannel complexity captures cross-channel information flow that can impact predictive uncertainty. These metrics serve as effective proxies for performance gains achievable through fine-tuning. Based on the two metrics, we develop Time-PEFT, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that incorporates a frequency adapter for top-$k$ filtering and a channel adapter for multichannel modeling. Multichannel complexity measures information flow between channels that can affect predictive uncertainty. abstract: Analytical diffusion models offer a mathematically transparent path to generative modeling by formulating the denoising score as an empirical-Bayes posterior mean. However, this interpretability comes at a prohibitive cost: the standard formulation necessitates a full-dataset scan at every timestep, scaling linearly with dataset size. In this work, we present the first systematic study addressing this scalability bottleneck. We challenge the prevailing assumption that the entire training data is necessary, uncovering the phenomenon of Posterior Progressive Concentration: the effective golden support of the denoising score is not static but shrinks asymptotically from the global manifold to a local neighborhood as the signal-to-noise ratio increases. Capitalizing on this, we propose Dynamic Time-Aware Golden Subset Diffusion (GoldDiff), a training-free framework that decouples inference complexity from dataset size. Instead of static retrieval, GoldDiff uses a coarse-to-fine mechanism to dynamically pinpoint the "Golden Subset" for inference. Theoretically, we derive rigorous bounds guaranteeing that our sparse approximation converges to the exact score. Empirically, GoldDiff achieves a 71$\times$ speedup on AFHQ while matching or achieving even better performance than full-scan baselines. Most notably, we demonstrate the first successful scaling of analytical diffusion to ImageNet-1K.

The standard approach is costly because every denoising step scans the entire dataset. This paper investigates whether all those examples remain necessary throughout generation.

The authors identify Posterior Progressive Concentration: as the signal-to-noise ratio increases, the examples that effectively support the score concentrate from the global data manifold into a local neighborhood. GoldDiff uses this changing support through a coarse-to-fine retrieval process. It dynamically selects a relevant subset instead of using a fixed retrieved set or repeatedly scanning all data.

summary.tldr: GoldDiff accelerates analytical diffusion by dynamically narrowing the data subset used for denoising as the relevant posterior support concentrates.

title: Fast and Scalable Analytical Diffusion

abstract: Model merging offers an efficient solution for integrating task-specific knowledge from multiple fine-tuned models. Most existing approaches focus on manipulating the difference vectors between fine-tuned and pretrained weights, often overlooking the generalization capabilities inherent in the pretrained parameters. In this work, we revisit the role of pretrained weights in model merging and investigate their efficacy from a subspace perspective. We find that the components of pretrained weights residing in the core subspace—defined by the dominant singular vectors—are essential for maintaining generalization across diverse tasks. Specifically, we present empirical evidence that pretrained weights are nearly first-order stationary and exhibit predominantly non-negative curvature within this core subspace with respect to multi-task loss landscapes, indicating near-optimality. These findings suggest that task-specific adaptations should be injected primarily into the orthogonal complement of the core subspace, thereby preserving the generalization properties of the pretrained model. Extensive experiments on vision and vision-language tasks show that this subspace-aware strategy consistently yields improvements over state-of-the-art training-free merging methods, including Task Arithmetic, LOT Merging, ISO, and TSV. The source code is available at https://github.com/SunWenJu123/model-merging.

paragraphs: Model merging combines knowledge from separately fine-tuned models without training a new model from scratch. Many methods manipulate the weight differences created by fine-tuning. This paper instead examines which parts of the original pretrained weights support generalization, asking whether preserving particular parameter directions can improve the merged result.

The authors define a core subspace using dominant singular vectors. They find that pretrained weight components in this subspace are essential to generalization across diverse tasks. Empirically, the multi-task loss has nearly zero first-order change and predominantly non-negative curvature there, indicating near-optimality within that subspace. This evidence motivates placing task-specific changes mainly in its orthogonal complement.

The resulting strategy preserves the core pretrained components while incorporating adaptations in complementary directions. Experiments on vision and vision-language tasks consistently improve on training-free merging methods including Task Arithmetic, LOT Merging, ISO, and TSV. The findings support a subspace-aware merging strategy; the near-optimality evidence concerns the identified core subspace rather than a claim of global optimality.
summary.tldr: Preserving a core subspace of pretrained weights while merging adaptations into complementary directions improves training-free model merging.

title: Revisiting the Role of Pretrained Weights in Model Merging: On Near-Optimality within the Core Subspace

abstract: Reliable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems depend fundamentally on the retriever’s ability to find relevant information. We show that neural retrievers used in RAG systems have blind spots, which we define as the failure to retrieve entities that are relevant to the query, but have low similarity to the query embedding. We investigate the training-induced biases that cause such blind-spot entities to be mapped to inaccessible parts of the embedding space, resulting in low retrievability. Using a large-scale dataset constructed from Wikidata relations and first paragraphs of Wikipedia, and our proposed Retrieval Probability Score (RPS), we show that blind spot risk in standard retrievers (e.g., Contriever, ReasonIR) can be predicted pre-index from entity embedding geometry, avoiding expensive retrieval evaluations. To address these blind spots, we introduce ARGUS, a pipeline that enables the retrievability of high-risk (low-RPS) entities through targeted document augmentation from a knowledge base (KB), first paragraphs of Wikipedia, in our case. Extensive experiments on BRIGHT, ImpliRet, and RAR-b show that ARGUS achieves consistent improvements across all evaluated retrievers (averaging +3.4 nDCG@5 and +4.5 nDCG@10 absolute points), with substantially larger gains in challenging subsets. These results establish that preemptively remedying blind spots is critical for building robust and trustworthy RAG systems (Code and data: github.com/ZeinabTaghavi/With_Argus_Eyes)

paragraphs: A retrieval system can miss an entity that is relevant to a question because its embedding has low similarity to the query embedding. This paper calls such failures blind spots and investigates how training biases place relevant entities in poorly retrievable regions of the embedding space. These omissions can deprive retrieval-augmented generation of needed information.

The authors introduce a Retrieval Probability Score that predicts blind-spot risk from entity embedding geometry before indexing. Using data built from Wikidata relations and Wikipedia introductions, they show that this assessment can avoid expensive retrieval evaluations. Their ARGUS pipeline then targets low-scoring entities with document augmentation drawn from a knowledge base.

Experiments on BRIGHT, ImpliRet, and RAR-b show consistent improvements across all evaluated retrievers. Average gains are 3.4 absolute nDCG@5 points and 4.5 nDCG@10 points, with larger gains on challenging subsets. The results support diagnosing and addressing likely retrieval failures before they appear in downstream answers, using targeted augmentation to improve access to information already relevant to the query.
summary.tldr: ARGUS predicts retrieval blind spots from embedding geometry and improves retrieval through targeted augmentation of high-risk entities.

title: With Argus Eyes: Assessing Retrieval Gaps via Uncertainty Scoring to Detect and Remedy Retrieval Blind Spots

abstract: DiLoCo is a powerful framework for training large language models (LLMs), enabling larger optimal batch sizes and increased accelerator utilization under networking constraints. However, DiLoCo’s performance has been shown to degrade as the number of workers (K) increases (Charles et al., 2025). In this work, we posit that a related but often overlooked factor in DiLoCo’s behavior is the choice of inner optimizer, which shapes the pseudogradient used by the outer optimizer. Given the recent success of Muon relative to AdamW for data parallel (DP) training, we examine how Muon’s normalized optimizer steps can affect the pseudogradient’s quality. We find that, relative to AdamW, Muon yields more directionally correct pseudogradients as the number of workers ($K$) increases. In our experiments pre-training language models, we conduct extensive hyperparameter tuning across 150M, 416M, 914M, 1.76B, and 3.1B models for DiLoCo, MuLoCo, AdamW DP, and Muon DP. Consistently across all scales, we find that with $K\geq1$ workers, MuLoCo (Muon inner optimizer DiLoCo) achieves superior performance to DiLoCo in absolute terms and for $K>2$ it outperforms DiLoCo relative to their data parallel baselines, while being compatible with quantization, streaming, and long synchronization intervals. At $K=1$, we find that MuLoCo can even outperform the data-parallel gold standard while having larger critical batch sizes and faster training times as a result.

paragraphs: DiLoCo supports language-model training under networking constraints, but its performance can deteriorate as the number of workers increases. This paper investigates the inner optimizer as a contributor to that behavior. Inner optimization shapes the pseudogradient supplied to the outer optimizer, so its influence extends beyond each worker's local training progress.

The proposed variant, MuLoCo, uses Muon as DiLoCo's inner optimizer. The authors find that Muon's normalized steps produce pseudogradients with more accurate directions than AdamW as worker counts rise. They extensively tune and compare both distributed approaches and their data-parallel counterparts across language models ranging from 150 million to 3.1 billion parameters.

Across the tested scales, MuLoCo outperforms DiLoCo in absolute performance for one or more workers. Above two workers, it also performs better relative to the respective data-parallel baselines. It remains compatible with quantization, streaming, and long synchronization intervals. At one worker, it can even exceed the data-parallel reference while supporting larger critical batch sizes and faster training, highlighting the practical importance of the inner optimizer.
summary.tldr: Replacing DiLoCo's inner optimizer with Muon improves pseudogradient directions and training performance across the tested model scales.

title: MuLoCo: Muon is a Practical Inner Optimizer for DiLoCo

abstract: Reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs) enable test-time scaling, with dataset-level accuracy improving as the token budget increases, motivating adaptive reasoning—spending tokens when they improve reliability and stopping early when additional computation is unlikely to help. However, setting the token budget, as well as the threshold for adaptive reasoning, is a practical challenge that entails a fundamental risk-accuracy trade-off. We re-frame the budget setting problem as risk control, limiting the error rate while minimizing compute. Our framework introduces an upper threshold that stops reasoning when the model is confident (risking incorrect output) and a novel parametric lower threshold that preemptively stops unsolvable instances (risking premature stoppage). Given a target risk and a validation set, we use distribution-free risk control to optimally specify these stopping mechanisms. Empirical results across diverse reasoning tasks and models demonstrate the effectiveness of our risk control approach, demonstrating computational efficiency gains from the lower threshold and ensemble stopping mechanisms, all while adhering to the user-specified risk target.

paragraphs: Giving a reasoning language model more tokens can improve accuracy across a dataset, but deciding how much computation to spend on each instance is difficult. Conformal Thinking treats this decision as a risk-control problem: reduce computation while keeping error within a user-specified target. This connects stopping decisions to an explicit reliability objective.

The framework uses two stopping mechanisms. An upper threshold ends reasoning when confidence is sufficiently high, accepting the possibility of an incorrect answer. A parametric lower threshold stops instances judged unlikely to be solved, accepting the possibility of ending too soon. Given a validation set and a target risk, distribution-free risk control selects these mechanisms to balance their risks against computation.

Experiments across several reasoning tasks and models show efficiency gains from the lower threshold and ensemble stopping mechanisms while adhering to the specified risk target. The lower threshold contributes a distinct source of savings: it can curtail unproductive reasoning as well as ending successful reasoning early. The reported control concerns the chosen risk objective, rather than a promise that every individual stopping decision is correct.
summary.tldr: Conformal Thinking calibrates when to stop confident or apparently unproductive reasoning to reduce computation while meeting a chosen risk target.

title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget

abstract: In interactive task learning (ITL), AI agents learn new capabilities from limited human instruction provided during task execution. STAND is a new method of data-efficient rule precondition induction specifically designed for these human-in-the-loop training scenarios. A key feature of STAND is its self-awareness of its own learning—it can provide accurate metrics of training progress back to users. STAND beats popular methods like XGBoost, decision trees, random forests, and version spaces at small-data precondition induction tasks, and is highly accurate at estimating when its performance improves on holdout examples. In our evaluations, we find that STAND shows more monotonic improvement than other models with low rates of error reoccurrence. These features of STAND support a consistent training experience, enabling human instructors to estimate when they have finished training and providing active-learning support by identifying trouble spots that require more training. STAND achieves this by efficiently learning a compact space of greedy classifiers consistent with training data, rather than a finite ensemble of alternatives.

paragraphs: In interactive task learning, people teach an agent while it performs a task, often with only a small number of examples. The agent must learn the conditions under which its rules apply. STAND addresses this precondition-learning problem while also estimating its own training progress so instructors can judge where further teaching is useful.

The method efficiently represents a compact space of greedy classifiers consistent with the training data. This gives it a different way to maintain possible rules than keeping a finite ensemble of alternatives. Its self-awareness refers to measurable feedback about learning progress, including whether performance is improving on held-out examples.

In small-data evaluations, STAND outperforms XGBoost, decision trees, random forests, and version spaces. Its performance improves more monotonically than the compared models, with relatively few previously corrected errors returning. These properties support a steadier teaching experience: instructors can better estimate when training is sufficient, while identified trouble spots can guide additional examples. The findings connect predictive performance with the practical experience of teaching an agent.
summary.tldr: STAND learns rule preconditions from limited instruction and estimates its learning progress to help people teach agents more consistently.

title: STAND: Self-Aware Precondition Induction for Interactive Task Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for post-training large reasoning models (LRMs) using policy-gradient methods such as GRPO. To stabilize training, these methods typically center trajectory rewards by subtracting the empirical mean for each prompt. Statistically, this centering acts as a control variate (or baseline), reducing the variance of the policy-gradient estimator. Typically, the mean reward is estimated using per-prompt empirical averages for each prompt in a batch. Drawing inspiration from Stein’s paradox, we propose using shrinkage estimators that combine per-prompt and cross-prompt means to improve the overall per-prompt mean estimation accuracy, particularly in the low-generation regime typical of RLVR. Theoretically, we construct a shrinkage-based baseline that provably yields lower-variance policy-gradient estimators across algorithms. This baseline serves as a drop-in replacement for existing per-prompt mean baselines, requiring no additional hyperparameters or computation. Empirically, shrinkage baselines consistently outperform standard empirical-mean baselines, leading to lower-variance gradient updates and improved training stability.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains reasoning models using outcomes that can be checked. Policy-gradient methods commonly subtract a prompt’s average reward to reduce variation in gradient estimates. When only a few responses are generated per prompt, that empirical average can itself be an imprecise estimate.

The paper draws on shrinkage estimation to combine each prompt’s reward mean with information from means across prompts. This sharing improves overall estimation of prompt-level means, particularly when generation counts are low. The authors construct a shrinkage baseline and prove that it yields lower-variance policy-gradient estimators across algorithms.

The proposed baseline can replace existing prompt-level empirical means without additional hyperparameters or computation. Empirical results consistently favor shrinkage baselines, showing lower-variance gradient updates and improved training stability. The significance is that a statistical change to reward centering can improve the learning signal without requiring a new reward source or a more elaborate training procedure. The contribution targets the baseline already used to stabilize policy-gradient learning.
summary.tldr: Shrinkage reward baselines combine within-prompt and cross-prompt information to reduce policy-gradient variance and improve training stability.

title: Shrinking the Variance: Shrinkage Baselines for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

abstract: Realistic simulation is critical for applications ranging from robotics to animation. Video generation models have emerged as a way to capture real-world physics from data, but they often face challenges in maintaining spatial consistency and object permanence, relying on memory mechanisms to compensate. As a complementary direction, we present 3DGSim, a learned 3D simulator that directly learns physical interactions from multi-view RGB videos. 3DGSim adopts MVSplat to learn a latent particle-based representation of 3D scenes, a Point Transformer for the particle dynamics, a Temporal Merging module for consistent temporal aggregation, and Gaussian Splatting to produce novel view renderings. By jointly training inverse rendering and dynamics forecasting, 3DGSim embeds physical properties into point-wise latent features. This enables the model to capture diverse behaviors, from rigid and elastic to cloth-like dynamics and boundary conditions (e.g., fixed cloth corners), while producing realistic lighting effects. We show that 3DGSim can generate physically plausible results even in out of distribution cases, e.g. ground removal or multi-object interactions, despite being trained only on single-body collisions.
