paragraphs: Learning physical behavior from video requires tracking how objects persist and move through space. Video generation models can struggle with spatial consistency and object permanence. 3DGSim explores a complementary approach: it learns a three-dimensional simulator directly from multi-view RGB videos, giving the dynamics an explicit 3D scene representation.

The system uses MVSplat to construct latent scene particles and a Point Transformer to predict their dynamics. A Temporal Merging module aggregates information consistently over time, while Gaussian Splatting renders the scene from new viewpoints. Joint training of inverse rendering and future dynamics embeds physical properties into the latent features associated with individual points.

The authors report rigid, elastic, and cloth-like behavior, including boundary conditions such as fixed cloth corners, alongside realistic lighting effects. Although trained only on single-body collisions, the model produces physically plausible results in tested unfamiliar settings such as ground removal and multi-object interactions. These examples indicate transfer beyond the training interaction type while keeping the claim at the level of reported physical plausibility.
summary.tldr: 3DGSim learns particle-based 3D dynamics from multi-view videos and produces physically plausible simulations, including reported cases beyond its single-body-collision training.

title: Learning 3D-Gaussian Simulators from RGB Videos

abstract: Recent work uses human cognitive benchmarks to evaluate how LLMs represent concepts, claiming to assess "human-like" understanding. This position paper argues that this approach is misguided: these benchmarks come from narrow, typically Western populations yet are treated as universal standards, despite cross-cultural research showing culture shapes how people think, not just what they think about. LLMs trained on global multilingual data should not be expected to mirror thinking patterns from limited groups. Moreover, LLM outputs can shift with minor changes in prompting, unlike the stable human mental structures these benchmarks were designed to measure. These problems show up as contradictory findings across studies, making benchmark results poor evidence for claims about how LLMs represent concepts. We call for evaluation approaches designed for what LLMs actually are—systems trained on diverse global data—rather than tests measuring how closely they match a single population’s way of thinking.

paragraphs: The paper questions using human cognitive benchmarks to claim that language models represent concepts in human-like ways. These benchmarks often originate in narrow, typically Western populations, yet are interpreted as universal standards. The authors draw on cross-cultural research showing that culture influences patterns of thinking themselves, which complicates treating one population’s responses as a general reference for understanding.

This matters because language models learn from global, multilingual data. The paper argues that they should not be expected to reproduce the cognitive patterns of a limited population. It also highlights a measurement mismatch: small prompt changes can shift model outputs, whereas the benchmarks were intended to assess comparatively stable human mental structures.

The authors connect these problems to contradictory findings across studies and argue that the resulting scores provide weak evidence about model concept representations. They call for evaluations grounded in the nature of language models and the diversity of their training data. The proposed change concerns what counts as evidence of understanding and whose thinking supplies the reference.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that culturally narrow human benchmarks provide poor evidence about how globally trained language models represent concepts.

abstract: The label ranking problem consists of learning a model that maps instances to total orders over a finite set of predefined labels. This paper introduces new methods for label ranking that complement and improve upon existing approaches. More specifically, we propose extensions of two methods that have been used extensively for classification and regression so far, namely instance-based learning and decision tree induction. The unifying element of the two methods is a procedure for locally estimating predictive probability models for label rankings.
originalAbstract: The label ranking problem consists of learning a model that maps instances to total orders over a finite set of predefined labels. This paper introduces new methods for label ranking that complement and improve upon existing approaches. More specifically, we propose extensions of two methods that have been used extensively for classification and regression so far, namely instance-based learning and decision tree induction. The unifying element of the two methods is a procedure for locally estimating predictive probability models for label rankings.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a model to order a fixed collection of labels for each input. The prediction is a complete ranking rather than one selected category or one numerical value. Learning therefore has to account for how labels relate to one another within the order assigned to an instance.

The paper adapts two familiar learning approaches to this output type: instance-based learning and decision tree induction. Both have been widely used for classification and regression. Extending them to rankings broadens the available methods for a problem in which the output contains several coordinated ordering decisions.

The shared ingredient is a procedure that locally estimates predictive probability models over label rankings. This supplies a common probabilistic basis for the two otherwise different approaches. Local estimation connects the ranking prediction to the relevant part of the input data, while the probability model represents possible orders. The authors present the resulting methods as complementing and improving existing approaches, with the main contribution being this adaptation of established learners through a unified ranking-model estimation procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper extends decision trees and instance-based learning to label ranking using local probability models over complete label orders.

title: Decision tree and instance-based learning for label ranking

abstract: Standard inductive learning requires that training and test instances come from the same distribution. Transfer learning seeks to remove this restriction. In shallow transfer, test instances are from the same domain, but have a different distribution. In deep transfer, test instances are from a different domain entirely (i.e., described by different predicates). Humans routinely perform deep transfer, but few learning systems, if any, are capable of it. In this paper we propose an approach based on a form of second-order Markov logic. Our algorithm discovers structural regularities in the source domain in the form of Markov logic formulas with predicate variables, and instantiates these formulas with predicates from the target domain. Using this approach, we have successfully transferred learned knowledge between molecular biology, social network and Web domains. The discovered patterns include broadly useful properties of predicates, like symmetry and transitivity, and relations among predicates, like various forms of homophily.

In deep transfer, test instances are from a different domain entirely (i.e., described by different predicates). Our algorithm discovers structural regularities in the source domain in the form of Markov logic formulas with predicate variables, and instantiates these formulas with predicates from the target domain. paragraphs: Transfer learning seeks to reuse knowledge when training and test settings differ. This paper studies a particularly substantial change: the target domain is described using different predicates, or kinds of relations, from the source domain. The authors call this deep transfer, distinguishing it from a distribution change within the same domain.

Their approach uses a form of second-order Markov logic to discover structural regularities. Learned formulas contain variables standing for predicates, allowing a pattern to be expressed without permanently tying it to the source domain's vocabulary. The algorithm then instantiates these formulas using predicates from the target domain.

The authors report successful knowledge transfer between molecular biology, social network, and Web domains. Discovered patterns include symmetry, transitivity, and forms of homophily, which concern how relations behave or interact. These findings illustrate why relational structure can be useful across domains with different descriptions. The transferable knowledge is expressed as a reusable pattern among predicates, enabling the target domain to supply its own concrete relations.
summary.tldr: Second-order Markov logic transfers relational patterns across domains by replacing source predicates with target predicates in learned formulas.

title: Deep transfer via second-order Markov logic

abstract: The analysis of the formation and evolution of networks over time is of fundamental importance to social science, biology, and many other fields. While longitudinal network data sets are increasingly being recorded at the granularity of individual time-stamped events, most studies only focus on collapsed cross-sectional snapshots of the network. In this paper, we introduce a dynamic egocentric framework that models continuous-time network data using multivariate counting processes. For inference, an efficient partial likelihood approach is used, allowing our methods to scale to large networks. We apply our techniques to various citation networks and demonstrate the predictive power and interpretability of the learned statistical models.

While longitudinal network data sets are increasingly being recorded at the granularity of individual time-stamped events, most studies only focus on collapsed cross-sectional snapshots of the network. In this paper, we introduce a dynamic egocentric framework that models continuous-time network data using multivariate counting processes. For inference, an efficient partial likelihood approach is used, allowing our methods to scale to large networks. paragraphs: Networks evolve through events, but many analyses summarize their history using snapshots. The paper focuses on data recorded at the finer level of individual time-stamped events. Its motivation is that a model of network formation and change can work directly with that temporal information, rather than first collapsing it into cross-sectional views.

The authors introduce a dynamic egocentric framework for continuous-time network data. The framework uses multivariate counting processes to model events over time. For inference, it employs an efficient partial-likelihood approach, which allows the methods to scale to large networks. Temporal modeling and computational scalability are therefore addressed together within the proposed framework.

Applications to several citation networks demonstrate both predictive power and interpretability of the learned statistical models. These findings matter because the objective is more than describing a final arrangement of links: the models address how a network develops over time. The reported results support the usefulness of modeling time-stamped network events while retaining statistical descriptions that can be interpreted.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time egocentric framework models network events at scale and yields predictive, interpretable models of citation networks.

title: Dynamic Egocentric Models for Citation Networks

abstract: Recent work on probabilistic latent feature models have shown great promise in predicting unseen links in social network and relational data. We present a max-margin nonparametric latent feature model, which unites the ideas of max-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics to discover discriminative latent features for link prediction and automatically infer the unknown latent social dimension. By minimizing a hinge-loss using the linear expectation operator, we can perform posterior inference efficiently without dealing with a highly nonlinear link likelihood function; by using a fully-Bayesian formulation, we can avoid tuning regularization constants. Experimental results on real datasets appear to demonstrate the benefits inherited from max-margin learning and fully-Bayesian nonparametric inference.

We present a max-margin nonparametric latent feature model, which unites the ideas of max-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics to discover discriminative latent features for link prediction and automatically infer the unknown latent social dimension. By minimizing a hinge-loss using the linear expectation operator, we can perform posterior inference efficiently without dealing with a highly nonlinear link likelihood function; by using a fully-Bayesian formulation, we can avoid tuning regularization constants. Experimental results on real datasets appear to demonstrate the benefits inherited from max-margin learning and fully-Bayesian nonparametric inference.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction of unseen links in social networks and relational data. It combines maximum-margin learning with Bayesian nonparametrics to discover latent features that discriminate between link outcomes. The formulation also infers the unknown latent social dimension automatically, making the size of the hidden representation part of learning.

The method minimizes hinge loss using a linear expectation operator. This enables efficient posterior inference without requiring a highly nonlinear link likelihood function. A fully Bayesian formulation also avoids tuning regularization constants. Together, these choices connect a prediction-oriented margin objective with Bayesian inference over the latent representation and its complexity.

Experiments on real datasets appear to show benefits from both maximum-margin learning and fully Bayesian nonparametric inference. The abstract presents this evidence cautiously, so it supports a promising combination rather than an unconditional superiority claim. The central contribution is a link-prediction model that learns discriminative hidden features, adapts their dimension, and offers an inference route built around the margin-based objective.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric maximum-margin model learns discriminative latent features and their dimension for link prediction.

title: Max-Margin Nonparametric Latent Feature Models for Link Prediction
